title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning for Practitioners
text:
Preface
This is the practitioner edition of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning. It is for people who build, review and audit machine-learning systems that handle personal data, and who need to know what each result says, when it applies, how to use it and what goes wrong in practice, without working through its proof.
It covers the same topics as the full edition, in the same parts and chapters. Each topic is explained in four steps: the idea and why it works, the result or rule, a worked example with real numbers, and the pitfalls that catch people in practice. Each chapter ends with a cheat sheet and a link to the full edition’s chapter, where every result is derived step by step.

title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning for Practitioners
text:
How this book is organized

Prerequisites collects the mathematics the later parts use: distributions, tail bounds, ways to compare distributions, hypothesis testing, and the basics of information theory, optimization, stability and cryptography.
Threat models and attacks shows how models and data leak: membership inference, attribute and property inference, memorization and extraction, gradient inversion, re-identification, and reconstruction from aggregate statistics.
Differential privacy foundations defines the guarantee those attacks call for, builds its mechanisms, composes them, and says what privacy costs.
Privacy accounting tracks the guarantee through the many steps of private training, and ends with how to choose an accountant and what to report.
Differential privacy in machine learning trains models with the guarantee: where the noise goes, how the knobs of noisy, clipped gradient descent trade privacy for accuracy, what else spends the budget, who pays for the noise, which ε to choose, and how to audit the result.

The numbers in the text are computed by the scripts in the repository’s code/ directory, the same ones the full edition uses, and tests check that the scripts still produce them.

title: Prerequisites
text:
The common thread
This part collects the mathematics the rest of the book stands on. It has no privacy in it: it is standard probability, statistics, optimization, information theory and cryptography, chosen because a later part needs it and taken only as far as that need goes. You need the basics of probability (expectation, variance, independence), enough machine learning to recognise a loss function and stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and enough Python to read a short script. If you know a topic, skim its cheat sheet; each later chapter restates in a sentence what it uses and links back here.
Later parts study algorithms whose output is random, and they keep asking the same few questions about them. How far is a random output from its expected value? How different are the outputs on two inputs that differ in one example, and how well could anyone tell them apart? How much does a trained model depend on a single training example? How much does an observation reveal about something hidden, and what can an observer with limited computing power learn?
Two ideas answer most of them. The first is the likelihood ratio \(p(x)/q(x)\): how many times more likely an observation is under one distribution than under another. It measures what one observation says about which distribution produced it, so telling two distributions apart always comes down to it: divergences summarize it, the best test thresholds it, and when it is bounded no single observation is strong evidence. The second idea is the effect of one input: how far one example can move an average, a minimizer or a loss. A quantity that no single input can move much has little room to vary, so small influence turns into narrow error bars, and in learning into a model that generalizes.

title: Prerequisites
section: Why the chapters come in this order
text:
Why the chapters come in this order
The first four chapters build one argument, each on the last. Probability distributions introduces the few families that model counts and noise, and ends by comparing a noise density with a copy of itself moved sideways: the normal’s likelihood ratio grows without bound in the tails, the Laplace’s is capped. That raises the question of how often the extreme ratios occur, and Concentration inequalities answers it by turning what you know about a random quantity into an error bar that fails with a chosen small probability. Divergences then compresses the difference between two distributions into one number, and shows that each candidate number answers a different question. Hypothesis testing says what those numbers mean for anyone trying to tell the two distributions apart: the best test, the curve of its two errors, and why a detector should be judged where false alarms are rare.
Information theory continues the same thread from a different angle, asking how much an observation reveals about a hidden value, on average and for a single best guess. Optimization and Algorithmic stability and generalization take up the second idea: how fast training converges, how far its result moves when one example changes, and why a model that depends little on each example generalizes. Cryptography basics stands somewhat apart. It defines what an efficient observer must not learn, as two worlds an attacker must tell apart, and can wait until a later chapter needs it.

title: Prerequisites
text:
How to read a chapter
Each chapter opens with its practical question and the idea that answers it, then reasons each result from a problem, with a worked example and the consequences for practice, and closes with a cheat sheet. The derivations and the scripts that check every number are in the full edition, linked at the end.

title: Prerequisites
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do
By the end of this part you will be able to put an error bar on a noisy answer, a measured rate or the maximum of many noise draws, and choose the inequality that gives the narrowest valid one. You will be able to compute the Kullback–Leibler (KL), Rényi, total variation and hockey-stick divergences between two normal or two Laplace distributions, and explain why processing data cannot increase any of them. You will know the best test between two distributions, read its trade-off curve, report a detector by its true positive rate at a low false positive rate, and size a test set to measure that rate. You will also be able to say how fast gradient descent converges and how much a trained model moves when one example changes, compute what an observation leaks about a hidden value, and state a security property as a game between an attacker and two worlds.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.1 Why this matters
Later parts keep asking two questions about a random output: how wide is it, and how hard is it to tell apart from a slightly different one? Both answers depend on its distribution, and a handful of families cover almost every case: counts of events, such as errors on a test set, and additive noise, usually normal or Laplace.
These families are built from one another. A binomial is a sum of coin flips, a Poisson is a binomial with many unlikely trials, a Laplace is two exponential waiting times back to back, and a normal is what many small independent pieces add up to. Each family’s spread and tail follow from how it is built, and so does what matters most later: how far a density drifts from a shifted copy of itself.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.2 Counts: binomial and Poisson
Every measured rate (accuracy, error rate, false positive rate) is a count of yes/no outcomes divided by the number of trials. With \(n\) independent trials, each a yes with probability \(p\), the count is \(\mathrm{Binomial}(n, p)\). Its mean is \(np\) and its variance \(np(1-p)\), because one trial has variance \(p(1-p)\) and variances add over independent terms. Dividing the count by \(n\), the measured rate \(\hat p\) has standard deviation \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\): four times the data only halves the error.
The variance vanishes near \(p = 0\), which sounds like good news for rare events but is not. What matters is the error relative to the rate, and the count’s standard deviation, about \(\sqrt{np}\), divided by its mean \(np\) is about \(1/\sqrt{np}\). So relative precision is set by the expected count, not by the number of trials. A classifier that errs with probability 0.05 on 2,000 test examples makes about 100 errors, with standard deviation about 9.7, and the measured rate is typically within about half a point of 5%. At an error rate of 0.001 the same test set expects 2 errors, with standard deviation about 1.4, a relative error of about 70%, and one test set in seven shows no error at all.
When the trials are many and each is unlikely, the binomial depends only on the expected count \(\mu = np\), and the limit is the Poisson distribution \(\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)\). Its variance equals its mean, \(\mu\), because the factor \(1 - p\) in the binomial variance tends to 1. A training loop that includes each of 60,000 examples independently with probability 0.01 gets batches whose size is close to \(\mathrm{Poisson}(600)\): mean 600, standard deviation about 24.5 (Figure 1.1).






Figure 1.1: \(\mathrm{Binomial}(n, 5/n)\) for \(n = 10\) and 100 against \(\mathrm{Poisson}(5)\) and its normal approximation. At \(n = 100\) the binomial and the Poisson almost coincide.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.3 Laplace and exponential
The waiting time for a rare event, with many independent chances each unlikely, follows the exponential distribution \(\mathrm{Exp}(b)\): density \(\frac1be^{-y/b}\) on \(y \ge 0\), mean \(b\), tail \(e^{-t/b}\). The Laplace distribution puts one exponential on each side of a centre. \(\mathrm{Lap}(\mu, b)\), with centre \(\mu\) and scale \(b\), has density \[f(x) = \frac{1}{2b}e^{-|x - \mu|/b}. \tag{1.1}\] So the size \(|X - \mu|\) is exactly \(\mathrm{Exp}(b)\): the average absolute error is \(b\), the variance is \(2b^2\) (so a standard deviation \(\sigma\) means \(b = \sigma/\sqrt2\)), and the two-sided tail is exact, \[\Pr[|X - \mu| \ge t] = e^{-t/b}. \tag{1.2}\]
The Laplace has heavier tails than a normal of the same variance, and the log scale shows why (Figure 1.2). The logarithm of each density is its exponent: two straight lines \(-|x|/b\) for the Laplace, a parabola \(-x^2/(2\sigma^2)\) for the normal. Far enough out a parabola always falls below a line, so the normal’s tail eventually becomes far lighter. With the same variance, the Laplace exceeds three times its scale with probability \(e^{-3} \approx 0.050\), the normal only with probability about 0.034, and the gap widens. So a tail bound shaped for the normal fails for Laplace noise far enough out.






Figure 1.2: Normal and Laplace densities with variance 2, on linear and log scales. The log of the normal density is a parabola; the log of the Laplace density is two straight lines.



Libraries differ in whether they take the scale \(b\) or the rate \(1/b\) (NumPy’s rng.exponential(b) takes the scale), so check before trusting a noise level.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.4 Normal
\(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) has density \(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), and every probability reduces to the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(\Phi\), through \(\Pr[X \le x] = \Phi((x - \mu)/\sigma)\). It stays normal under sums: \(\sum_ia_iX_i\) for independent normals is normal with mean \(\sum_ia_i\mu_i\) and variance \(\sum_ia_i^2\sigma_i^2\).
That rule explains normal noise in many dimensions. A vector \(X \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\) has \(d\) independent coordinates, so its squared length is a sum of \(d\) terms of mean \(\sigma^2\), and like any sum of many independent terms its relative spread shrinks: the length sits at \(\sigma\sqrt d\), with relative spread about \(1/\sqrt{2d}\) (Table 1.1). Yet the projection onto a fixed unit vector is a weighted sum whose squared weights add to 1, so it is just \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). Noise \(\mathcal N(0, 0.01^2I_d)\) on a model with \(d = 10^6\) parameters has length about \(0.01 \times 1000 = 10\), yet along any direction fixed in advance it is only \(\mathcal N(0, 0.01^2)\): large in norm, small in every direction.

The central limit theorem (CLT) explains why the normal is everywhere: the standardized sum of \(n\) independent draws with finite variance approaches \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\). But the skew of the summands averages out only like \(1/\sqrt n\): for sums of exponentials the largest error in the CDF is still 0.0243 at \(n = 30\). That is fine for the bulk and useless in the far tail, whose probabilities are much smaller than that error; tails need Concentration inequalities. Small tails need care in code too: \(1 - \Phi(x)\) subtracts two nearly equal numbers and loses every digit, so compute the tail directly as \(\frac12\operatorname{erfc}(x/\sqrt2)\).

title: 1  Probability distributions
section: 1.5 A density against its shifted copy
text:
1.5 A density against its shifted copy
You observe \(x = \mu + X\) with noise density \(f\), and \(\mu\) is either 0 or a known shift \(s\). The two candidates give \(x\) the densities \(f(x)\) and \(f(x - s)\), the same curve moved sideways, and how much one observation favours the first is the log ratio \[L(x) = \ln f(x) - \ln f(x - s). \tag{1.3}\] If \(|L(x)|\) is bounded, no single observation can settle the question; if not, some observations settle it almost for certain.
The log of each density is its exponent, so the answer comes from the shapes in Figure 1.2. Two copies of the normal’s parabola have the same curvature, so subtracting them cancels the \(x^2\) terms and leaves a straight line, unbounded: \[L(x) = \frac{s^2 - 2sx}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{1.4}\] The Laplace’s log density is \(-|x|/b\), a distance from the centre divided by \(b\). Moving the centre by \(s\) changes the distance from any point by at most \(|s|\), so \[L(x) = \frac{|x - s| - |x|}{b}, \qquad |L(x)| \le \frac{|s|}{b}, \tag{1.5}\] and the bound is reached on whole half-lines, every \(x \le 0\) and every \(x \ge s\), where both distances change by exactly \(s\).
Take \(s = 1\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(b = 1\) (Table 1.2 and Figure 1.3). At \(x = 10\) the normal log ratio is \(-9.5\): the observation is about 13,360 times more likely under \(\mu = 1\). The Laplace never says more than \(e \approx 2.72\) times, however far out \(x\) lies.

Rules of thumb

A measured rate has standard deviation \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\); its relative precision is set by the expected count \(np\).
Normal noise in \(d\) dimensions has norm \(\approx \sigma\sqrt d\) and is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) along every fixed direction.
Laplace shifted by \(s\): log ratio at most \(|s|/b\). Normal: unbounded, but large only in the tails, which carry very little probability.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.1 Why this matters
Almost every number in a private system is random. The noise added to a count is random by design. An error rate measured on a test set depends on which examples happened to be in it. The number of examples in a randomly sampled minibatch changes from one step to the next. Before you can use any of these numbers, you need to know how far each one can stray from the value you care about.
A concentration inequality answers that question. It tells you how wide to make an interval around your estimate so that the true value falls outside it only rarely, say once in a thousand runs. This chapter calls that rare event a failure, and the chance of it the failure probability, written \(\beta\). It calls the distance from the estimate to either end of the interval the width, so the interval reaches one width on each side.
How wide the interval must be depends on how much you know about the random quantity. If you know only its variance, the width grows quickly as you ask for a smaller failure probability. If you also know the shape of its distribution far from the centre, the width grows very slowly. For a 95% interval the difference is modest, under a factor of two in the examples below. But later parts of this book often ask for failure probabilities of one in a hundred thousand or less. At one in a million, knowing that shape can make an interval a hundred times narrower. This chapter shows how to use everything you know.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.2 Knowing only the variance: Markov and Chebyshev
text:
2.2 Knowing only the variance: Markov and Chebyshev
Start with the weakest thing you could know about a quantity: it is never negative, and you know its average. That alone limits how often it can be large. Suppose customers wait 2 minutes at a counter on average. Then at most a quarter of them can wait 8 minutes or more, because if more than a quarter did, those customers alone would push the average above 2 minutes. This is Markov’s inequality. For a quantity \(X\) that is never negative, with average \(\mathbb E[X]\), and any positive threshold \(a\), it says that \(\Pr[X \ge a] \le \mathbb E[X]/a\).
On its own, Markov’s inequality is rarely useful, because it ignores how spread out the quantity is. What makes it useful is that you can apply it to other quantities built from \(X\), and the first of these is the squared distance from the mean. Write \(\mu\) for the mean of \(X\) and \(\sigma^2\) for its variance, the average squared distance from \(\mu\). A squared distance is never negative, so Markov’s inequality applies to it, with \(\sigma^2\) as the average. Now pick a distance \(t\). Being at least \(t\) from the mean is the same as having a squared distance of at least \(t^2\), so the chance of it is at most \(\sigma^2/t^2\). This is Chebyshev’s inequality: \[\Pr[|X - \mu| \ge t] \le \frac{\sigma^2}{t^2}. \tag{2.1}\]
To turn the bound into an interval, set the right side equal to \(\beta\) and solve for \(t\), which gives \(t = \sigma/\sqrt\beta\). So with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the quantity lies within \(\sigma/\sqrt\beta\) of its mean. The same works for an average of \(n\) independent samples. Averaging divides the variance by \(n\), so the width becomes \(\sigma/\sqrt{n\beta}\).
Chebyshev’s bound is weak because it must hold for every distribution with the given variance. Some of those distributions hide their spread in a rare spike far from the mean. To cover them, the width has to grow like \(1/\sqrt\beta\) as the failure probability falls. Most noise is better behaved. Its tail, the chance of landing far from the centre, falls off quickly. For a quantity whose tail falls off like a normal distribution’s, the width is only \(\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\beta)}\), and the next section shows where this comes from. Table 2.1 compares the two widths.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.3 Normal and Laplace noise
When you know the distribution of the noise, you don’t need a general inequality. You can read the width directly off the distribution’s tail. The two noise distributions this book uses most are the Laplace and the normal distributions (Probability distributions), both centred at zero.
Laplace noise, written \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\), has a scale \(b\) that sets its typical size. Its tail has an exact formula: a draw lands more than \(t\) from zero with probability \(e^{-t/b}\). Setting this chance equal to \(\beta\) and solving for \(t\) gives the width. With probability \(1 - \beta\), the noise stays within \(b\ln(1/\beta)\) of zero.
Compare this with Chebyshev’s inequality, which uses only the variance of Laplace noise, \(2b^2\). For scale 1 and a 95% interval, Chebyshev gives a width of about 6.3. The exact tail gives about 3.0. At a failure probability of one in a million, Chebyshev gives 1,414 and the exact tail gives 13.8. Ignoring the shape of the noise makes the interval a hundred times wider.
Normal noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\) has no simple formula for its tail, but a simple bound on it is enough to compute the width. A draw lands more than \(t\) from zero with probability at most \(e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}\). Solving for \(t\) in the same way gives the width \(\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\beta)}\) from Table 2.1.
The shapes of the two tails explain why the widths grow at different rates. The Laplace tail falls like \(e^{-t}\), so its width grows like \(\ln(1/\beta)\). The normal tail falls like \(e^{-t^2}\), so it is the squared width that grows like \(\ln(1/\beta)\). The width itself grows like the square root of the logarithm, which is why it grows so slowly.
Sometimes you add noisy values together, for example to compute a total from several noisy counts. Write \(S\) for the sum of \(k\) independent Laplace draws with scale \(b\). Near its centre the sum looks like a normal distribution, as the central limit theorem (CLT) predicts. Far from the centre, though, its tail keeps the slow decay of a single Laplace draw, like \(e^{-t}\) rather than \(e^{-t^2}\). A bound that is valid everywhere has to describe both regions: \[\Pr[S \ge t] \le \exp\Big(-\min\Big(\frac{t^2}{8kb^2}, \frac{t}{4b}\Big)\Big). \tag{2.2}\] The constants come from the derivation in the full edition. What matters here is the shape. Up to \(t = 2kb\), where the two terms inside the minimum are equal, the first term is the smaller one, and the bound has the normal shape. Beyond that point the second term takes over, and the bound falls only like \(e^{-t}\), as a Laplace tail does.
The difference matters whenever you need a guarantee. Take 10 draws with scale 1, and approximate their sum by a normal distribution with the same mean and variance. That approximation says the sum reaches 20 with probability \(3.9\times10^{-6}\). Simulation gives \(3.4\times10^{-5}\), about nine times more (Figure 2.1). A system that trusted the approximation would fail nine times as often as it promised. The bound above gives \(6.7\times10^{-3}\) at the same point. It is far from the truth, but it is never below it. When the answer must be a guarantee, use a bound, not the CLT.






Figure 2.1: Empirical tail of a sum of 10 \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\) draws, against the bound above and the normal approximation, which badly underestimates the far tail.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.4 Many quantities at once: the union bound
text:
2.4 Many quantities at once: the union bound
Often you need many random quantities to stay close to their targets at the same time. A system might release \(k\) noisy counts and need every one of them to be accurate. The union bound handles this. It says that the chance that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their separate chances. The sum can overcount, because an outcome in which two events happen is counted twice, but it never misses an outcome. So if you want all \(k\) counts to be accurate except with probability \(\beta\), ask each one to fail with probability at most \(\beta/k\).
Dividing the failure probability by \(k\) adds only \(\ln k\) to the logarithm in each width, since \(\ln(k/\beta) = \ln k + \ln(1/\beta)\). All \(k\) Laplace draws then stay within \(b\ln(k/\beta)\) of zero, and all \(k\) normal draws within \(\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(k/\beta)}\). Because the number of quantities enters only through a logarithm, controlling many of them at once is cheap.
The union bound looks crude, but for rare, independent failures it is nearly exact. When the failures are independent and each is rare, two at once are rarer still, so the double counting adds almost nothing. For an example, take 100 Laplace draws with scale 1, and look at the one furthest from zero. With a failure probability of 0.05, the union bound gives the width \(\ln(100/0.05) = 7.60\). In simulation, the draw furthest from zero lands beyond 7.60 in 4.86% of runs. That is just under the 5% the bound allows (Figure 2.2). The bound is far less exact when the failures are correlated. If all \(k\) events were the same event, the sum would count it \(k\) times.






Figure 2.2: Left: the width \(b\ln(k/\beta)\) for the draw furthest from zero among \(k\) Laplace draws grows like \(\ln k\). Right: the simulated probability that this draw lands beyond the width stays near \(\beta = 0.05\) for every \(k\).

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.5 Counts: the Chernoff bound
Many quantities in machine learning are counts: errors on a test set, examples in a sampled minibatch, records that match a query. A count adds up many independent yes-or-no outcomes. Chebyshev’s bound for it is far too loose when you need a very small failure probability. The Chernoff bound gives a bound on its tail that falls exponentially, using one more idea.
The idea is to apply Markov’s inequality to \(e^{\lambda X}\) instead of to \(X\) itself, where \(\lambda\) is a positive number you are free to choose. The exponential keeps the order of values, so \(X\) is at least \(t\) exactly when \(e^{\lambda X}\) is at least \(e^{\lambda t}\). Markov’s inequality then gives \[\Pr[X \ge t] \le \frac{\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}]}{e^{\lambda t}}. \tag{2.3}\] The exponential turns a modest gap between \(X\) and \(t\) into a huge gap between \(e^{\lambda X}\) and \(e^{\lambda t}\). The threshold on the bottom of the fraction is then far above the typical values on top, so the bound becomes small. The bound holds for every positive \(\lambda\), and you pick the one that makes it smallest. For a count, the average on top, \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}]\), is also easy to compute. The exponential of a sum is a product of exponentials, and for independent outcomes the average of that product is the product of the averages, one factor per outcome.
Carrying out this calculation for a count \(S\) gives a bound in terms of two numbers. The first is the expected count, written \(\mu\). The second is the relative deviation you ask about, written \(\delta\), so that \(\delta = 0.2\) means 20% above or below \(\mu\). The two Chernoff bounds are \[\Pr[S \ge (1+\delta)\mu] \le \exp\Big(-\frac{\delta^2\mu}{2+\delta}\Big), \qquad \Pr[S \le (1-\delta)\mu] \le \exp\Big(-\frac{\delta^2\mu}{2}\Big). \tag{2.4}\] The first bounds the chance that the count overshoots its mean by the fraction \(\delta\). The second bounds the chance that it undershoots, and holds for \(\delta\) between 0 and 1. For small \(\delta\), setting either bound to \(\beta\) gives a one-sided width of about \(\sqrt{2\mu\ln(1/\beta)}\).
The exponent contains the expected count \(\mu\), not the number of trials. This has a cost and a benefit. The cost is that a count of rare events has a small error relative to its mean only once you expect many of them. A million trials that each succeed with probability one in a million expect a single success. The count is far from concentrated: no success at all and two successes are both common outcomes.
The benefit is that the calculation works with each outcome’s own probability before adding them up into \(\mu\). An outcome that is a yes with probability \(p\) has variance \(p(1-p)\). When \(p\) is small, that is about \(p\). The variance of a count is the sum of its outcomes’ variances, so a count of rare events has a variance of about \(\mu\). The Chernoff bound adapts to that small variance. A bound that knew only that each outcome is 0 or 1 would have to assume the largest variance such an outcome can have, which is 0.25. The next section shows how much that costs.
The overshoot and undershoot bounds also differ. For large \(\delta\), the exponent of the overshoot bound grows like \(\delta\mu\) rather than \(\delta^2\mu\), so the overshoot bound falls more slowly. Counts have long right tails, like the Poisson distribution, so a count can overshoot its mean by a lot far more easily than it can undershoot it.
Here is how the bound is used in practice. A training loop forms each minibatch by including each of 60,000 examples independently with probability 0.01. The batch size is a count with expected value \(\mu = 600\). If your code or your analysis assumes a batch size near 600, you need to know how often that assumption fails. With \(\delta = 0.2\), the overshoot bound says a batch is more than 20% too large with probability at most \(1.8\times10^{-5}\). The undershoot bound gives \(6.1\times10^{-6}\) for a batch more than 20% too small. Adding the two, a single batch leaves the range \(600 \pm 20\%\) with probability about \(2.4\times10^{-5}\). Over 1,000 training steps, the union bound multiplies this by 1,000. So the chance that any batch leaves the range is about 0.024.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.6 Averages of bounded quantities: Hoeffding and Bernstein
text:
2.6 Averages of bounded quantities: Hoeffding and Bernstein
Often you know neither the distribution nor the variance, only the range. A loss clipped to lie between 0 and 1 is an example, and so is a 0/1 indicator of a mistake. Knowing the range already tells you a lot. A quantity confined to an interval cannot have a heavy tail, one that reaches far out with sizable probability, because it cannot go past the ends at all. Its variance cannot be large either. The most spread-out quantity on an interval puts half its probability on each end, like a fair coin. Its variance is a quarter of the squared length of the interval.
Hoeffding’s inequality turns this into a width for an average. Take \(n\) independent quantities, each in the same interval from \(a\) to \(b\). Write \(\bar X_n\) for their average and \(\mu\) for its expected value. Hoeffding’s inequality says that the average has a normal-shaped tail, as if each quantity had the largest variance its range allows. With probability at least \(1-\beta\), \[|\bar X_n - \mu| < (b - a)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\beta)}{2n}}. \tag{2.5}\] The 2 inside the logarithm appears because the interval has two sides, and each side is allowed half the failure probability. The width shrinks like \(1/\sqrt n\) as you add samples. As you lower the failure probability, it grows only like the square root of a logarithm, as for normal noise.
The most common use is to compare a model’s error on its training data with its true error, its average loss on new data from the same source. For one fixed model, the training error is an average of \(n\) losses between 0 and 1, so Hoeffding’s inequality applies directly. A learner, however, picks its model after seeing the data. The model it picks is the one that looks best on the training data, which makes it the one whose training error is most likely to be too optimistic. So the bound must hold for every model the learner might pick.
Suppose the candidates form a finite set \(H\), and write \(|H|\) for their number. The union bound puts an extra \(\ln|H|\) inside the logarithm. With probability at least \(1-\beta\), every candidate’s training error is then within \(\sqrt{\ln(2|H|/\beta)/(2n)}\) of its true error. The number of candidates enters only through its logarithm, so even a huge set of them costs little.
Knowing only the range is Hoeffding’s strength, since there is nothing to estimate. It is also its weakness, because the inequality assumes the largest variance that the range allows. A 0/1 quantity that is rarely 1 has a much smaller variance than that. The gap is widest exactly when you measure small rates, such as a false-positive rate.
Suppose a classifier makes 1 false positive on 1,000 negative examples, and you want a 95% upper bound on its true false-positive rate. An upper bound needs only one side of the interval, so it uses \(\ln(1/\beta)\) in place of \(\ln(2/\beta)\). With \(n = 1{,}000\), this one-sided Hoeffding bound adds about 0.039 to the measured rate. The added width alone is about 40 times the rate you measured. The cause is the variance Hoeffding’s inequality assumes: 0.25, the variance of a fair coin. A single 0/1 outcome that is 1 with probability near 0.001 has a variance of only about 0.001.
Bernstein’s inequality fixes this by using the variance. Write \(\sigma^2\) for the variance of each quantity, and \(M\) for the largest distance it can be from its mean. Then the one-sided width is about \[\sqrt{\frac{2\sigma^2\ln(1/\beta)}{n}} + \frac{2M\ln(1/\beta)}{3n}. \tag{2.6}\] The first term is the normal-shaped width, computed with the true variance. The second term pays for the range, but it shrinks like \(1/n\) instead of \(1/\sqrt n\). For the classifier, take \(M = 1\) and estimate the variance as 0.001. Bernstein’s inequality then adds about 0.0045, against Hoeffding’s 0.039. This calculation is only a heuristic, because the variance was estimated from the same data. A rigorous version, empirical Bernstein, gives a wider interval.
The exact answer comes from the binomial distribution itself, through the Clopper–Pearson interval. Its one-sided 95% upper bound on the rate is 0.0047, a little below the measured rate plus Bernstein’s 0.0045. The same number is the upper end of a two-sided 90% interval, which is how Hypothesis testing computes it.
Figure 2.3 shows the cost of ignoring the variance on a second example. It averages 200 yes-or-no outcomes (Bernoulli variables), each a yes with probability 0.1. The question is how likely the average is to reach 0.15. Hoeffding’s inequality bounds that chance by 0.37. Chebyshev’s inequality, which uses the variance, does better here with 0.18. At this moderate deviation, Chebyshev’s \(1/t^2\) has not yet fallen far behind an exponential tail, so knowing the variance counts for more. The Chernoff bound has both, and gets 0.135. Even that is far above the true chance of about \(9.6\times10^{-3}\), because a bound must cover every case its assumptions allow.






Figure 2.3: Empirical tail of the mean of 200 Bernoulli(0.1) variables against the Markov, Chebyshev, Hoeffding and Chernoff bounds.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.7 Functions of many inputs: McDiarmid and Azuma
text:
2.7 Functions of many inputs: McDiarmid and Azuma
So far, every quantity was a sum of independent pieces. Two common situations break this. A trained model’s error is a complicated function of its training data, not a sum. And in a sequential procedure, each step can depend on what happened before, so the pieces are not independent. Concentration still holds in both situations, provided that no single input or step can move the result by much.
Start with a function \(f\) of independent inputs \(X_1, \dots, X_n\), and write \(X\) for all of them together. Suppose that changing only the \(i\)-th input, with the others held fixed, moves the result by at most an amount \(c_i\). McDiarmid’s inequality says that the result then concentrates around its average as tightly as a sum of pieces with ranges \(c_i\) would: \[\Pr[f(X) - \mathbb E f(X) \ge t] \le \exp\Big(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_ic_i^2}\Big). \tag{2.7}\]
The reason is easiest to see if you reveal the inputs one at a time and keep a running best guess of the result. Before you see any input, the best guess is the average result. After you see the first input, it is the average over the inputs you have not seen yet, with the first one fixed. Each revealed input updates the guess in this way, and after the last one the guess is the result itself. So the deviation you want to bound is the sum of \(n\) updates.
Two facts about these updates make the sum concentrate. First, an update is zero on average. Before you see an input, you cannot predict which way it will move your guess, or that prediction would already be part of the guess. Second, the \(i\)-th update is small. Changing the \(i\)-th input moves the result by at most \(c_i\), so it moves the guess by at most \(c_i\) too. The updates are not independent, since each one depends on the inputs before it. The next paragraphs explain why the two facts are enough anyway.
For the training error of a fixed model, with losses between 0 and 1, changing one example moves the average by at most \(1/n\). With \(c_i = 1/n\) for every input, McDiarmid’s inequality gives back Hoeffding’s bound. Its real use is for functions that are not averages, such as the error of a model retrained on the data, and Algorithmic stability and generalization uses it that way. The amount \(c_i\) must hold for every possible change to the \(i\)-th input, not just for typical ones, because the argument charges each input its largest possible move. This per-record influence returns in later parts under the name sensitivity.
Hoeffding’s inequality was stated for independent pieces, but its conclusion needs less. It is enough that each piece averages zero given everything before it, and lies in a short interval. A running total whose steps average zero given the past is called a martingale. Azuma’s inequality bounds how far it drifts. Suppose the \(k\)-th step always lies in an interval of length \(d_k\). Then the total drifts upward by \(t\) or more with probability at most \(\exp(-2t^2/\sum_kd_k^2)\). This is McDiarmid’s bound, with the step lengths \(d_k\) in place of the influences \(c_i\).
Azuma’s inequality covers procedures that adapt as they go. Flip a coin 200 times. If the previous flip was heads, flip a coin that lands heads with probability 0.7. Otherwise, including for the first flip, use a coin that lands heads with probability 0.3. The flips depend on each other, so Hoeffding’s inequality does not apply. What you can bound is the drift. Count the heads, and subtract the number of heads you would expect from the coins you chose. Each step of the drift is the flip’s outcome, 1 or 0, minus the chosen coin’s probability of heads. Given the past, it averages zero and lies in an interval of length 1. Azuma’s inequality bounds the chance of an upward drift of 20 or more by \(1.83\times10^{-2}\). Simulation gives \(1.12\times10^{-3}\) (Figure 2.4).






Figure 2.4: Empirical tail of the drift in the adaptive coin game against the Azuma bound.



The bound is loose partly for the same reason as Hoeffding’s. It assumes that each step has the largest variance its interval allows, which is 0.25. The true variance of each step is 0.21 for either coin, since \(0.7 \times 0.3 = 0.3 \times 0.7\).

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.1 Why this matters
How far is a fitted model from the truth? How many samples reveal a drift? Later parts ask the same about an algorithm’s outputs on two different inputs. Each time you need one number for how different two distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) are, and there are several candidates because there are several questions.
All of them summarize the likelihood ratio \(r(x) = p(x)/q(x)\), how many times more likely an outcome is under \(P\) than under \(Q\); its logarithm \(L(x) = \ln r(x)\) is the evidence for \(P\), in nats. The running example is a die, fair (\(Q\)) or loaded so that a six comes up half the time (\(P\)). A six has \(r = 0.5/(1/6) = 3\); any other roll has \(r = 0.1/(1/6) = 0.6\).

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.2 KL divergence
Roll the loaded die many times and add up the evidence \(\sum_i\ln r(x_i)\). Sixes are frequent, so the sum drifts upward. That rate, the average evidence per observation from \(P\), is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_P\left[\ln\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\right] = \sum_x p(x)\ln\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}. \tag{3.1}\] Independent observations multiply their likelihoods, so their evidence adds: \(n\) samples carry \(n\) times the KL of one. And since the drift grows like \(n\) while its fluctuation grows like \(\sqrt n\), telling the two apart takes on the order of \(1/\mathrm{KL}\) samples. For the die, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = 0.2939\) per roll.
KL is never negative and is zero only when \(P = Q\), but it averages over its first argument, so it is asymmetric. The fair die proves its innocence more slowly, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P) = 0.2426\), because its evidence is the absence of sixes.
The direction also shapes fitted models. Maximum likelihood minimizes the forward KL, averaged over the data, so wherever the data go and the model has almost no mass, \(\ln(p/q)\) explodes: the fit must cover everything. Variational inference minimizes the reverse KL, averaged over the model, which only punishes mass where the data aren’t. Fitting one Gaussian to two separated bumps, the forward fit spreads over both and the reverse fit locks onto one; the second has forward KL 15.307, against 0.724 for the first. If \(Q\) gives zero probability to anything \(P\) can produce, that outcome is infinite evidence and KL is infinite.
For two normals with the same variance and means \(\mu\) standard deviations apart, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = \mu^2/2\); for \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\) against \(\mathrm{Lap}(s, b)\), with \(t = s/b\), \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = t + e^{-t} - 1\). The normal’s is quadratic in the shift, which is why small drifts need many samples.

title: 3  Divergences
section: 3.3 Rényi divergence and the worst case
text:
3.3 Rényi divergence and the worst case
KL is the average of \(\ln r\), so \(e^{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\) is the geometric mean of \(r\). Other means weight large ratios more: for the die under \(P\), the geometric mean is 1.3416, the arithmetic mean 1.8000, the largest value 3.0000. The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is the logarithm of the power mean of \(r\) with exponent \(\alpha - 1\): for \(\alpha > 0\), \(\alpha \ne 1\), \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_Q\big[r^\alpha\big] = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\sum_x p(x)^\alpha q(x)^{1-\alpha}. \tag{3.2}\] The order is a dial: \(\alpha \to 1\) gives KL, larger \(\alpha\) weighs large ratios more, so \(D_\alpha\) never decreases, and \(\alpha \to \infty\) gives the max-divergence \(D_\infty(P\|Q) = \ln\max_x r(x)\), the largest log ratio \(\ln P(A)/Q(A)\) of any event. Every order adds over samples.
The normal pair’s log ratio is a straight line, so higher orders keep finding larger ratios further out: \(D_\alpha = \alpha\mu^2/2\) and \(D_\infty = \infty\). The Laplace pair’s is capped at \(t\), so \(D_\alpha\) levels off at \(D_\infty = t\): \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)t} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha t}\right) \qquad (\alpha \ne \tfrac12, 1). \tag{3.3}\] At equal variance, the Laplace pair is further apart at low orders, because its sharp peak moves visibly, and the normal pair above order 2.98, where its unbounded tail takes over (Table 3.1, Figure 3.1). “More different” must name the order.

Unbounded is not frequent, and Rényi divergences say how rare large evidence is, which an average cannot. Markov’s inequality applied to \(r^\alpha\), whose \(Q\)-average is what \(D_\alpha\) measures, gives for any \(\alpha > 0\) \[Q[L \ge c] \le \exp\big(-\alpha c + (\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)\big). \tag{3.4}\] For the normal pair with \(\mu = 1\), a draw from \(Q\) gives at least 2 nats of evidence for \(P\) with probability 0.0062. The bound gives 0.1353 at \(\alpha = 1\), valid for any pair, and 0.0439 at \(\alpha = 2.5\).

title: 3  Divergences
section: 3.4 Total variation and the hockey-stick divergence
text:
3.4 Total variation and the hockey-stick divergence
Draw \(p\) and \(q\) on the same axes. Where they overlap, an observation can’t tell you which one produced it. Total variation (TV) is the mass that doesn’t overlap: \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \max_A|P(A) - Q(A)| = \frac12\sum_x|p(x) - q(x)|. \tag{3.5}\] The best single guess says “\(P\)” exactly where \(p > q\), so with equal priors it is right with probability \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}\), and no classifier does better. The mean of any statistic with values in \([a, b]\) likewise moves by at most \((b - a)\,\mathrm{TV}\). For the normal pair, with \(\Phi\) the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF), \(\mathrm{TV} = 2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\); at \(\mu = 1\) it is 0.3829, so the best guess is right with probability 0.6915.
TV is capped at 1 and does not add over samples. A shift of a tenth of a standard deviation has TV 0.0399 in one sample, yet the best test on 400 samples is right with probability 0.8413. So compute KL or Rényi for \(n\) samples, where they add, and convert at the end (Section 3.5).
TV counts all excess mass, however weak its evidence. To keep only strong evidence, scale \(q\) up by \(\gamma \ge 1\) and measure the mass of \(p\) still above \(\gamma q\), the hockey-stick divergence: \[E_\gamma(P\|Q) = \max_A\big[P(A) - \gamma Q(A)\big] = \sum_x\big(p(x) - \gamma q(x)\big)_+, \tag{3.6}\] with \((y)_+ = \max(y, 0)\). Only outcomes with ratio above \(\gamma\) count, so \(E_1 = \mathrm{TV}\), \(E_\gamma\) falls as \(\gamma\) grows, and it reaches zero at \(\gamma = e^{D_\infty}\). For the die only the six counts, and \(E_\gamma = 0.5 - \gamma/6\) hits zero at \(\gamma = 3\). For the Laplace pair, \(E_\gamma = 1 - e^{-(t - \ln\gamma)/2}\) up to \(\gamma = e^t\), zero beyond. The normal pair never reaches zero, \[E_\gamma = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac{\ln\gamma}\mu\Big) - \gamma\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac{\ln\gamma}\mu\Big), \tag{3.7}\] giving \(E_2 = 0.1906\) and \(E_4 = 0.0692\) at \(\mu = 1\) (Figure 3.2): its large ratios exist but carry little mass.






Figure 3.2: The hockey-stick divergence \(E_\gamma(P\|Q)\) against \(\ln\gamma\) for the loaded die, a Laplace pair and a normal pair with the same variance. The die and Laplace curves reach zero at their max-divergences; the normal curve stays positive.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.5 Data processing and Pinsker’s inequality
Binning, thresholds and added noise map several outcomes to one, and the output’s likelihood ratio is then an average of theirs. Report the die’s parity, and the six (ratio 3) joins the two and four (0.6 each) in an even result with ratio \((3 + 0.6 + 0.6)/3 = 1.4\). Averaging pulls strong evidence toward weak, and a divergence, a convex summary of the ratios, can only shrink. That is the data processing inequality (DPI): if both inputs go through the same channel \(K\), even a randomized one, then \(D(PK\|QK) \le D(P\|Q)\) for KL, TV, \(E_\gamma\), every \(D_\alpha\) and \(D_\infty\), and every f-divergence \(\mathbb E_Q[f(r)]\) with \(f\) convex and \(f(1) = 0\).
Nothing is lost when processing keeps the ratio: parity drops the die’s KL from 0.2939 to 0.0823, while “is it a six?” keeps all of it. Thresholding draws from \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) or \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\) at the midpoint lowers KL from 0.5 to 0.3090 but keeps all of the TV, since it is the best test. The DPI bounds the best test only: processing can help a bad classifier, never beat the best test on raw data.
Pinsker’s inequality turns the KL you can compute into a bound on the TV you want to report, and Bretagnolle–Huber stays below 1: \[\mathrm{TV} \le \sqrt{\tfrac12D_{\mathrm{KL}}}, \qquad \mathrm{TV} \le \sqrt{1 - e^{-D_{\mathrm{KL}}}}. \tag{3.8}\] Pinsker is tight for nearly equal distributions but passes 1 at KL \(= 2\); Bretagnolle–Huber is better above 1.59 (Table 3.2). There is no converse: a tiny TV is compatible with infinite KL.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.1 Why this matters
A spam filter, a fraud detector and a drift monitor all face one problem: an observation came from one of two distributions, and you must decide which. Later parts ask it about any test anyone could run, so you need the best test, how good it can be, and how to measure a given test from finite data.
The answer runs through the likelihood ratio \(\Lambda(x) = q(x)/p(x)\), how many times more likely the observation is under the alternative \(Q\) than under the default \(P\). The best test thresholds it, and sliding the threshold traces a curve of the best achievable errors that belongs to \(P\) and \(Q\) alone. Most of what goes wrong in practice comes from summarizing that curve by one number and losing the corner where false alarms are rare.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.2 Errors and the Neyman–Pearson lemma
Test the null hypothesis \(H_0: X \sim P\) against the alternative \(H_1: X \sim Q\) with a rule \(\phi(x) \in [0, 1]\), the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) on seeing \(x\). Its false positive rate (FPR), or type I error, is \(\alpha = \mathbb E_P[\phi]\); its type II error is \(\beta = 1 - \mathbb E_Q[\phi]\), and \(1 - \beta\) is its power or true positive rate (TPR). The two pull against each other: rejecting one more outcome raises \(\alpha\) and lowers \(\beta\). A coin that rejects with probability \(\alpha\) ignoring the data has \(\beta = 1 - \alpha\); a useful test beats it.
For the most power on a fixed false-alarm budget, note that rejecting an outcome \(x\) costs \(p(x)\) of budget and buys \(q(x)\) of power, an exchange rate of \(\Lambda(x)\). So spend the budget on the best rates first: reject where \(\Lambda(x)\) is above a cut-off \(\eta\). That is the Neyman–Pearson lemma: the test that rejects when \(q(x) > \eta\,p(x)\), keeps \(H_0\) when \(q(x) < \eta\,p(x)\), and randomizes on ties so its FPR is exactly \(\alpha\), has the smallest \(\beta\) of any test with FPR at most \(\alpha\).
A spam filter counts suspicious words, capped at 3 (Table 4.1). The ratio increases with the count, so the best tests are thresholds on it, but on discrete data a threshold only reaches a few FPRs: rejecting counts of 3 spends 0.1, counts of 2 or 3 spend 0.3. To spend a budget of exactly 0.25, reject a count of 3 always and a count of 2 with probability 0.75, for power 0.625. No test does better: the best of 200,000 random tests with FPR at most 0.25 reaches 0.587.

Whenever \(\Lambda\) increases with a statistic, “ratio above \(\eta\)” is “statistic above some \(t\)”, which is why thresholding a score works. A calibrated score \(\Pr[H_1 \mid x]\) increases with \(\Lambda(x)\), so thresholding it is optimal; a score that ranks outcomes differently from \(\Lambda\) can be beaten by re-ranking.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.3 Trade-off curves
A single test is one point \((\alpha, \beta)\). To say how hard it is to tell \(P\) from \(Q\), take the best \(\beta\) at every \(\alpha\): the trade-off function \(T(\alpha) = \inf\{\beta_\phi : \alpha_\phi \le \alpha\}\). It lies below the coin flip’s \(1 - \alpha\), and the further below, the easier the problem. Its slope is minus the likelihood ratio at the threshold, since rejecting a little more of \(x\) trades \(p(x)\) of FPR for \(q(x)\) of power. The best test adds outcomes in decreasing order of \(\Lambda\), so the curve flattens as it goes and is convex. Plotted as power against FPR, it is the optimal receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.
For \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\), with \(\Phi\) the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF), the best test thresholds \(x\), and \[T(\alpha) = \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu\big). \tag{4.1}\] With \(n\) draws, the log ratios add up to a function of the sample mean, which shifts by \(\delta\) with standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt n\), so the same curve applies with \(\mu = \delta\sqrt n/\sigma\): distinguishability grows like \(\sqrt n\). A monitor that averages 100 readings to detect a drift of \(0.2\sigma\) has \(\mu = 2\), power 0.6388 at \(\alpha = 0.05\), and only 0.1378 at \(10^{-3}\). Solving for \(n\) gives the sample size for power \(1 - \beta'\) at level \(\alpha\), \[n \ge \left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) + \Phi^{-1}(1 - \beta')}{\delta/\sigma}\right)^2, \tag{4.2}\] so power 0.9 at \(\alpha = 0.01\) for \(\delta/\sigma = 0.25\) needs 209 readings.
Near \(\alpha = 0\) the normal curve is vertical, because the normal likelihood ratio is unbounded far out: the first sliver of false-alarm budget buys power at an unbounded rate. A Laplace shift is different. For \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\) against \(\mathrm{Lap}(s, b)\), with \(\kappa = s/b\), the ratio is clipped to \([e^{-\kappa}, e^\kappa]\), so the ends of the curve are straight lines with those slopes: \[T(\alpha) = \begin{cases} 1 - e^{\kappa}\alpha, & \alpha < \tfrac12 e^{-\kappa}, \\ e^{-\kappa}/(4\alpha), & \tfrac12 e^{-\kappa} \le \alpha \le \tfrac12, \\ e^{-\kappa}(1 - \alpha), & \alpha > \tfrac12. \end{cases} \tag{4.3}\] No test can buy power faster than \(e^\kappa\) per unit of FPR, so no test has power above \(e^\kappa\alpha\). Table 4.2 compares a Laplace pair (\(\kappa = 1\)) with a normal pair (\(\mu = 1.0301\)) with the same best advantage, 0.3935 (Section 4.4). At \(\alpha = 10^{-6}\) the normal pair is 36 times easier, because its unbounded ratio lets a test find rare, overwhelming evidence (Figure 4.1). Plan for the level you will use.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.4 One-number summaries
The advantage of a test, \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\), is how much more often it fires under \(Q\) than under \(P\). Its maximum over all tests is the total variation (TV) distance \(\frac12\sum_x|q(x) - p(x)|\), reached by rejecting where \(q > p\): \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\) for the normal pair and \(1 - e^{-\kappa/2}\) for the Laplace pair. But that is one point of the curve, at \(\eta = 1\), and the two pairs above share it, 0.3935, despite their 36-fold gap at small \(\alpha\).
The area under the curve (AUC) of a ROC curve is the probability that a random positive scores above a random negative. It weights all FPRs equally, so the region below \(10^{-3}\) barely moves it. If negatives score \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and positives \(\mathcal N(m, \sigma^2)\), then \(\mathrm{AUC} = \Phi(m/\sqrt{1 + \sigma^2})\) and \[\mathrm{TPR}(\mathrm{FPR}) = 1 - \Phi\Big(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - m}{\sigma}\Big). \tag{4.4}\] Detector A has positives scoring \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\), detector B \(\mathcal N(1.5811, 2^2)\). Both have AUC 0.7602, but at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) their TPRs are 0.0183 and 0.2253: B catches 12 times as many positives (Figure 4.2). Report the TPR at a fixed low FPR chosen by the application, and plot ROC curves on log–log axes, where that corner is visible.






Figure 4.2: ROC curves of two detectors with the same AUC of 0.760. Left, linear axes: the curves cross and look comparable. Right, log axes: at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) detector B has 12 times the TPR of detector A.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.5 Base rates: the Bayesian view
With a known base rate, the useful question is how likely \(H_1\) is given the observation, and the likelihood ratio answers it in one multiplication. With prior probability \(\pi\) for \(H_1\), \[\frac{\Pr[H_1 \mid x]}{\Pr[H_0 \mid x]} = \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} \times \Lambda(x). \tag{4.5}\] If all you know is that the test fired, the likelihood ratio of that event is \(\mathrm{TPR}/\mathrm{FPR}\). Use the \(\mu = 2\) test where 1% of cases are positive. At an FPR of 0.05 an alarm has ratio \(0.6388/0.05 = 12.8\), and the chance it is real is only 0.114. At \(10^{-3}\) the ratio is 137.8 and the chance is 0.582. When positives are rare, the FPR, not the power, decides whether an alarm is worth acting on.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.6 Measuring rates from finite trials
A measured FPR is \(k\) false positives among \(n\) negatives, a binomial count. A count of \(k\) fluctuates by about \(\sqrt k\), so the relative uncertainty, about \(1/\sqrt k\), is set by the number of events. The Clopper–Pearson interval at confidence \(1 - a\) is the range of rates \([l, u]\) that make the observed count unsurprising: \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, l) \ge k] = a/2\) and \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, u) \le k] = a/2\). It covers the true rate with probability at least \(1 - a\). With no events the 95% upper bound is about \(3/n\), the rule of three. Measuring an FPR of \(\alpha\) to within a factor of about 1.2 takes some 100 expected events, so about \(100/\alpha\) negatives.
Evaluate the \(\mu = 2\) monitor at its \(10^{-3}\) threshold on 10,000 negatives and 10,000 positives. One run gives 1,350 true positives, interval \([0.1284, 0.1419]\), but only 10 false positives, interval \([0.00048, 0.00184]\): the FPR is known only to within a factor of two. To certify an FPR below \(10^{-3}\) at 95% confidence you need 2,995 negatives with no false positive at all.
The normal-approximation (Wald) interval is symmetric, too narrow for a skewed count, and collapses to \([0, 0]\) at \(k = 0\). Hoeffding’s interval uses only the range and ignores the tiny variance: its half-width here is 0.0136, over 13 times the rate. And a threshold tuned on the same data has a true FPR as uncertain as that interval, so choose it on one split and measure on another.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.7 Code
The normal trade-off curve and the Clopper–Pearson interval need only the standard library; bisection on the upper tail keeps precision when \(\alpha\) is tiny:
from collections.abc import Callable
from math import erfc, exp, lgamma, log, log1p, sqrt


def normal_cdf(x: float) -> float:
    return 0.5 * erfc(-x / sqrt(2))


def upper_quantile(a: float) -> float:
    """The point a standard normal exceeds with probability a, found by bisection on the tail."""
    lo, hi = -40.0, 40.0
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if 0.5 * erfc(mid / sqrt(2)) > a else (lo, mid)
    return lo


def gaussian_power(alpha: float, mu: float) -> float:
    """Best power at false positive rate alpha between N(0, 1) and N(mu, 1)."""
    return 1 - normal_cdf(upper_quantile(alpha) - mu)


def binom_cdf(k: int, n: int, p: float) -> float:
    """Pr[Binomial(n, p) <= k], summed in log space."""
    if p <= 0.0:
        return 1.0
    if p >= 1.0:
        return 1.0 if k >= n else 0.0
    total = 0.0
    for i in range(k + 1):
        log_pmf = lgamma(n + 1) - lgamma(i + 1) - lgamma(n - i + 1) + i * log(p) + (n - i) * log1p(-p)
        total += exp(log_pmf)
    return total


def clopper_pearson(k: int, n: int, confidence: float = 0.95) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Exact two-sided interval for a rate after k successes in n trials."""
    a = (1 - confidence) / 2

    def solve(f: Callable[[float], float], target: float) -> float:
        """The rate p at which f, a binomial CDF that falls as p grows, equals target."""
        lo, hi = 0.0, 1.0
        for _ in range(100):
            mid = (lo + hi) / 2
            lo, hi = (mid, hi) if f(mid) > target else (lo, mid)
        return lo

    # Lower end: Pr[Bin(n, l) >= k] = a, that is Pr[Bin(n, l) <= k - 1] = 1 - a.
    lower = 0.0 if k == 0 else solve(lambda p: binom_cdf(k - 1, n, p), 1 - a)
    # Upper end: Pr[Bin(n, u) <= k] = a.
    upper = 1.0 if k == n else solve(lambda p: binom_cdf(k, n, p), a)
    return lower, upper


print(f"{gaussian_power(0.05, 2.0):.4f} {gaussian_power(1e-3, 2.0):.4f}")  # 0.6388 0.1378
low, high = clopper_pearson(10, 10_000)
print(f"[{low:.5f}, {high:.5f}]")  # [0.00048, 0.00184]
print(f"{1 - 0.05 ** (1 / 3000):.3e}")  # 9.981e-04
The last line is the exact 95% upper bound after no events in 3,000 trials, close to the rule of three’s \(3/n\).

To find the best test, compute the likelihood ratio and threshold it.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.1 Why this matters
How much does an observation tell you about something you cannot see, such as the word “offer” about whether an email is spam? There are two honest answers, because there are two questions. How many bits does the observation save you, on average, when you describe the hidden value? Shannon entropy and mutual information answer that. How much more likely is a single best guess to be right? Min-entropy and vulnerability answer that.
Every quantity here is the logarithm of a probability, and the two families differ only in where the logarithm sits: Shannon’s quantities average the log over all outcomes, the one-guess quantities take the log of the best probability. Usually they agree. When a rare outcome reveals a lot they disagree by orders of magnitude, and knowing which to trust is the skill this chapter builds.
Logarithms are base 2, so quantities are in bits; one nat, the unit of natural logarithms, is \(1/\ln 2 \approx 1.443\) bits.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.2 Entropy
A measure of uncertainty should give a fair coin one unit and two independent fair coins two. Probabilities of independent events multiply, so to make uncertainties add you take a logarithm: an outcome of probability \(p(x)\) has surprisal \(\log(1/p(x))\), one bit for a fair coin’s heads, nothing for a certainty. Entropy is the average surprisal, \[H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x), \qquad 0 \le H(X) \le \log\lvert\mathcal X\rvert, \tag{5.1}\] zero for a constant and largest when all values are equally likely, since then no outcome is less surprising than another. For a coin with heads probability \(p\) it is the binary entropy \(h(p)\). The conditional entropy \(H(X \mid Y) = \sum_y p(y)\,H(X \mid Y = y)\) is the uncertainty left after seeing \(Y\), averaged over what you might see.
Take a spam filter. One email in eight is spam; every spam contains “offer”, and so does one ham email in seven. Before reading, \(H(X) = h(1/8) = 0.5436\) bits. If the word is absent the email is certainly ham: 0 bits. If it is present, which happens a quarter of the time, spam and ham are equally likely: a full bit, more than before. On average the word still helps, \(H(X \mid Y) = 0.25\) bits, because the common observation settles the question and the rare one only muddies it (Figure 5.1). So observing never increases uncertainty on average, \(H(X \mid Y) \le H(X)\), but a particular observation can.






Figure 5.1: Entropy of the spam label before observing the keyword, after each of the two possible observations, and on average. The rare observation raises the entropy above \(H(X)\) (dashed line); the average falls below it.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.3 Mutual information and data processing
What \(Y\) tells you about \(X\) is the drop in uncertainty it causes, the mutual information \[I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = D\big(P_{XY}\,\big\|\,P_XP_Y\big). \tag{5.2}\] The second form, a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (Divergences), says why it behaves as it does: \(Y\) helps exactly to the extent that the joint distribution differs from what independence would give. So it is non-negative, zero only under independence, and symmetric. For the keyword, \(I(X; Y) = 0.5436 - 0.25 = 0.2936\) bits.
The data processing inequality says that if \(Z\) is computed from \(Y\) alone, possibly with fresh randomness, then \(I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y)\). \(Z\) has no access to \(X\) except through \(Y\), so whatever it knows about \(X\) it learned from \(Y\), and the computation can only lose some on the way. Detect the keyword with a tokenizer that errs 10% of the time, and the feature keeps 0.1668 bits, 57% of the clean one. Denoising, feature extraction and training are all processing; they can make information easier to use, never larger. So a bound on the raw observation covers everything anyone computes from it.
But mutual information is an average over \(x\) and \(y\), and a small average can hide a few outcomes on which \(Y\) gives \(X\) away completely (Section 5.5).

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.4 Min-entropy and one-guess leakage
Someone with one guess does not care how many bits describe a value on average, only how likely their best guess is: the probability of the most likely value. That is the vulnerability, and its log the min-entropy, \[V(X) = \max_x p(x), \qquad H_\infty(X) = -\log V(X) \le H(X). \tag{5.3}\] A uniform 4-digit PIN has 13.2877 bits of both. If 10% of people choose 1234, the Shannon entropy barely moves, to 12.4278 bits, because the other 90% is still spread evenly and dominates the average. The min-entropy falls to 3.3219 bits: one guess in ten succeeds.
If the guesser sees \(Y\) first, the best strategy is the maximum a posteriori (MAP) guess, the value most likely given \(y\). On observation \(y\) it wins with probability \(\max_x p(x \mid y)\), and weighting by \(p(y)\) gives the posterior vulnerability, the sum of the largest entry in each column of the joint table: \[V(X \mid Y) = \sum_y\max_x p(x, y). \tag{5.4}\] The min-entropy leakage \(\mathcal L = \log\big(V(X \mid Y)/V(X)\big)\) is the factor by which the observation multiplies the chance of a correct first guess, in bits: 1 bit doubles it. For four secret values with prior \((0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1)\), observed through the channel of Section 5.7, a blind guess wins with probability 0.4 and the MAP guesser with 0.66 (Figure 5.2), a leakage of 0.7225 bits.






Figure 5.2: The joint distribution \(p(x, y) = \pi(x)C[x, y]\) of four secret values and three observations. The MAP guesser picks the boxed cell in each column, and its success probability is their sum \(V(X \mid Y) = 0.66\).



Because the formula is a success probability, two shortcuts are wrong. The guesser compares joint probabilities, not channel entries \(C[x, y] = p(y \mid x)\): on \(y_3\) it picks \(x_3\) over \(x_4\), which produces \(y_3\) more often, because \(x_3\) is twice as likely to begin with. And the log comes after averaging: averaging per-observation min-entropies gives 0.6548 bits instead of 0.5995, a number that is no guesser’s success rate. When you do not know the prior, use the worst case over priors, the min-capacity \(\log\sum_y\max_x C[x, y]\), which needs only the channel: 1.2630 bits here.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.5 Shannon against min-entropy leakage
Shannon leakage, the mutual information, and min-entropy leakage agree when every outcome reveals the same amount: reveal the lowest \(m\) bits of a uniform \(n\)-bit secret and both say \(m\). They disagree when a channel reveals everything on a few outcomes and nothing on the rest. Suppose it reveals the whole secret when its lowest \(j\) bits are zero, with probability \(2^{-j}\). Shannon averages the log, so that outcome’s \(n\) bits count with weight \(2^{-j}\): about \(2^{-j}n\) in all. The guesser, though, now wins whenever the reveal happens, so the success rate jumps from \(2^{-n}\) to more than \(2^{-j}\), a min-entropy leakage close to \(n - j\) (Figure 5.3).






Figure 5.3: Shannon leakage against min-entropy leakage for two families of deterministic channels on a uniform 64-bit secret. Revealing the low \(m\) bits gives equal leakages (diagonal). Revealing the whole secret with probability \(2^{-j}\) gives a small Shannon leakage but a min-entropy leakage close to \(64 - j\).



In Table 5.1, Shannon calls the first channel less leaky, yet a one-shot guesser does better against it by a factor of more than \(10^{15}\). When the adversary gets one try, use min-entropy.

Both measures still average over the secret, so neither says how exposed one value is. Revealing a 32-bit secret only when it is all zeros leaks \(7.786\times10^{-9}\) Shannon bits and 1 min-entropy bit, yet exposes that one value completely. Later parts build a worst-case measure.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.6 Fano’s inequality
Mutual information can also show that no estimator beats some error rate. Suppose a guess of \(X\) from \(Y\) is wrong with probability \(P_e\). The uncertainty left about \(X\) is then at most the uncertainty about whether the guess is right, \(h(P_e)\), plus, when it is wrong, which of the other \(M - 1\) values is true: \[H(X \mid Y) \le h(P_e) + P_e\log(M - 1), \qquad\text{so}\qquad P_e \ge \frac{H(X \mid Y) - 1}{\log M}. \tag{5.5}\] Solve the left form numerically; the right form bounds \(h(P_e)\) by 1 and is weaker. A label uniform over 8 classes (3 bits), with features carrying at most 1 bit, keeps at least 2 bits, so every classifier errs at least 0.3730 of the time (the weak form gives 0.3333).
For estimation, take \(M\) candidate parameters whose sample distributions are within KL divergence \(\kappa\) bits of each other: \(n\) samples carry at most \(n\kappa\) bits about which is true, so \(P_e \ge 1 - (n\kappa + 1)/\log M\). With 1024 candidates and \(\kappa = 0.01\), 100 samples leave \(P_e \ge 0.8000\) and 400 leave \(P_e \ge 0.5000\).
The bound is tight only when a wrong guess leaves the truth spread evenly over the other values. If errors go to one neighbour, little uncertainty remains after a wrong guess and Fano underestimates: shifting each of 8 symbols to its neighbour with probability 0.2 gives a bound of 0.0954 against a true MAP error of 0.2000.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.7 Code
Everything in Section 5.4 comes from the joint table. This computes the guessing example:
from math import log2

prior = [0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1]
channel = [  # channel[x][y] = probability of observation y given secret x
    [0.8, 0.2, 0.0],
    [0.1, 0.8, 0.1],
    [0.0, 0.5, 0.5],
    [0.0, 0.2, 0.8],
]


def joint(prior: list[float], channel: list[list[float]]) -> list[list[float]]:
    return [[px * c for c in row] for px, row in zip(prior, channel)]


def mutual_information(p: list[list[float]]) -> float:
    """Shannon leakage I(X; Y) in bits, from the joint table p[x][y]."""
    px = [sum(row) for row in p]
    py = [sum(col) for col in zip(*p)]
    return sum(
        pxy * log2(pxy / (px[x] * py[y]))
        for x, row in enumerate(p)
        for y, pxy in enumerate(row)
        if pxy > 0
    )


def posterior_vulnerability(p: list[list[float]]) -> float:
    """Success probability of the best one-shot guess after seeing y: sum of column maxima."""
    return sum(max(col) for col in zip(*p))


p = joint(prior, channel)
v_prior = max(prior)
v_post = posterior_vulnerability(p)
print(f"{v_prior:.4f} {v_post:.4f}")  # 0.4000 0.6600
print(f"{log2(v_post / v_prior):.4f}")  # 0.7225
print(f"{mutual_information(p):.4f}")  # 0.6865
print(f"{log2(sum(max(col) for col in zip(*channel))):.4f}")  # 1.2630
It prints the two vulnerabilities, the min-entropy leakage, the Shannon leakage and the min-capacity. The full edition’s script, information_theory.py, computes every number in this chapter:
uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/information_theory.py

\(0 \le H \le \log\lvert\mathcal X\rvert\)


Conditional entropy
\(H(X \mid Y) = \sum_y p(y)H(X \mid Y = y)\)
\(\le H(X)\) on average only


Mutual information
\(I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = D(P_{XY}\,\Vert\,P_XP_Y)\)
Symmetric; zero iff independent


Data processing
\(Z\) computed from \(Y\): \(I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y)\)
Bound the raw observation


Vulnerability, min-entropy
\(V(X) = \max_x p(x)\), \(H_\infty = -\log V\)
\(H_\infty \le H\)


Posterior vulnerability
\(V(X \mid Y) = \sum_y\max_x p(x, y)\)
Success of the MAP guesser


Min-entropy leakage
\(\log V(X \mid Y)/V(X)\)
1 bit doubles one-guess success


Min-capacity
\(\log\sum_y\max_x C[x, y]\)
Worst case over priors


Fano
\(H(X \mid Y) \le h(P_e) + P_e\log(M - 1)\)
Lower bound on any estimator’s error






Rules of thumb

Shannon quantities average logs; min-entropy quantities take the log of a best-case probability. Use the one that matches how many tries the adversary gets.
Both are averages over the secret; neither says how exposed a single value is.
Bound the raw observation: processing never adds information.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.1 Why this matters
Training a model minimizes the average loss over the training set, \(F(w) = \frac1n\sum_i\ell(w, z_i)\), over parameters \(w\), almost always with stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Two questions come up every time. How fast does SGD get there, and how should you set its step size when its gradients are noisy? And how much does the answer depend on any single training example: if you replace one and retrain, does the minimizer barely move, or can it jump?
Both answers come from a few constants of the loss: how steep it can be, how fast its slope can change, how strongly it curves upward, and how much the random gradients scatter. Every result here is a statement about them, so know which ones a result assumes, and whether your loss has them.

title: 6  Optimization
section: 6.2 Lipschitz, smooth and strongly convex losses
text:
6.2 Lipschitz, smooth and strongly convex losses
Four properties of the loss matter. A loss is \(L\)-Lipschitz when its gradient norm never exceeds \(L\), so moving the parameters by \(d\) changes the loss by at most \(Ld\). It is \(\beta\)-smooth when its gradient changes by at most \(\beta\) per unit of distance; then the tangent is a trustworthy guide for a step of about \(1/\beta\), and that is the largest safe step size. It is convex when its curvature is never negative, and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex when the curvature is at least \(\lambda\) in every direction; adding \(\frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\) to a convex loss makes it so.
The logistic loss \(\ln(1 + e^{-y\langle w, x\rangle})\), with features scaled to \(\|x\| \le 1\), is the standard example. Its slope is a probability times \(x\), so it is 1-Lipschitz; its curvature is \(p(1 - p) \le \frac14\), so it is \(\frac14\)-smooth. It is convex but not strongly convex, because far from the data it flattens out. A ridge term makes it \(\lambda\)-strongly convex and \((\frac14 + \lambda)\)-smooth.
Lipschitz and smooth bound different derivatives, so neither implies the other: \(|w|\) is 1-Lipschitz but its slope jumps at zero, and \(w^2/2\) is 1-smooth but its slope is unbounded. The parabola is the general case: a strongly convex function curves upward everywhere, so its slope grows at least in proportion to the distance from the minimizer, and it cannot be Lipschitz on all of \(\mathbb R^d\). The ridge-regularized logistic loss is therefore Lipschitz only on a ball \(\|w\| \le R\), with gradient at most \(1 + \lambda R\) there. Algorithms keep the iterates in the ball by projection, \(\Pi(u) = u\min(1, R/\|u\|)\), which never moves a point farther from anything inside the ball.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.3 SGD convergence
SGD steps against the gradient of one random example, or of a small random batch: cheap, right on average, but noisy. Even at the minimizer the individual gradients are not zero, so with a fixed step the iterates keep jumping around it. Averaging the iterates cancels the jumps; shrinking the step makes them smaller.
For a convex loss, the error of the averaged iterate after \(T\) steps of size \(\eta\), starting within \(R\) of the minimizer, with random gradients of mean squared size at most \(G^2\), is \[\mathbb E[F(\bar w_T)] - F^* \le \frac{R^2}{2\eta T} + \frac{\eta G^2}{2}. \tag{6.1}\] The two terms are a trade-off. The first is the cost of travelling the distance \(R\) with steps of size \(\eta\): small steps take long. The second is the jitter each step adds: large steps overshoot. Balancing them gives the best step \(\eta = R/(G\sqrt T)\) and an error of \(RG/\sqrt T\), with \(G = L\) for an \(L\)-Lipschitz loss. The bound holds for the average of the iterates, not the last one, so average.

The bound holds, loose by a factor of 11 at \(T = 100\) and 65 at \(T = 10{,}000\). The gap grows because the observed error falls much faster than \(1/\sqrt T\), closer to \(1/T\): the data curve the loss near the minimizer, and the convex bound does not know it. Every constant in a bound is a worst case the run does not reach, so trust how a bound scales, not its size.
Curvature is what speeds SGD up. On a \(\lambda\)-strongly convex loss, the farther the iterate is from the minimizer, the harder the gradient pulls it back, and with steps \(\eta_t = 2/(\lambda(t + 1))\) and an average that weights later iterates more, the error falls to \(2G^2/(\lambda(T + 1))\). The price is the \(1/\lambda\): a weak regularizer gives a fast rate only after many steps.
On a non-convex loss, such as a neural network’s, no gradient method can promise the global minimum. What smoothness guarantees is a point where the gradient is small: for a \(\beta\)-smooth loss that can fall at most \(\Delta\) from the start, with gradient variance \(\sigma^2\) and \(\eta \le 1/\beta\), \[\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E\|\nabla F(w_t)\|^2 \le \frac{2\Delta}{\eta T} + \beta\eta\sigma^2. \tag{6.2}\] It is the same trade-off, progress against noise, and a small gradient is all you get: the point may be a saddle or a poor local minimum.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.4 Gradient noise and minibatches
Every bound above pays for the mean squared size of the random gradients, which is the squared true gradient plus the variance of the estimate. Averaging a batch of \(B\) independent gradients divides the variance by \(B\), from \(\sigma_1^2\) to \(\sigma_1^2/B\), a little less when drawn without replacement. Noise of mean zero added to each gradient adds its mean squared size \(\sigma^2\): independent of the gradient and zero on average, it neither reinforces nor cancels it. So the convex bound holds with \(G^2 = L^2 + \sigma^2\): \[\eta^* = \frac{R}{\sqrt{(L^2 + \sigma^2)T}}, \qquad \frac{R\sqrt{L^2 + \sigma^2}}{\sqrt T}. \tag{6.3}\] To reach a fixed error, \(T\) must grow in proportion to \(L^2 + \sigma^2\), so noise multiplies the steps needed by \(1 + \sigma^2/L^2\). Noise of size \(\sigma = 3L\) makes that ten times as many.

Larger batches are not free either: a batch of \(B\) costs \(B\) gradient evaluations and divides the variance by \(B\), so per evaluation the gain cancels, and batches pay mainly through parallelism.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.5 Sensitivity of regularized ERM
The last question is about the problem, not the optimizer. Regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) returns the minimizer of \(J(w; D) = \frac1n\sum_i\ell(w, z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\). Replace one example: how far can the minimizer move?
The argument has two steps. Each example carries weight \(1/n\), and its gradient is at most \(L\) long, so swapping it changes the gradient of \(J\) at any point by at most \(2L/n\), the old one’s \(L/n\) out and the new one’s \(L/n\) in. At the old minimizer the new objective’s gradient is therefore at most \(2L/n\). Strong convexity says the gradient grows by at least \(\lambda\) per unit of distance from the minimizer, so a point where it is that small lies within \((2L/n)/\lambda\) of the new minimizer: \[\|w^*(D) - w^*(D')\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{6.4}\] The loss at any point then changes by at most \(L\) times that, \(2L^2/(\lambda n)\). Later parts call this movement a sensitivity.
With \(n = 1{,}000\) and \(\lambda = 0.1\) the bound is \(2/(0.1 \times 1{,}000) = 0.02\), and over 20 replacements in regularized logistic regression the largest observed move is \(6.66\times10^{-3}\): smaller, because real data add curvature of their own and two gradients rarely point in opposite directions at full length. Because one example weighs \(1/n\), ten times the data gives a tenth of the movement (Figure 6.1).






Figure 6.1: Left: largest observed movement of the regularized logistic minimizer when one of \(n\) examples is replaced (solid), against \(2L/(\lambda n)\) (dashed), for three values of \(\lambda\). Right: the same at \(n = 1000\) as a function of \(\lambda\): the bound blows up as \(\lambda \to 0\), while the observed movement levels off.



The argument shows what the bound needs. It is about the exact minimizer, so an optimizer stopped early adds its own error. And it needs the curvature: without a regularizer, the absolute loss gives the median, and on data made of 0s and 1s one replaced value can move it by 1 whatever \(n\) is. On a non-convex loss with two valleys, one label can flip which valley is deeper, and the minimizer of a double-well loss jumps by 2.0854 at \(n = 11\) and still by 2.0010 at \(n = 1{,}001\). For non-convex models, bound one example’s influence on the algorithm instead, such as a fixed number of SGD steps (Algorithmic stability and generalization).
