There the true effect is small, the noise in the shadow models swamps it, and the meta-classifier finds the separating direction badly: the attack is weaker than the best test, not the model safer. So an auditor should report the accuracy predicted from \(\kappa\) next to the measured one. Shadow models also need data from both groups, the victim’s algorithm and its dataset size, or they sample the wrong distribution.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.5 Neural networks and permutation invariance
Swap two hidden units of a network, with their incoming and outgoing weights, and it computes the same function. For tanh units, flipping the signs of a unit’s weights in and out also changes nothing, because tanh is odd. Training from a symmetric random start keeps these symmetries, so each weight slot holds a random one of the network’s units with a random sign. The property shows in which units the network has, not in which slot holds which, and averaging slot by slot washes it out: for tanh networks every raw weight has mean zero under both hypotheses, and a linear meta-classifier on raw weights is at chance (Ganju et al. 2018).
The fix is a representation that ignores order and sign. A canonical form flips each unit so its outgoing weight is positive and sorts the units by it; ReLU networks have no sign symmetry, so sorting alone suffices. It is fragile when two units have nearly equal outgoing weights, which swap places from one network to the next. A set representation sums a function of each unit’s parameter vector \(u_j\), and a sum ignores order; \(\sum_ju_ju_j^\top\) ignores signs too, and a learned DeepSets network (Zaheer et al. 2017) is the general form. Probe outputs, the model’s answers on fixed inputs, need no fix: they measure the function, which is what the property changes, and a function does not depend on how it is parameterized. Table 12.3 compares them on tanh networks with 4 hidden units, trained on 200 records with share 0.2 or 0.8, 150 shadow and 150 target networks per side.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.6 Code
The ceiling of Equation 12.1 and the two advantages of Section 12.3 take a few lines:
from math import erf, exp, lgamma, log, sqrt


def binom_pmf(n: int, t: float) -> list[float]:
    """Pr[Bin(n, t) = k] for k = 0..n, in log space so that large n does not overflow."""
    return [exp(lgamma(n + 1) - lgamma(k + 1) - lgamma(n - k + 1) + k * log(t) + (n - k) * log(1 - t)) for k in range(n + 1)]


def property_ceiling(n: int, t0: float, t1: float) -> float:
    """Best advantage of any property attack when the group is visible: TV(Bin(n, t0), Bin(n, t1))."""
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(p - q) for p, q in zip(binom_pmf(n, t0), binom_pmf(n, t1)))


def property_normal(n: int, t0: float, t1: float) -> float:
    """The normal approximation 2 Phi(sqrt(n) |t1 - t0| / (2 sqrt(tbar (1 - tbar)))) - 1."""
    tbar = (t0 + t1) / 2
    z = sqrt(n) * abs(t1 - t0) / (2 * sqrt(tbar * (1 - tbar)))
    return erf(z / sqrt(2))  # equals 2 Phi(z) - 1


def membership_best(n: int, t: float) -> float:
    """Best advantage for one subgroup record from the same count: (1 - t) max_k Pr[Bin(n - 1, t) = k]."""
    return (1 - t) * max(binom_pmf(n - 1, t))


print(f"{property_ceiling(100, 0.45, 0.55):.4f} {property_normal(100, 0.45, 0.55):.4f}")  # 0.6827 0.6827
print(f"{property_ceiling(1000, 0.45, 0.55):.4f} {property_normal(1000, 0.45, 0.55):.4f}")  # 0.9985 0.9984
print(f"{membership_best(100, 0.5):.4f} {membership_best(10000, 0.5):.4f}")  # 0.0398 0.0040

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.1 Why this matters
A language model trained on scraped text sees phone numbers, addresses, keys and private messages. Ask it to continue “Anna Smith’s phone number is” and it may finish with the real number. Nothing was breached: the number is stored in the weights and comes out through the normal interface. That is training-data extraction. Membership inference asks whether a record you already hold was in the training set; extraction hands the attacker the record itself, often one it did not know existed.
The idea that organizes the chapter is the rank of a secret under the model. A language model gives every string a probability. Fix the context in which a secret appears, say “my pin is”, and list every possible filler in order of the model’s probability, most likely first. The secret’s rank is its position in that list, and it is also the number of guesses an attacker needs if it tries the most likely fillers first. Memorization is the model putting a training string far above the strings that could have stood in its place. Every measure below reads that rank in its own way.
The examples use one toy: a contact list of 5,000 background lines like toneka 14524 (a made-up name and a five-digit pin), plus 600 secret lines, 100 each repeated 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 times. The model is a character \(n\)-gram model, which predicts each character from the previous \(n - 1\) by counting. Its order \(n\) plays the role of model size.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.2 Verbatim, approximate, discoverable, extractable
“The model memorized its training data” can mean several things, and the numbers differ by orders of magnitude between them, so a report must say which it measures. The definitions differ in what the attacker is assumed to know. A string is extractable (Carlini et al. 2021) if some prompt makes greedy decoding, which appends the most likely next symbol at each step, emit it. That is the real attacker, who has only the model, but measuring it means searching over all prompts. A suffix is discoverable (Carlini et al. 2023) if prompting with its own training prefix makes greedy decoding emit it. That assumes an attacker who holds the prefix, which is strong, but it is easy to measure: prompt with each training prefix and compare. Discoverable implies extractable, since the prefix is one prompt among all. A string is \(k\)-eidetic if it is extractable and appears in at most \(k\) training documents; small \(k\) is the worrying case, a secret seen once and given back.
The definitions also differ in how close the output must be. The ones above are verbatim; a string is approximately memorized (Ippolito et al. 2023) if the output is within some distance of it. Verbatim matching misses near copies, and a phone number with one digit changed has still leaked to anyone who reads it. Ippolito et al. show that prompts which change the style slip approximate copies past a filter that blocks verbatim training text. A verbatim rate is therefore a lower bound on the leak, not a measure of it, and a verbatim filter is not a defence.
Greedy decoding is a convenience for measurement; deployed models sample. A string greedy decoding never emits can still come out. If one sample reproduces it with probability \(p\), then \(m\) independent samples all miss it with probability \((1 - p)^m\), which is at most \(e^{-pm}\), so \[m \ge \frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{p} \tag{13.1}\] samples extract it with probability at least \(1 - \beta\). The budget is inversely proportional to \(p\): a string with probability \(10^{-3}\) after its prefix comes out with 99% confidence (\(\beta = 0.01\)) within about 4,600 samples. In the toy, an order-5 model reproduces a secret’s pin in one sample with probability \(1.4\times10^{-3}\) on average at 4 copies and 0.142 at 32 copies, which means 3,252 and 31 samples for a 99% chance. Duplication made the search trivial.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.3 Duplication and model size
Which strings get memorized? In the \(n\)-gram toy the answer can be read off the counts. Greedy decoding follows the largest count at each step, so memorization is a vote. Each copy of a training line adds one vote for the line’s own next symbol in every context the line passes through. The line comes out when, at every step, its votes beat the strongest rival from the rest of the corpus, so the number of copies it needs, \(k^*\), is its largest gap to a rival plus one, set by its most contested step. The fraction of lines memorized at \(k\) copies is the fraction with \(k^* \le k\); this matched greedy decoding exactly in all 36 cells of Table 13.1, because it is a restatement of what greedy decoding does with counts.
Model size works by splitting the vote. A longer context is a finer partition of the training positions: fewer positions share a given context of length 7 than of length 2. So rival counts shrink as the order grows, while the line’s own \(k\) votes stay with it in every context it passes through. In the limit every line has contexts of its own and is memorized from a single copy. That is the toy version of “larger models memorize more”: a larger model can afford to give rare strings parameters of their own.
Table 13.1 shows both effects. Along a row, at order 5, the verbatim rate climbs from 0 at one copy to 0.70 at 32. Down a column, a line seen once is safe up to order 5, memorized 8% of the time at order 6, 70% at order 7 and 98% at order 8; those singletons are 1-eidetic.

For real models, Carlini et al. (2023) found that discoverable memorization grows log-linearly with duplication, model size and prompt length, and that the largest model they measured, GPT-J, reproduces at least 1% of its training data from 50-token prefixes.
The vote picture also says who is exposed first. A line whose name shares little with other names reaches a context of its own sooner, so rare and atypical strings are memorized first; this is the high self-influence of atypical examples from Algorithmic stability and generalization, which can only be fitted by memorizing them. Deduplication lowers \(k\) for every repeated string, so it is the cheapest defence: Lee et al. (2022) found that models trained on deduplicated data emit memorized text about ten times less often without losing quality. But it cannot touch a singleton in a large model, where \(k = 1\) already suffices; deduplicating the order-8 model’s data would barely change its 98%. And because larger models memorize from fewer copies, an audit passed at one size must be redone after scaling up.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.4 Canaries and the exposure metric
Discoverable memorization is all or nothing; an auditor wants a graded answer with a known false alarm rate. Carlini et al. (2019) plant canaries, random secrets of a fixed format such as “my pin is” followed by five random digits, in the training data, then read off the trained model’s rank of the canary among all values of that format. Because you chose the canary at random, you know the answer and the size of the space \(\mathcal R\). The exposure reads the rank on a log scale, \[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) = \log_2|\mathcal R| - \log_2\operatorname{rank}(\hat r). \tag{13.2}\] Before seeing the model, an attacker guessing the canary faces \(|\mathcal R|\) equally likely values; guessing in the model’s order, it needs \(\operatorname{rank}\) tries. Exposure is the difference in bits, the number of halvings of the search the model has done for the attacker.
What makes exposure an audit tool is that its behaviour without memorization is known exactly. If the model does not depend on the canary, for instance because it was never inserted, the canary is just a uniformly random value, so its rank is uniform over the list. The chance of landing in the top fraction \(2^{-e}\) of the list is then \(2^{-e}\): \[\Pr[\mathrm{exposure} \ge e] \le 2^{-e}. \tag{13.3}\] So exposure is \(-\log_2\) of a p-value, and the test “inserted if exposure \(\ge e\)” has false positive rate (FPR) at most \(2^{-e}\). “Was this canary inserted?” is a membership question, but where membership inference calibrates its test with shadow models, here the canary’s own randomness does the calibration. In the toy, uninserted pins show mean exposure 1.443 bits, the \(\log_2 e\) the uniform rank predicts, and a fraction \(1/32 = 2^{-5}\) with exposure at least 5.
For “my pin is 58745”, \(|\mathcal R| = 10^5\) and the maximum exposure is 16.61 bits. Table 13.2 gives the exact exposure, from scoring all \(10^5\) pins. The order-4 model reaches the maximum at 16 copies. The order-2 model barely moves even at 64, because its one-character contexts are shared with every line, the vote-splitting argument run backwards.

For a large space the rank must be estimated. Counting how many of \(m\) random candidates score above the canary is reliable, but a canary above all of them only says its rank fraction is below about \(1/m\), so it cannot resolve exposures above \(\log_2 m\). Fitting a distribution to the scores reaches further, but only as far as its tail is right, and the tail is the part you cannot sample. At order 3 with 8 copies, counting 10,000 random pins gives 5.35 bits against an exact 5.24, while a normal fit gives 8.28, because the scores have a heavier right tail than a normal. Ties are a further trap: a model that has never seen a context gives every candidate the same score, so every rank is the last and every exposure 0, which hides rather than measures.
Because you control what was planted, use canaries to compare training runs that differ in one thing: with and without deduplication, before and after an unlearning method, or with private training (Part 3). Carlini et al. (2019) found that differentially private training kept their canaries at the exposure of canaries never inserted.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.5 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
text:
13.5 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
A real attacker has only the model. Carlini et al. (2021) extracted training data from GPT-2 in three steps: generate many samples, rank them by how likely they are to be memorized, and verify the top of the ranking against a search or public sources. The ranking is the hard step, and it is a hypothesis test. A model can find a string likely because text like it is common, or because it memorized it, and only the second is a leak. Ranking by the target’s likelihood alone surfaces the common, such as licences and boilerplate, which reveal nothing. A reference model, trained on similar data that excludes the target’s training set, stands in for “common text”, and the right score is how much more likely the target finds \(x\) than the reference does: \[\Lambda(x) = \ln p_\theta(x) - \ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x). \tag{13.4}\] Text both models know cancels. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma of Hypothesis testing, this likelihood ratio is the most powerful ranking at every FPR; it is the per-example calibration of membership inference again. The reference can be crude: a smaller model of the same family, the zlib-compressed length of the text, or the target’s own likelihood on the lowercased text.
In the toy, the attacker draws 20,000 lines from the order-6 model, whose training set also contains 50 public lines repeated 100 times each. Among the 14,852 distinct samples are 197 private training lines. Of the top 100 by likelihood only 45 are private, since the public lines are the most likely strings the model knows. Ranked by Equation 13.4, with a reference trained on an independent contact list that also contains the public lines, 85 of the top 100 are private (Figure 13.2).






Figure 13.2: Fraction of the top-ranked distinct generations that are private training lines (solid) or public lines (dashed), from 20,000 samples of an order-6 model. Ranking by likelihood puts the public lines first; ranking by the likelihood ratio to a reference model puts the private lines first.



Without the prefix the attacker gets much less than is discoverable: none of the secrets inserted 1, 2 or 4 times appear in the samples, though 76% of the 4-copy secrets are discoverable at order 6. A sample must first produce the right name before it can produce the pin, and only heavily duplicated lines make their names likely enough.
“Less than discoverable” can still be a great deal. Nasr et al. (2023) attacked an aligned chat model, which rarely emits training data in normal use because alignment taught it to answer as an assistant, not to continue documents. Asked to repeat a single word forever, it diverged into text that looked like pretraining documents; about 200 US dollars of queries extracted over 10,000 unique memorized examples, including personal contact details. Alignment changed how the model usually responds, not what it had memorized, so it is not a defence, and a red team should test prompts that escape the chat behaviour. Verify outputs against the training set, or against a large public corpus as a lower bound. Report precision at the top of the ranking, which is the low-FPR operating point an attacker checking candidates by hand cares about, not recall over all memorized strings.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.1 Why this matters
A phone keyboard learns from what its users type, and the raw text never leaves the phones. The server sends the current model to each phone, the phone computes the gradient of the loss on its own few examples, and only that gradient goes back. This is federated learning (FL), often described as private because “the data stay on the device”. If you design, review or red-team such a system, the question is: what does one client’s gradient reveal about the client’s data?
Often, everything, because many entries of a gradient are simple functions of the input. Take a fully connected layer, which computes \(a = Wx + b\). The weight \(W_{jk}\) multiplies the input \(x_k\), so nudging \(W_{jk}\) changes \(a_j\) by \(x_k\) times the nudge, and the loss responds to \(a_j\) at some rate \(\delta_j = \partial\ell/\partial a_j\) set by everything above the layer. The chain rule multiplies the two rates, and the bias, which is added to \(a_j\) directly, gets \(\delta_j\) alone: \[\nabla_W\ell = \delta\,x^\top, \qquad \nabla_b\ell = \delta. \tag{14.1}\] The weight gradient is an outer product: row \(j\) is the input \(x\) scaled by the single number \(\delta_j\), so the layer’s input sits in every row. The rest of the network, the loss and the label only set the scales. With one example the scale can be divided out; with a batch the gradient is a sum of one outer product per example, and the attacker’s job is to pull the sum apart.
The attacker here is an honest-but-curious server in the sense of Threat models and privacy games: it follows the protocol, sends the real model and only analyses what it receives. It knows the architecture and every parameter, because it chose them, and it sees each client’s update \(g = \frac1B\sum_i\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i, y_i)\), the average gradient over the client’s \(B\) examples. Reconstructions are scored by the relative error \(\lVert\hat x - x\rVert/\lVert x\rVert\) against the closest true example. The experiments use \(8\times8\) images of four shapes and a network with one hidden layer of 32 units at its random initialization: 2,212 gradient entries against 64 unknown pixels per example.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.2 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
text:
14.2 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
For a single example, Equation 14.1 already gives the attack (Phong et al. 2018). Row \(j\) of the first layer’s weight gradient is \(\delta_{1,j}x^\top\), and entry \(j\) of its bias gradient is the same number \(\delta_{1,j}\), so dividing one by the other cancels the only unknown scale. Every unit \(j\) with a nonzero bias gradient gives \[x = \frac{(\nabla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:}}{(\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j}. \tag{14.2}\] No search, no prior on the data and no label are needed, and the attack checks itself: all usable units must give the same answer, so if their ratios agree, the attacker knows it has the input.
Take a two-unit ReLU network with \(W_1 = \begin{pmatrix}0.4 & -0.2 & 0.1\\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.4\end{pmatrix}\), \(b_1 = (0.1, -0.1)\), \(W_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\ 0.5 & 0.5\end{pmatrix}\) and no output bias, and an input \(x = (0.5, 1, 0.2)\) with the first class as label. The backward signal at the first layer is \(\delta_1 = (-0.3279, 0.9838)\), so the two rows of the weight gradient are \((-0.1640, -0.3279, -0.0656)\) and \((0.4919, 0.9838, 0.1968)\), visibly the same vector at two scales. Dividing each by its bias entry gives \((0.5, 1, 0.2)\) twice; Section 14.6 runs it. On an \(8\times8\) image and the 32-unit network, 13 units are switched on, and each of the 13 ratios equals the image to a relative error of at most \(6.7\times10^{-17}\), rounding error (Figure 14.1).






Figure 14.1: Exact recovery from the first-layer gradient of a ReLU network with 32 hidden units. Left: the client’s input. Middle: the weight gradient, one row per hidden unit, next to the bias gradient; every nonzero row is the image times its bias entry, and switched-off units give zero rows. Right: one row divided by its bias entry, which is the input exactly.



Because the division cancels \(\delta_1\), whatever produced \(\delta_1\) is irrelevant: twenty layers above the first, or a custom loss, change nothing. A ReLU unit switched off on \(x\) has \(\delta_{1,j} = 0\) and gives nothing, but one active unit is enough. Without a bias there is no denominator, yet every row still points along \(x\), so \(x\) is known up to one number that a one-dimensional search finds. The same division at a deeper fully connected layer yields that layer’s input, an intermediate feature vector. What really breaks the closed form is a convolutional first layer: a convolution applies one small filter at every position of the image, so its gradient is a sum of outer products over all the image patches, and no single division separates them. A batch of more than one example is a sum too, and breaks it only partly (Section 14.5).

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.3 Label recovery from the last layer
text:
14.3 Label recovery from the last layer
The label is often the most sensitive part of an example (the diagnosis, the next word typed), and the last layer gives it away by a sign (Zhao, Mopuri & Bilen 2020). With softmax and cross-entropy, the backward signal at the logits is the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot label, \(p - e_y\). Softmax probabilities lie strictly between 0 and 1, so every entry is positive except the one at the true label, \(p_y - 1\). By Equation 14.1 the last-layer bias gradient is exactly this signal, so for one example the label is the position of its only negative entry: \[y = \arg\min_k(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.3}\] Without a bias the weight gradient tells the same story: its row \(k\) is the signal’s entry \(k\) times the hidden activations, and if those are never negative (ReLU or sigmoid) the multiplication keeps the sign, so the label is the only row with a negative sum. Both rules were right in 1,000 of 1,000 trials. Nothing in the argument depends on how good the model is, so they are exact at any point of training; only a probability that rounds to 1 in floating point hides the sign.
For a batch of \(B\), the bias gradient is the average of \(p_i - e_{y_i}\). The one-hot parts add up to the label histogram, and the probability parts to the model’s total predicted probability for each class, so the number \(n_k\) of examples of class \(k\) is \[n_k = \sum_{i=1}^Bp_{ik} - B\,(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.4}\] The equation is exact; the only unknown is the total prediction \(\sum_ip_{ik}\). The attacker knows the model, so it estimates that total as \(B\) times the model’s average prediction on data of its own, and rounds. Since true counts are integers, rounding is exact whenever the estimate is off by less than one half for every class.
A batch of 16 has true counts \((4, 2, 4, 6)\). With the average prediction taken over 200 of the attacker’s own images, Equation 14.4 gives \((3.88, 2.00, 4.19, 5.92)\), which rounds to the truth. Assuming the model predicts every class equally gives \((2.12, 3.01, 4.27, 6.60)\), which does not, because even an untrained network is not uniform. Over 200 random batches, the averaged estimate gets all counts exact for 1.000 of batches of 4, 0.975 of batches of 16 and 0.525 of batches of 64 (Figure 14.2): the error of the estimate grows with \(B\), and once it passes one half, rounding starts to miss, though the counts stay close.






Figure 14.2: Labels from the last-layer bias gradient. Left: for one example it has a single negative entry, at the true label. Right: for a batch of 16, the counts estimated with the model’s average prediction on the attacker’s own images are close to the true counts; with a uniform guess they are off by up to about half an example.



So a batch leaks its label histogram even when no input is recovered. And knowing the label helps the next attack: it removes a discrete unknown, so the search of Section 14.4 runs over the input only.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.4 Deep Leakage from Gradients
Convolutions, normalization layers or missing biases leave no closed form. Deep Leakage from Gradients (DLG) (Zhu, Liu & Han 2019) needs none: guess an input, compute the gradient it would produce, and move the guess until that gradient matches the one observed. If only the true input produces the observed gradient, a matching guess is the input. With the labels fixed as above, DLG minimizes the matching loss, the squared distance between the gradient of the guessed batch and \(g\): \[\hat x = \arg\min_{x'}R(x'), \qquad R(x') = \Big\lVert\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i', y_i) - g\Big\rVert^2. \tag{14.5}\] It starts from random noise and runs a gradient method on \(R\), which automatic differentiation provides by differentiating through the backward pass.
Two consequences follow from that construction. Since \(R\) is built from gradients, its own gradient is made of second derivatives of the network. ReLU’s slope is constant on each side of zero, so its second derivative is zero almost everywhere and the search gets no signal through it; that is why Zhu et al. replaced ReLU by the sigmoid, as the experiments here do. And since the true input has \(R = 0\), the smallest possible value, the final \(R\) reports the outcome: at rounding error the match is exact, while a loss that stopped falling well above zero means the search is stuck, because \(R\) is not convex.
On one image, the sigmoid network with 32 hidden units, and 600 steps of the Adam optimizer from uniform noise, the relative error is \(7.5\times10^{-2}\) at step 50, already visually correct, and \(5.8\times10^{-14}\) at step 600, with matching loss \(1.3\times10^{-27}\) (Figure 14.3).






Figure 14.3: Deep Leakage from Gradients on one image, sigmoid network with 32 hidden units. Top: the reconstruction at selected iterations, starting from noise, and the true input. Bottom: the matching loss and the relative error on a log scale; both fall until they reach rounding error.



A failed run is therefore an optimization failure, not evidence of privacy, and the attacker sees it and retries with restarts, better optimizers or image priors. Geiping et al. (2020), comparing gradients by cosine distance and penalizing differences between neighbouring pixels, recover recognizable images from trained networks and from batches.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.5 Batches and averaging
Clients usually send a batch average, and averaging is often said to protect individuals: the gradient describes the batch, not anyone in it. Averaging does break Equation 14.2 and makes DLG harder, but the outer-product structure survives it.
The first-layer gradient is now a sum of \(B\) outer products, one per example. Every row is a combination of the \(B\) inputs, and the matrix has rank at most \(B\), so the server learns the subspace that contains the batch, which for \(B\) much smaller than the input dimension already rules out almost every input. A unit’s ratio from Equation 14.2 is now a weighted average of the inputs, each weighted by its share of the unit’s backward signal, and it equals one input exactly when the unit is active for that example only, when it isolates it. If each of \(m\) ReLU units fires on each example like an independent fair coin, a unit isolates a given example with probability \(2^{-B}\), and the example escapes only if all \(m\) units miss it: \[P_{\text{iso}}(B, m) = 1 - (1 - 2^{-B})^m. \tag{14.6}\] Each extra example halves the chance per unit, and each extra unit adds a chance. An even chance at \(B = 10\) needs 710 units, and real first layers have thousands.
A batch of 4 through the 32-unit ReLU network gives a rank-4 gradient, and the unit ratios recover all 4 images exactly, where the formula predicts 0.873 per example. Table 14.1 tests the formula more widely. For Gaussian inputs, whose units really do fire like coins, it matches. For images it is far too optimistic about privacy at large batches: at \(B = 16\) in the 1024-unit network it predicts 1.6% exposed, and 69.1% is. Images are correlated, so a unit tends to fire on many of them or on few, and units that fire on exactly one are much more common than coin flips allow (Figure 14.4).

DLG has to untangle \(B\) inputs from one sum. On the sigmoid network it recovers all single images, 0.67 of examples in batches of 2, 0.29 at \(B = 4\) and none at \(B = 8\), where the matching loss stalls near \(10^{-5}\) and the reconstructions are blends. That is a stuck search, not missing information: 2,212 equations remain.
So batching is not a defence. The label histogram, the span and every isolated example come out exactly. Sending the parameter change after several local steps does not help either: every step’s first-layer gradient is built from outer products with the same inputs, so for one example the change is still a multiple of \(x^\top\) in every row, and the division still recovers \(x\). And all of this is what an honest server can do with random weights. A malicious server chooses the weights, and can plant units that fire on rare inputs only (Boenisch et al. 2023) or that sort inputs into bins by a feature (Fowl et al. 2022), so that most of a large batch is isolated by design. Defences have to change what the server sees: differential privacy (Part 3) bounds what any update reveals, and secure aggregation, which reveals only the sum over many clients, is introduced in Local, shuffle and distributed trust models.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.6 Code
The hand example of Section 14.2, with the label rule and the isolation formula, in plain Python. The script indexes classes from 0, so label 0 is the first class.
from math import ceil, exp, log

Vector = list[float]
Matrix = list[Vector]


def client_gradient(w1: Matrix, b1: Vector, w2: Matrix, x: Vector, y: int) -> tuple[Matrix, Vector, Vector]:
    """What a client sends for one example: the gradients of W1, b1 and b2 (one ReLU layer, softmax, cross-entropy)."""
    a = [sum(wk * xk for wk, xk in zip(row, x)) + bj for row, bj in zip(w1, b1)]
    h = [max(aj, 0.0) for aj in a]
    z = [sum(wk * hk for wk, hk in zip(row, h)) for row in w2]
    total = sum(exp(zk) for zk in z)
    delta2 = [exp(zk) / total - (1.0 if k == y else 0.0) for k, zk in enumerate(z)]  # p - e_y
    delta1 = [sum(delta2[k] * w2[k][j] for k in range(len(w2))) * (1.0 if a[j] > 0 else 0.0) for j in range(len(a))]
    grad_w1 = [[dj * xk for xk in x] for dj in delta1]  # outer product delta1 x^T
    return grad_w1, delta1, delta2  # the bias gradients equal the backward signals


def recover_input(grad_w1: Matrix, grad_b1: Vector) -> Vector:
    """Exact recovery: a row of the weight gradient divided by its bias entry."""
    j = next(j for j, g in enumerate(grad_b1) if g != 0.0)
    return [g / grad_b1[j] for g in grad_w1[j]]


def recover_label(grad_b2: Vector) -> int:
    """The only negative entry of the last-layer bias gradient is the label."""
    return min(range(len(grad_b2)), key=lambda k: grad_b2[k])


def isolation(batch: int, units: int) -> float:
    """Chance that some ReLU unit fires for one given example of the batch only, under the coin-flip model."""
    return 1 - (1 - 2.0**-batch) ** units


def width_for_even_odds(batch: int) -> int:
    """Smallest number of units that isolates each example with probability at least 1/2."""
    return ceil(log(2) / -log(1 - 2.0**-batch))


w1 = [[0.4, -0.2, 0.1], [0.3, 0.5, -0.4]]
b1 = [0.1, -0.1]
w2 = [[1.0, -1.0], [0.5, 0.5]]
gw1, gb1, gb2 = client_gradient(w1, b1, w2, x=[0.5, 1.0, 0.2], y=0)
print([round(v, 4) for v in recover_input(gw1, gb1)])  # [0.5, 1.0, 0.2]
print([round(v, 4) for v in gb2], recover_label(gb2))  # [-0.6559, 0.6559] 0
print(f"{isolation(4, 32):.3f}")  # 0.873
print(width_for_even_odds(10))  # 710
The full edition’s script runs every attack in this chapter on the image network, including DLG with a hand-written double backpropagation, in about half a minute:
uv run python code/part02-attacks/gradient_inversion.py

Rules of thumb

One example through a fully connected layer with a bias: the input costs one division, the label one sign.

An honest server can already do all of this; a malicious one can do it for large batches by design. Protect updates with differential privacy and secure aggregation, not with batching or local steps.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.8 Further reading

Zhu, Liu & Han, “Deep Leakage from Gradients” (NeurIPS 2019): the gradient-matching attack on images and text.
Geiping, Bauermeister, Dröge & Moeller, “Inverting Gradients — How easy is it to break privacy in federated learning?” (NeurIPS 2020): cosine matching with an image prior, and attacks on trained networks, local steps and batches.
Huang, Gupta, Song, Li & Arora, “Evaluating Gradient Inversion Attacks and Defenses in Federated Learning” (NeurIPS 2021): how attack strength depends on assumptions such as known labels and untrained models; read it before trusting a published attack number.
Boenisch, Dziedzic, Schuster, Shamsabadi, Shumailov & Papernot, “When the Curious Abandon Honesty: Federated Learning Is Not Private” (IEEE EuroS&P 2023): trap weights and exact recovery from large batches by a malicious server.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.1 Why this matters
A hospital shares its discharge records with researchers after deleting names and addresses, keeping postcode, date of birth, sex and diagnosis. But most people are the only person with their postcode, birth date and sex, so anyone holding a table with names and those three columns, such as a voter roll, can join the two and put a name back on most rows. This is a linkage attack, and naming a “de-identified” record is re-identification. It needs only the release and some auxiliary data, so run it before you sign off on sharing a dataset.
What makes it work is that identifying information is measured in bits, and bits add up. Picking one person out of \(n\) takes \(\log_2 n\) bits, because each bit halves the candidates: 27.9 bits for the 248.7 million people in the United States in 1990, 32.9 for 8 billion. An attribute with \(v\) equally likely values carries at most \(\log_2 v\) bits, and for independent attributes the bits add, because probabilities multiply and the logarithm turns the product into a sum. Once the bits an adversary knows exceed \(\log_2 n\) by a few, almost everyone is unique.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.2 Quasi-identifiers and the linkage attack
Direct identifiers, such as a name, name a person on their own. Sensitive attributes, such as a diagnosis, are what the release is about. Quasi-identifiers sit in between: they name nobody alone, but in combination they single people out, and they also appear in other datasets next to names. ZIP code, birth date and sex are the classic example. Deleting the first kind and keeping the third is the most common form of “de-identification”, and linkage is aimed at exactly that gap.
Group the records of a release into equivalence classes, sets of records with identical quasi-identifiers. An adversary who knows the target is in the release, and knows the target’s quasi-identifiers, finds the target’s class and picks a record from it: right for sure if the class has one record, one time in \(k\) if it has \(k\). Each class therefore contributes exactly one record’s worth of wins however large it is, and the best possible success is \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n}, \tag{15.1}\] the number \(J\) of distinct quasi-identifier combinations divided by the number \(n\) of records.

Join Table 15.1 with Table 15.2. Ana, Carla and Dan are each alone in their class, so their diagnoses come out with certainty; Ben shares his class with one other record, so the adversary is right about him half the time. The classes have sizes 1, 1, 1, 2 and 3, so \(J = 5\) for \(n = 8\) and the success is \(5/8 = 0.625\). Sweeney re-identified the governor of Massachusetts this way in the late 1990s: on the Cambridge voter roll, six people shared his birth date, three were men, and one lived in his ZIP code.
Every unique record is a certain win, so the fraction of unique records is a floor on the success, and predicting uniqueness is the core of a risk assessment. Conversely, if every class has at least \(k\) records then \(J \le n/k\) and the success is at most \(1/k\). That is the promise of k-anonymity, and it holds against this adversary only: had all three women born on 1990-01-01 had asthma, the adversary would learn it without picking a record, the gap studied in Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks. And which columns are quasi-identifiers is not a property of the table but a guess about what auxiliary data exist; in sparse data, every column is one (Section 15.4).

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.3 How many people are unique?
To predict uniqueness for a release not yet made, use a model of the population. Call a person’s combination of attribute values their cell, and suppose each person falls in cell \(c\) with probability \(p_c\), independently. A person in cell \(c\) is unique when all \(n - 1\) others land elsewhere, which happens with probability \((1 - p_c)^{n-1}\); averaging over the person’s own cell gives the expected fraction unique, \[\frac{\mathbb E U}{n} = \sum_c p_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}. \tag{15.2}\]
With \(M\) equally likely cells this becomes the bits picture. Each person stays alone with probability about \(e^{-n/M}\), where \(n/M\) is the average occupancy of a cell. With \(b = \log_2 M\) bits the occupancy is \(2^{\log_2 n - b}\), so the fraction unique is about \(\exp(-2^{\log_2 n - b})\): it depends only on the bits beyond the \(\log_2 n\) needed to name one person, the same curve for a town and for the planet (Figure 15.1, right). Every extra bit halves the occupancy, so the curve is steep: half the people are unique at 0.53 bits beyond \(\log_2 n\), 99% at 6.64 bits beyond.
So “33 bits identify anyone” is misleading: 33 bits for 8 billion people put about one person in the average cell, where only a fraction 0.394 is unique, because random labels collide often. 99% uniqueness takes 39.5 bits.
Sweeney’s attributes show the accounting. About 40,000 ZIP codes are worth 15.3 bits, a birth date over 80 years 14.8, and sex 1.0: at most 31.1 bits against the 27.9 that single out one American, so about 0.106 people per cell and a uniqueness of \(e^{-0.106} = 0.899\) if cells were equally likely. From 1990 census tables she estimated 87%. The gap is skew: people crowd into popular cells, which hold nobody unique, while rare cells stay empty. Correlation pulls the same way, because correlated attributes (ZIP code and income) say partly the same thing, so their joint bits are less than the sum. A bits sum is a quick screen, not an estimate. Table 15.3 reveals the attributes of a synthetic census of 10,000 people one at a time (\(\log_2 n = 13.29\) bits).

With 12.90 bits, just under \(\log_2 n\), a third of people are unique; about 7 bits beyond it, 97.5% are. The uniform model overstates uniqueness, by up to 0.27, because the attributes are skewed: a few large regions hold many people, who are not unique. A floor that never overstates comes from the collision probability \(\sum_c p_c^2\), the chance that two random people share a cell: \(\mathbb E U/n \ge (1 - \sum_c p_c^2)^{n-1}\). For independent attributes it is a product over columns, since two people share a cell exactly when they agree on every attribute, so the floor needs only each column’s frequencies. It is loose when a few crowded cells hold most people and tight once most cells are nearly empty. For a real audit, compute Equation 15.2 from a model of the joint distribution, such as the Gaussian copula of Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye (2019).

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
section: 15.4 Sparse, high-dimensional data: the Netflix attack
text:
15.4 Sparse, high-dimensional data: the Netflix attack
In 2006 Netflix released about 100 million ratings by 480,189 subscribers, names replaced by random numbers. There are no columns to join on, and what an adversary knows (“she watched these films around these dates”) is partial and noisy, so the release looks safe. Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008) showed that it is not, by the same accounting. Most films are rated by few people, so each film in a record carries many bits: one rated by 1% of subscribers is worth \(\log_2 100 = 6.64\) bits, and three such films carry 19.9 bits, more than the 18.9 that single out a subscriber.
Since no record matches exactly, the attack scores every record by how well it agrees with the auxiliary information \(\mathrm{aux}\), item by item: \[\mathrm{Score}(\mathrm{aux}, r) = \sum_{i \in \mathrm{aux}} w_i\,\mathrm{Sim}(\mathrm{aux}_i, r_i), \tag{15.3}\] where \(\mathrm{Sim}\) is 1 if record \(r\) agrees on item \(i\) (say, within one star) and 0 otherwise. Rarer items get larger weights, because agreeing on a film half the subscribers rated says little and agreeing on an obscure one says a lot; Narayanan and Shmatikov used \(w_i = 1/\ln\lvert\mathrm{supp}(i)\rvert\), with \(\lvert\mathrm{supp}(i)\rvert\) the number of records that rated item \(i\). The likelihood ratio of “target” against “unrelated” gives the principled version, \(w_i \approx \ln(1/s_i) + \ln\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\), with \(s_i\) the chance an unrelated record agrees on item \(i\) and \(\varepsilon\) the chance the adversary is wrong about it. Because the score adds up evidence, noise costs little: a wrong item costs the target one term, and unrelated records rarely gain one. On Netflix, 8 ratings of which 2 may be wrong, with dates known within 14 days, identify 99% of records.

A synthetic matrix of 5,000 users with Netflix-like density shows the bits deciding (Table 15.4). An item carries a median of 5.83 bits against \(\log_2 5000 = 12.29\) needed, so two items fall a little short and re-identify about 43% of targets, while four clear the bar and re-identify 93%. The weighting barely matters except when some items are wrong: then equal weights drop to 94%, because a wrong popular item lets many unrelated records score. For a defender, perturbing a few values does not protect sparse data; the score needs a margin, not a perfect match.
If the target might not be in the release, the adversary must also decide when to trust the top score. The eccentricity test declares a match only when the best score \(s_1\) stands out from the second best \(s_2\), in standard deviations \(\sigma\) of all scores: \((s_1 - s_2)/\sigma \ge \varphi\). How often an outsider’s top score stands out by chance depends on the score distribution, so no threshold is safe in the abstract. With 8 items of which 2 are wrong, the popular \(\varphi = 1.5\) matches 94.8% of insiders but also “matches” 26.3% of outsiders. Holding false matches to 1% of outsiders takes \(\varphi = 4.83\), which still re-identifies 73.0% of insiders. So calibrate the threshold on records known not to be the target, and read the attack at a small false positive rate (Figure 15.2).

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.5 Does releasing a sample protect?
Agencies often release a 1% sample, arguing plausible deniability: a record unique in the sample need not be unique in the population. Let each person be in the release with probability \(\pi\), the sampling fraction, and let \(\lambda\) be the expected number of other people in the target’s cell.
Suppose the adversary knows a person’s cell and finds exactly one record there. Either the target was sampled and nobody else in the cell was, or the target was left out and one other person was. Each other person in the cell supplies a wrong story as likely as the right one, and since the release shows no second record, those others are all unsampled, about \(\lambda(1 - \pi)\) of them. The match is right with probability right over right plus wrong: \[\kappa \approx \frac{1}{1 + \lambda(1 - \pi)}. \tag{15.4}\] Going the other way, a record alone in the sample is named by a population register, such as a voter roll, when nobody unsampled shares its cell, which has probability \[\xi \approx e^{-\lambda(1 - \pi)}. \tag{15.5}\]
Sampling enters both only through \(1 - \pi\), which is already close to 1 for any small sample. So what protects a person is a crowded cell, not the sampling: shrinking the sample can never push \(\kappa\) below \(1/(1 + \lambda)\) or \(\xi\) below \(e^{-\lambda}\), and for a rare cell both stay near 1 (Table 15.5). Going from a 50% to a 1% sample lowers \(\kappa\) by only 0.04 for a rare cell, and by 0.16 for a crowded one.

0.500
0.138
0.368






Over a whole release, a small sample grants deniability only to people who were not unique in the population anyway. In a synthetic population of 100,000 with seven attributes, 82.8% of people are unique, and in a 1% sample 0.8301 of the sample-unique records are population-unique. Nor does “any match might be wrong” help, because a sample is a fair picture of the population: the adversary can estimate each cell’s \(\lambda\) from the sample itself and compute \(\xi\) record by record. Doing that from one 1% sample predicts 0.817 on average against an actual 0.824, and the records it rates above 0.95 are population-unique 99.3% of the time.
Removing names, perturbing values and sampling all failed the same way: they left enough bits in each record and bet on what the adversary didn’t know. A defence has to hold whatever auxiliary data exist. The classic attempts, k-anonymity and its successors, are tested against that requirement in Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks, and The definition of differential privacy gives the guarantee that meets it.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.6 Code
Three numbers summarise the linkage risk of a release you hold: \(J/n\), the fraction of unique records and the smallest class size. For a planned release, the uniform-cells formula and Equation 15.4 give quick estimates.
from collections import Counter
from math import exp, log2


def linkage_report(rows: list[tuple[str, ...]]) -> tuple[float, float, int]:
    """Linkage success J/n, fraction of unique records, and smallest class size of a release."""
    sizes = Counter(rows).values()  # one count per distinct quasi-identifier combination
    n = len(rows)
    return len(sizes) / n, sum(1 for k in sizes if k == 1) / n, min(sizes)


def uniform_unique(n: float, cells: float) -> float:
    """Expected fraction of n people who are unique when they fall in `cells` equally likely cells."""
    return exp(-n / cells)


def match_correct(lam: float, pi: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """In a sample of fraction pi, with lam expected others in the cell: (kappa, xi)."""
    return 1 / (1 + lam * (1 - pi)), exp(-lam * (1 - pi))


release = [
    ("02138", "1961-03-14", "F"), ("02138", "1972-11-02", "M"), ("02138", "1972-11-02", "M"),
    ("02139", "1958-06-21", "F"), ("02139", "1990-01-01", "F"), ("02139", "1990-01-01", "F"),
    ("02139", "1990-01-01", "F"), ("02141", "1983-09-30", "M"),
]
success, unique, k = linkage_report(release)
print(f"{success:.3f} {unique:.3f} {k}")  # 0.625 0.375 1
cells = 40_000 * 365 * 80 * 2  # ZIP code x birth date over 80 years x sex
print(f"{log2(cells):.1f} {uniform_unique(248.7e6, cells):.3f}")  # 31.1 0.899
kappa, xi = match_correct(0.1, 0.01)
print(f"{kappa:.3f} {xi:.3f}")  # 0.910 0.906

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.1 Why this matters
Linkage and re-identification showed that deleting names does not anonymize a table: the remaining quasi-identifiers, such as age, ZIP code and sex, single out most people. Between 1998 and 2008 a family of definitions answered by constraining the released table itself, each one proposed to stop an attack on the one before. k-anonymity hides every record in a crowd of at least \(k\) look-alikes. l-diversity asks each crowd to hold several different sensitive values. t-closeness asks each crowd to look like the whole table. They are syntactic: each is a property of the published table that you can check by reading it, with no reference to how it was produced or what else the adversary knows. Statistics offices, regulators’ guidance and tools such as ARX still use them.
What they share is also what breaks them: each fixes the adversary’s knowledge in advance. k-anonymity assumes the adversary knows the quasi-identifiers and nothing else, l-diversity allows a few facts about the target, t-closeness the table’s overall distribution. Each attack in this chapter hands the adversary one piece of knowledge the definition did not anticipate, and the guarantee then says nothing. A second release, the most ordinary auxiliary information there is, breaks all three. Those failures are the specification for differential privacy.
One fact drives every attack below. Records are grouped into equivalence classes, sets of records with the same (generalized) quasi-identifiers, and each record has one sensitive attribute \(S\), such as a diagnosis. An adversary who knows the target’s quasi-identifiers can find the target’s class \(E\) but not its record, so the best it can believe, its posterior, is that the target looks like a random member of the class: \[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}] = \frac{n_E(v)}{\lvert E\rvert} = P_E(v), \tag{16.1}\] where \(n_E(v)\) counts the records of \(E\) with value \(v\). If the adversary also knows the target’s value is not \(u\), it crosses out the records with \(u\) and renormalizes over the rest.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.2 k-anonymity
Sweeney and Samarati’s answer to linkage was to make sure no combination of quasi-identifiers singles out fewer than \(k\) people. A release is k-anonymous if every equivalence class has at least \(k\) records. A custodian gets there by generalization (age 37 becomes 35–39, ZIP code 02139 becomes 021**) and by suppression, deleting the few records that still stand out. What this buys follows from the linkage game: an adversary who finds the target’s class must guess among its records, so each class yields one record’s worth of wins, and the success is the number of classes \(J\) over the number of records \(n\). Classes of at least \(k\) records cannot number more than \(n/k\), so \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n} \le \frac{1}{k}. \tag{16.2}\]
The price is precision, and it is larger than it looks. Cells of the generalized quasi-identifiers vary in size around their average, and the unlucky small ones violate the definition, so the average must be well above \(k\). For 10,000 people, keeping 99% of records in classes of at least 2 needs 4.61 people per cell on average, more than twice \(k\), which allows the quasi-identifiers 11.08 bits, 2.20 below \(\log_2 n\). Since 99% of people are unique 6.64 bits above it, the window between “almost everyone is unique” and “almost everyone is hidden” is only about 9 bits wide, and every column you publish spends some of it.
The Mondrian algorithm (LeFevre, DeWitt & Ramakrishnan, 2006) starts from the whole table as one box and repeatedly splits a box at the median of its widest quasi-identifier, as long as both halves keep \(k\) records. Because it recodes locally, classes stay close to size \(k\). Table 16.1 applies it to a synthetic hospital table of 10,000 patients, with age, ZIP code and sex as quasi-identifiers and one of eight diagnoses that depend on age. With exact quasi-identifiers the linkage success is 0.933.

16.3 Homogeneity, background knowledge and l-diversity

Alice, 26, is in the first class, where every record says heart disease, so by Equation 16.1 her posterior is 1: the homogeneity attack, full disclosure without re-identification. Bob, 35, is in the third class, with posterior \(\frac23\) for cancer. His neighbour knows he did not have flu, crosses out the flu record, and cancer has posterior 1: the background knowledge attack. Both work because one value dominates the class, so l-diversity asks each class for enough different values.
Its three versions differ in what they bound. A class is distinct \(\ell\)-diverse if it holds at least \(\ell\) different values, and entropy \(\ell\)-diverse if its distribution is as spread out as \(\ell\) equally common values (entropy at least \(\log_2 \ell\)). Neither limits the share of the most common value, so neither caps the posterior: an entropy 3-diverse class over 8 values can have one value in 73% of its records, because the other 27%, spread over seven values, add enough entropy. The third version targets the background knowledge attack directly. Sort a class’s value counts as \(r_1 \ge r_2 \ge \dots \ge r_m\); the class is recursive \((c, \ell)\)-diverse if \[r_1 < c\,(r_\ell + \dots + r_m). \tag{16.3}\] The right side is the tail left after setting aside the \(\ell - 1\) most common values. An adversary who rules out \(\ell - 2\) values cannot make the top count larger, and whatever it removes, the values that remain besides the top one add up to at least that tail. So the top value still holds less than \(c\) parts out of \(c + 1\). Every remaining value therefore keeps a posterior below \(c/(1 + c)\): 0.500, 0.667 and 0.750 for \(c = 1, 2, 3\). Even that cap lets the adversary be fairly sure. l-diversity protects against certainty, not likelihood, and only against an adversary who rules out at most \(\ell - 2\) values; one who knows something softer (“probably not flu”) is not covered.
To judge what a release teaches, compare with what the adversary would believe without it. On the hospital table (Table 16.3), the most common diagnosis overall is right for 18.5% of patients, but imputation, guessing the most likely diagnosis for each patient’s age from the population, is right for 53.6%. So most of the 59.3% that a 5-anonymous release achieves is the age–diagnosis pattern any study would report, a fact about the population rather than a secret about anyone. Measure attribute disclosure against imputation, or you will count the study’s findings as leaks.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.4 Skewness, similarity and t-closeness
Li, Li and Venkatasubramanian (2007) found two attacks that diversity does not see. In the skewness attack, 1% of the table has HIV, and a class that is half HIV is 2-diverse by every definition, yet it raises the belief that a member has HIV from 1% to 50% (Figure 16.1). In the similarity attack, a class holding gastric ulcer, gastritis and stomach cancer is 3-diverse and still says “stomach disease”. So counting values is the wrong yardstick: what matters is how far a class moves the adversary from what it would believe anyway, the whole table’s distribution \(P\).






Figure 16.1: The skewness attack: a table in which 1% of patients have HIV, and a class of it that is half HIV. The class is 2-diverse but at total variation 0.49 from the table.



A release is t-close if every class’s distribution is within distance \(t\) of the table’s, \(d(P_E, P) \le t\). With the total variation (TV) distance, \(\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \frac12\sum_v\lvert P(v) - Q(v)\rvert\), the guarantee has a direct reading. TV is the largest gap between the two distributions’ probabilities of any set of values, so every question the adversary can ask about the target’s value gets an answer within \(t\) of the table’s: \[\lvert P_E(A) - P(A)\rvert \le t \quad \text{for every set of values } A. \tag{16.4}\] In particular, guessing the class’s top value is right with probability at most \(\max_v P(v) + t\), and on the hospital table (Table 16.4) the accuracy stays under that bound.

The bound is additive, and that is its weakness. A difference of 0.15 is small next to a value held by 40% of patients and enormous next to one held by 1%: at \(t = 0.15\) a 1% value may rise to 16%, a sixteen-fold increase for exactly the people who most need protection. The half-HIV class sits at TV 0.49; a class with 10% HIV sits at 0.09, passes \(t = 0.1\), and still makes HIV ten times as likely. A guarantee for rare values has to bound the ratio of beliefs, not their difference.
t-closeness also fights the purpose of the release. If age predicts diagnosis, a class of similar ages has a different diagnosis distribution from the whole table, so making every class close to the table means mixing ages until the pattern is gone. In Table 16.4 the classes span about 30% of each quasi-identifier’s range, and guess accuracy falls to 0.222–0.275, far below the 0.536 of imputation. The release now hides a population fact that was never a secret.
The distance also decides what counts as similar, and TV, which treats all values as equally different, misses the similarity attack. Li et al. use the earth mover’s distance (EMD), the least work to reshape one distribution into the other when moving mass between two values costs their distance. With a ground distance that puts gastritis near gastric ulcer, a class full of stomach diseases is far from the table and fails. For \(m\) ordered values (salary bands, age groups) at spacing \(1/(m - 1)\), the work is the net mass that has to cross each gap between neighbouring values: \[\mathrm{EMD}(P_E, P) = \frac{1}{m - 1}\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\Big\lvert\sum_{j \le i}\big(P_E(j) - P(j)\big)\Big\rvert. \tag{16.5}\]

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.5 The composition attack
Every definition so far concerns one table. Ganta, Kasiviswanathan and Smith (2008) asked about two. Two hospitals in one city publish their tables, each properly k-anonymous or \(\ell\)-diverse, without coordinating. A patient treated at both sits in a class of each, and the true diagnosis is in both classes, because the patient’s own record carries it. So the adversary intersects the two sets of values, \(\{v : n_{E_A}(v) > 0\} \cap \{v : n_{E_B}(v) > 0\}\), and the diagnosis is pinned down when one candidate is left. Neither hospital did anything wrong.
How often this works depends on class size, for a clear reason: every other member of a class brings a wrong value, and each wrong value is another chance for the two classes to share one. In a model where the other members are drawn from the population, the probability of pinning is 0.8734 for classes of 2 and 0.1615 for classes of 5, falling to 0.0015 for classes of 10. On data, take a city of 15,000 people in which two hospitals each treat a random 10,000, so 6,649 are treated at both, and each publishes a 5-anonymous Mondrian release (Table 16.5).

Together, two 5-anonymous releases pin down the diagnosis of 9.9% of shared patients, more than three times either alone. With distinct 3-diversity neither release pins anyone, and together they pin 18 patients. The model understates the risk: a patient’s class here holds 6.8 records on average, and the model predicts only 2.9% pinned for classes of 7, because real classes group people of similar age, who share diagnoses more often than random draws.
No custodian can prevent this by checking its own table harder, since it cannot know every other release its patients appear in. A better definition must therefore do three things. It has to hold whatever the adversary knows, since another release is just auxiliary information. It has to say how leakage adds up when releases are combined. And it has to bound the ratio of beliefs with and without a person’s data, so that rare values are protected. The definition of differential privacy starts from these three requirements.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.6 Code
An auditor can check every definition of this chapter by grouping the rows. The snippet audits Table 16.2: smallest class, fewest distinct values, entropy-equivalent \(\ell\), recursive \((2, 2)\)-diversity and TV distance from the table.
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from math import log2


def classes(rows: list[tuple[str, str, str]]) -> list[Counter[str]]:
    """Group (ZIP, age, diagnosis) rows by their quasi-identifiers; count the diagnoses in each class."""
    groups: defaultdict[tuple[str, str], Counter[str]] = defaultdict(Counter)
    for zip_code, age, diagnosis in rows:
        groups[(zip_code, age)][diagnosis] += 1
    return list(groups.values())


def entropy_l(counts: Counter[str]) -> float:
    """2 ** entropy: the number of equally common values with the same spread."""
    total = sum(counts.values())
    return 2 ** -sum(c / total * log2(c / total) for c in counts.values())


def recursive_diverse(counts: Counter[str], c: float, l: int) -> bool:
    """Recursive (c, l)-diversity: the top count is below c times the counts from the l-th largest on."""
    r = sorted(counts.values(), reverse=True)
    return r[0] < c * sum(r[l - 1 :])


def tv_to_table(counts: Counter[str], table: Counter[str]) -> float:
    """Total variation between a class's distribution and the whole table's."""
    nc, nt = sum(counts.values()), sum(table.values())
    return sum(abs(counts[v] / nc - table[v] / nt) for v in table) / 2


rows = [
    ("130**", "<30", "heart disease"), ("130**", "<30", "heart disease"), ("130**", "<30", "heart disease"),
    ("148**", "4*", "cancer"), ("148**", "4*", "flu"), ("148**", "4*", "heart disease"),
    ("130**", "3*", "cancer"), ("130**", "3*", "cancer"), ("130**", "3*", "flu"),
]
table = Counter(diagnosis for _, _, diagnosis in rows)
found = classes(rows)
print(min(sum(e.values()) for e in found))  # 3
print(min(len(e) for e in found))  # 1
print(" ".join(f"{entropy_l(e):.2f}" for e in found))  # 1.00 3.00 1.89
print(all(recursive_diverse(e, 2, 2) for e in found))  # False
print(" ".join(f"{tv_to_table(e, table):.3f}" for e in found))  # 0.556 0.111 0.444

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.1 Why this matters
A hospital keeps one sensitive bit per patient, whether they tested positive, and never releases it. It only answers counting questions, “how many of patients 3, 17, 42, … tested positive?”, and adds a little noise to every answer. Is that safe? Dinur and Nissim (2003) showed that it is not, unless the noise is large. Each answer is a linear equation whose unknowns are the patients’ bits, so a table of aggregates is a system of equations, and enough equations with small enough errors determine the unknowns.
The error of the answers is therefore the only thing standing between the attacker and the solution, and it fails in two ways. It can be too small: to hide a wrong guess, the error must be as large as the amount by which that guess changes the answers, which for a random query is about \(\sqrt n\), where \(n\) is the number of people. Or there can be too many answers: errors that are independent from answer to answer are averaged away by asking more. Dwork and Roth call this the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery: overly accurate answers to too many questions destroy privacy. If you run or audit a system that answers aggregate queries, check both.
Throughout, the secret is a bit vector \(d = (d_1, \dots, d_n)\), one bit per person. A subset-sum query asks how many people in a set \(S\) have bit 1. The curator, the party holding \(d\), answers \(m\) queries, each with an error, and “error at most \(E\)” means every answer is within \(E\) of the truth.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.2 How accurate is too accurate?
Start with the strongest attacker, who may ask all \(2^n\) subset sums, and throws away every candidate database that contradicts an answer by more than the curator’s error allows. Any candidate \(c\) that survives is close to \(d\), for a simple reason. The bits where \(c\) is wrong form two sets: the ones it missed and the ones it invented. The attacker asked about both. On the set of missed ones, \(d\) sums to the size of the set and \(c\) to zero, yet both are within \(E\) of the same published answer, so the set has at most \(2E\) people; the same holds for the invented ones. A surviving candidate therefore has at most \(4E\) wrong bits, and the bound is tight. With \(n = 10^6\) people and every answer off by up to 1000, the attacker gets at most 4,000 bits wrong, 0.4% of them. Error well below \(n\) is useless against unlimited queries; a curator whose error lets the attacker recover all but a vanishing fraction of the bits is called blatantly non-private.
Dinur and Nissim’s main result replaces the \(2^n\) questions with random subsets, each including every person with probability \(\frac12\). The price is a lower threshold, and the reason is that a random query cannot aim. Suppose a candidate is wrong on \(k\) bits. A query aimed at exactly those bits would move the answer by \(k\), but a random query picks up each wrong bit with probability \(\frac12\), so its sum over them behaves like \(k\) coin flips and moves by only about \(\sqrt k\). An error below that scale cannot hide a candidate wrong on a constant fraction of the bits. So with error well below \(\sqrt n\) on a number of random queries slightly above \(n\), a linear-program decoder recovers all but a small fraction of the bits in polynomial time: it finds any vector with entries between 0 and 1 whose answers are within \(E\) of every published answer, and rounds it.
The proved constants are poor; at \(n = 1000\) the proof needs about \(33n\) queries. Don’t read them as a safety margin, because the scaling is what matters and real attacks beat the constants easily: least squares with \(m = 4n\) already recovers 96.55% of the bits under Gaussian noise of \(\sigma = 0.25\sqrt n\) (Section 17.3). Random queries aren’t needed either. Cohen and Nissim (2020) ran a linear-program reconstruction against a commercial query system that added noise to its answers and recovered most of a secret column.
The same logic says which distortions don’t count as noise. A curator that rounds every answer to a multiple of 4 has error at most 2, but the rounding is a known function of the true sum, so an attacker who applies it to each candidate’s answers recovers \(d\) exactly. And a few wildly wrong answers don’t help the curator: a variant of the decoder that minimises the total absolute error, instead of requiring every answer to fit, tolerates a constant fraction of them (Dwork, McSherry and Talwar, 2007).

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
section: 17.3 Least squares under random and worst-case error
text:
17.3 Least squares under random and worst-case error
The attack you would actually run is simpler. Least squares picks the vector whose answers come closest to the published ones in squared distance, then clips each coordinate to \([0, 1]\) and rounds it. Because its output is a linear function of the answers, its error is a linear function of the curator’s, and you can predict its success.
With independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) on each of \(m\) random subset sums, each decoded coordinate is off by a normal error with standard deviation about \(2\sigma/\sqrt{m - n}\). The reasoning is the familiar one for averages: \(n\) equations are needed to pin down \(n\) unknowns, and the \(m - n\) beyond those average the noise down by \(\sqrt{m - n}\); the factor 2 appears because a random query includes each person only half the time. A bit comes out wrong when its error crosses \(\frac12\), so the expected fraction recovered is \[\Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{m - n}}{4\sigma}\right), \tag{17.1}\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Two consequences follow. At a fixed ratio \(m/n\), only \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) matters, so \(\sqrt n\) is again the scale of the threat. And at a fixed \(\sigma\) the fraction tends to 1 as \(m\) grows, so to hold the attack at a fixed accuracy the noise must grow like \(\sqrt m\).

Noise of order \(\sqrt n\) is not automatically safe: at \(\sigma = 0.25\sqrt n\), 96.55% of the bits come back, and recovery degrades smoothly instead of switching off at a threshold. The column at \(\sigma = 2\sqrt n\) shows the second failure. That curator looks safe at \(m = 4n\), where only 0.5875 of the bits come back, but if it answers any number of queries at the same noise level, an attacker who asks \(m = 106.1\,n\) recovers 90% of them (Figure 17.1). A bound on the error of each answer protects nothing when the number of answers is unbounded; the error budget has to cover all of them together.






Figure 17.1: Fraction of bits recovered by least squares at \(n = 200\) as the number of queries grows, for three noise levels. Lines are Equation 17.1; dots are simulations. Near \(m = n\) the system is barely determined and the noise is amplified; beyond that, more queries average the noise away, and even at \(\sigma = 2\sqrt n\) the attack recovers most bits with \(64n = 12\,800\) queries.



Gaussian noise is also the friendly case. Least squares amplifies errors most along one direction, that of the smallest singular value \(s_{\min}(A)\) of the query matrix, and independent noise points in all directions equally. A curator that pushes every error along that weakest direction does far more damage: at \(E = 0.25\sqrt n = 5.59\) it causes 143 wrong bits, against about 17 for Gaussian noise of the same scale. The general guarantee, at most \(4mE^2/s_{\min}(A)^2\) wrong bits, covers every curator. So when a system’s errors are not independent random noise, test it with errors chosen against the decoder, not only with Gaussian noise of the same size.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
section: 17.4 The Fundamental Law: what stops reconstruction, and what doesn’t
text:
17.4 The Fundamental Law: what stops reconstruction, and what doesn’t
Is error of order \(\sqrt n\) enough to stop reconstruction? A sampling curator shows it can be. It keeps each person with probability \(p\) in a secret set, answers every query from that set, and scales up by \(1/p\) so that answers are right on average. Each answer’s error is then a sum of independent zero-mean terms, one per person, so it is of order \(\sqrt n\), and the largest of all \(m\) errors is only a logarithmic factor above that, of order \(\sqrt{n\log m}\). But the people left out never affect any answer, so nothing reveals their bits, and no attacker recovers more than a fraction \(p + \frac{1 - p}{2}\) of a uniformly random \(d\) on average: the sampled bits, plus a coin flip for the rest. At \(n = 500\), \(m = 2000\) and \(p = \frac12\), the largest error is 28.00, or \(1.25\sqrt n\), and least squares recovers 0.7560 of the bits, right at the ceiling of three quarters.
That is not privacy, though. The same curator answers exactly for the people in its sample, and an attacker with enough queries learns all of their bits: half the people are fully exposed so that the other half can be fully hidden. Stopping blatant reconstruction is a much weaker goal than protecting everyone. A guarantee has to hold for every individual, which is what The definition of differential privacy provides, and it has to control both halves of the law, the error scale and the number of answers. That is why differential privacy tracks a budget spent across queries.
How few queries can any attack use? Count bits. The secret carries \(n\) bits; an answer that takes at most \(V\) values carries at most \(\log_2 V\); and a guess that may be wrong on a fraction \(\beta\) of the bits still leaves \(h(\beta)\) bits of uncertainty per person, where \(h(\beta) = -\beta\log_2\beta - (1 - \beta)\log_2(1 - \beta)\) is the binary entropy. So any attack needs at least \[m \ge \frac{n\,(1 - h(\beta))}{\log_2 V} \tag{17.2}\] queries. At \(n = 1000\) and 5% wrong bits, exact counts need at least 71.6 queries, and rounding every count to a multiple of 32 raises the floor only to 141.5. Coarser answers carry fewer bits each, but this is a floor on what an attack needs, not a defence: a curator that answers unlimited queries has only roughly doubled the minimum the attacker must ask, and the attacker can simply ask more.

text:
17.5 Reconstructing a census block
Statistical offices publish tables, not query answers, but every cell is a query, and many tables come from the same confidential records. Garfinkel, Abowd and Martindale (2019) showed how far this goes with a toy block of seven people, each with an age, a sex, a race and a marital status, where nobody under 18 is married. Withholding a number rarely helps, because the remaining numbers usually imply it: eight of the twelve medians and means leave the block unique when withheld (Figure 17.2). Real publications are more exposed than the toy, not less: they cross-classify many variables at many geographic levels, which is the “too many questions” half of the law. And the usual protections leave most constraints exact. Swapping a small fraction of households between blocks, the main protection of the 2010 Census, changes some answers; coarsening ages and suppressing small cells remove some constraints; the rest still bind. The Census Bureau’s own reconstruction of the 2010 Census, described by Abowd (2021), rebuilt a record for each of the 308,745,538 people counted. About 46% matched a real person exactly on block, sex, age, race and ethnicity, and linking to commercial data confirmed the identity of about 17% of the population. The Bureau’s response was to move the 2020 Census to a method based on differential privacy.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.6 Code
To audit a query system or plan a release, three numbers come first: what fraction least squares would recover at your noise level, how many queries per person push it to a target, and the fewest queries any attack needs. The snippet computes all three, using the finite-\(m\) variance \(4\sigma^2 n/((n + 1)(m - n - 1))\) that the full edition derives, which is about \(4\sigma^2/(m - n)\).
from math import log2, sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist

PHI = NormalDist()


def ls_recovered(n: int, m: int, sigma: float) -> float:
    """Predicted fraction of n secret bits that least squares recovers from m noisy random subset sums."""
    sd = 2 * sigma * sqrt(n / ((n + 1) * (m - n - 1)))  # spread of each decoded bit's error
    return PHI.cdf(0.5 / sd)  # a bit comes out wrong when its error crosses 1/2


def queries_per_person(target: float, sigma_over_sqrt_n: float) -> float:
    """m/n at which least squares recovers a fraction `target` of the bits, for noise sigma = c * sqrt(n)."""
    return 1 + (4 * sigma_over_sqrt_n * PHI.inv_cdf(target)) ** 2


def binary_entropy(p: float) -> float:
    return -p * log2(p) - (1 - p) * log2(1 - p)


def min_queries(n: int, wrong: float, values: int) -> float:
    """Fewest answers, each taking at most `values` values, from which any attack gets all but n * wrong bits."""
    return n * (1 - binary_entropy(wrong)) / log2(values)


n, m = 500, 2000
print(" ".join(f"{ls_recovered(n, m, c * sqrt(n)):.4f}" for c in (0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)))  # 1.0000 0.9585 0.8069 0.6676 0.5858
print(f"{queries_per_person(0.9, 2.0):.1f}")  # 106.1
print(f"{min_queries(1000, 0.05, 1001):.1f}")  # 71.6
print(f"{min_queries(1000, 0.05, 1000 // 10 + 2):.1f}")  # 106.9
print(f"{min_queries(1000, 0.05, 1000 // 32 + 2):.1f}")  # 141.5
The first line is the prediction row of Table 17.1. The full edition’s script, reconstruction.py, runs the attacks themselves: the exponential attack, least squares under random and worst-case error, the sampling curator and the census-block search.
uv run python code/part02-attacks/reconstruction.py

text:
17.8 Further reading

Dinur & Nissim, “Revealing Information while Preserving Privacy” (PODS 2003): the original attacks and the notion of blatant non-privacy.
Dwork, Smith, Steinke & Ullman, “Exposed! A Survey of Attacks on Private Data” (Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application, 2017): a readable survey of reconstruction and tracing attacks.
Garfinkel, Abowd & Martindale, “Understanding Database Reconstruction Attacks on Public Data” (CACM 2019): the seven-person block reconstructed with a solver.
