text:
31.9 Further reading

Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi, “Privacy Amplification by Subsampling: Tight Analyses via Couplings and Divergences” (NeurIPS 2018): tight \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) amplification for each sampling scheme and neighbouring relation.
Mironov, Talwar & Zhang, “Rényi Differential Privacy of the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism” (2019): the subsampled Gaussian’s RDP curve and its stable computation, the basis of most RDP accountants.
Lebeda, Regehr, Kamath & Steinke, “Avoiding Pitfalls for Privacy Accounting of Subsampled Mechanisms under Composition” (IEEE SaTML 2025): fixed-size against Poisson sampling, and worst-case pairs that fail under composition.
Chua, Ghazi, Kamath, Kumar, Manurangsi, Sinha & Zhang, “How Private are DP-SGD Implementations?” (ICML 2024): why shuffle-and-partition batching can be much less private than the Poisson accountant reports.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.1 Why this matters
You trained a model with differential privacy (DP): 10,000 steps of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), each on a Poisson sample of the data with rate \(q = 0.01\), with clipped gradients and Gaussian noise of multiplier \(\sigma = 1\). This is DP-SGD, the running example of this part, and you need the smallest \(\varepsilon\) for which the whole run is \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Rényi differential privacy (RDP), from Rényi DP, gives an upper bound that loses an unknown amount in its conversion. The Gaussian central limit theorem (CLT) of f-DP and Gaussian DP gives an approximation that may err in either direction.
This chapter computes the answer itself. \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) depends on a mechanism only through the distribution of its privacy loss, a distribution on the real line, and composing steps adds losses, so a whole run’s distribution is a convolution that a computer can evaluate on a grid. Rounding in a chosen direction gives the grid’s error a known sign: you get a certified upper bound and a lower bound whose distance you know in advance.
crumbs: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.2 The privacy loss distribution
Let \(P\) be the distribution of the output on your dataset \(D\) and \(Q\) on a neighbour \(D'\). The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is \(L(y) = \ln\frac{P(y)}{Q(y)}\) (Composition). Draw \(y\) from \(P\) and the loss is a random variable; its distribution is the privacy loss distribution (PLD).
Why should this one-dimensional distribution carry everything? The definition lets each output’s probability under \(P\) be up to \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability under \(Q\), and \(\delta\) pays only for the excess. An output with loss \(\ell\) has \(P(y) = e^\ell Q(y)\), so its excess is a fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell}\) of its probability when \(\ell > \varepsilon\), and nothing otherwise. That fraction depends on the output only through its loss, so \(\delta\) is an average over the PLD: \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big] = P[L > \varepsilon] - e^{\varepsilon}\,Q[L > \varepsilon], \tag{32.1}\] where \((x)_+ = \max\{x, 0\}\). The second form reads it as a gap: the chance under \(P\) that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), minus \(e^\varepsilon\) times that chance under \(Q\). An output impossible under \(D'\) has infinite loss and counts fully. So the output space never enters: a run with millions of parameters and a one-dimensional mechanism with the same PLD have the same privacy curve.
The weight is 0 up to \(\ell = \varepsilon\) and rises slowly towards 1, so \(\delta\) is the PLD’s upper tail with losses just above \(\varepsilon\) discounted (Figure 32.1). That is why the plain tail \(P[L > \varepsilon]\) is a loose bound: it counts the barely-over outputs in full.
For the Gaussian mechanism, with \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma\) the sensitivity in noise standard deviations, the two densities have the same shape, so their log-ratio is linear in the output and the loss is itself Gaussian, \(\mathcal N(\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\). Its two tails give the closed form of The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, with \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function: \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^{\varepsilon}\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{32.2}\] With sensitivity 1 and \(\sigma = 1\), the PLD is \(\mathcal N(0.5, 1)\); at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the formula gives \(\Phi(-0.5) - e\,\Phi(-1.5) = 0.3085 - 0.1816 = 0.1269\), and solving \(\delta(\varepsilon) = 10^{-5}\) gives \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\).






Figure 32.1: The Gaussian PLD for \(\mu = 1\) (blue), the weight \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell})_+\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (orange, scaled by 0.4 to fit), and their product (green). The green area is \(\delta(1) = 0.1269\): only losses above \(\varepsilon\) count, and those just above it count little.
crumbs: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.3 Composition is convolution
For independent steps the probability of the tuple of outputs is a product, its log is a sum, and so the privacy loss of the run is the sum of the step losses. The distribution of a sum of independent variables is the convolution of their distributions, so the PLD of \(k\) steps is the \(k\)-fold convolution of the per-step PLDs.
This step is exact, which sets it apart from the theorems of Composition: they see each step only through its \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) and must cover the worst step with those values, while convolution uses each step’s actual shape. All the error in a PLD accountant comes from computing it. Gaussian steps give a check, since means and variances add: \(k\) steps with shift \(\mu\) behave like one Gaussian mechanism with \(\mu_k = \sqrt k\,\mu\). Ten steps with \(\sigma = 1\) are \((17.8566, 10^{-5})\)-DP and a hundred \((91.8173, 10^{-5})\)-DP, values any accountant must reproduce at \(q = 1\). The same picture explains why the CLT is plausible, since long sums look Gaussian; the PLD accountant computes the sum instead.
DP-SGD steps are adaptive: each gradient depends on the model, so the losses are not independent. The repair is a dominating pair, a fixed pair at least as easy to tell apart as the step, whatever came before; convolving the dominating pairs’ PLDs bounds the adaptive run (Zhu, Dong & Wang 2022). The bound is exactly as tight as the pair. For the Gaussian mechanism, \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) against \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) is produced by real datasets, so nothing is lost; for a subsampled mechanism the pair depends on how batches are drawn and must match your training code.
crumbs: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.4 Pessimistic and optimistic discretization
A computer convolves vectors, so the loss goes on a grid of width \(h\). The rounding can still give a guarantee, because the weight in Equation 32.1 never decreases as the loss grows: move every loss up and \(\delta\) can only rise, move every loss down and it can only fall.
The pessimistic PLD rounds every loss up to the next grid point and sends any truncated upper tail to \(+\infty\). The optimistic PLD rounds every loss down and drops the truncated lower tail. In any run, each step’s rounded-up loss is at least its true loss, which is at least its rounded-down loss, and adding over \(k\) steps keeps that order for the totals. So at every \(\varepsilon\) \[\delta_{\text{optimistic}}(\varepsilon) \;\le\; \delta(\varepsilon) \;\le\; \delta_{\text{pessimistic}}(\varepsilon). \tag{32.3}\] The same argument gives the width: each step’s two roundings are at most \(h\) apart, so the totals, and the two values of \(\varepsilon\) at your \(\delta\), are at most \(kh\) apart. For a continuous PLD the gap is almost exactly \(kh\): the error grows linearly in \(k\).
The two sides are not equally strong. Raising losses keeps the pessimistic distribution the PLD of a real pair that dominates the original, so the upper bound holds for adaptive composition too. Lowering them can produce a distribution no pair has, so the optimistic value bounds the mechanism from below only when real datasets produce the pair, as for the Gaussian and the subsampled Gaussian.
Randomized response with \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\), composed three times on the coarse grid \(h = 0.5\), has exact \(\delta(1) = 0.4190\) between the pessimistic 0.6758 and the optimistic 0.3648 (Figure 32.2). For Gaussian steps with \(\mu = 1\) on \(h = 10^{-3}\) (Table 32.1), the width is exactly \(kh\) and the exact value sits in the middle, because a loss spread evenly within a cell moves up by about \(h/2\) when rounded up and down by as much when rounded down. The midpoint, like rounding to the nearest point, is a good estimate, but only the two sides are guarantees.

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.5 Composition by FFT
On a common grid, adding two losses adds their grid indices, so composing two discretized PLDs is a discrete convolution of their mass vectors. A fast Fourier transform (FFT) turns it into a pointwise product of transforms, at a cost of order \(N\log N\) for length \(N\), and repeated squaring composes \(k\) steps in at most \(2\log_2k\) convolutions.
The FFT has one trap, which follows from how it works: it attaches to each index a power of an \(N\)-th root of unity, so indices add modulo \(N\), and mass that falls off one end of the window reappears at the other. Ten Gaussian steps with \(\mu = 1\) on \(h = 10^{-3}\) give a pessimistic \(\delta(1) = 0.81891018\), against the exact 0.81851782. On a circular window from loss 0 to 10, the same computation gives 0.83478562, wrong in the second decimal: negative losses, which should count nothing, wrap to the top of the window where they count almost fully. Width 40 gets it right. The error from wraparound can go either way, so a wrapped result is no bound at all; pad every convolution to the sum of its inputs’ lengths. Truncating tails at a tiny mass such as \(10^{-15}\) is safe only if the pessimistic side moves the cut mass up, to \(+\infty\).
Each tenfold refinement of \(h\) makes the vectors ten times longer. The privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant (Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz 2021) rounds to the nearest point and shifts the grid to preserve the mean loss, so the per-step errors have mean zero and grow like \(\sqrt k\,h\) instead of \(kh\); a grid of \(h \approx 1/\sqrt k\) then suffices, with explicit error bounds. Connect the dots (Doroshenko et al. 2022) builds the best pessimistic PLD on a given grid.
crumbs: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.6 The subsampled Gaussian
A DP-SGD step with Poisson sampling includes each record with probability \(q\). Without the record in question, the noisy sum is a Gaussian centred at 0; with it, the record is sampled with probability \(q\) and shifts the centre by 1, so the output is a mixture (Amplification by subsampling). Under add/remove neighbours the pair’s two orders differ. With \(D'\) the dataset that holds the record, the remove direction puts it first, \(P = M(D')\) and \(Q = M(D)\): \[P = (1 - q)\,\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2), \qquad Q = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2), \tag{32.4}\] and the add direction swaps them (Zhu, Dong & Wang 2022). Dividing the mixture by the base gives the remove loss, \(L_{\mathrm{rem}}(y) = \ln\big((1 - q) + q\,e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}\big)\), and the add loss is its negative.
The formula explains the asymmetry (Figure 32.3). For an ordinary output the exponential is small, so the remove loss never falls below \(\ln(1 - q)\); but a large output is far likelier from the shifted component, and there the loss grows without limit: a rare large gradient betrays that the record was used. The add loss is the mirror image, bounded above by \(-\ln(1 - q) = 0.0101\), and since \(\delta\) counts only losses above \(\varepsilon\), one add step costs nothing beyond that. For \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), one step is \((0.1995, 10^{-5})\)-DP in the remove direction and \((0.0091, 10^{-5})\)-DP in the add direction.






Figure 32.3: Left: the densities of \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) and of the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) for \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), on a log scale; they differ only in the far right tail. Right: the privacy loss as a function of the output for the remove pair (red) and the add pair (blue).



Composition narrows the gap, since many small add losses add up: after 10,000 steps the add direction’s upper bound is 5.6615. The remove direction stays larger here, but that is an observation, not a theorem, so compose both and report the larger \(\varepsilon\); an accountant using only the remove pair covers half of the add/remove relation. The pair also assumes Poisson sampling: if your loader shuffles and partitions instead, the mixture is the wrong model and these numbers do not apply.

RDP lies above them and the CLT below them.



After 10,000 steps the true \(\varepsilon\) lies in \([6.1377, 6.2377]\); report 6.2377. RDP’s 6.7127 is valid but over-states by 0.4750, and the single step shows why: 0.9555 against 0.1995. RDP keeps one moment of the loss per order \(\alpha\), and turning a moment into a tail bound costs about \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) whatever the true curve looks like.
The CLT errs the other way, which is worse: it falls below the PLD lower bound at every \(k\), so quoting its 1.62 for 1000 steps claims a guarantee the run does not have. The reason is the shape of the subsampled PLD (Figure 32.5): convolution makes its bulk bell-shaped, but its right tail stays heavy, and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) reads exactly that tail, where the Gaussian approximation is worst.






Figure 32.5: The pessimistic remove-direction PLD of DP-SGD with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) after 1, 10 and 100 steps (log scale; the dotted line is the mean). One step piles its mass just above \(\ln(1 - q)\) with a long right tail; convolution moves the bulk towards a bell shape, but the right tail stays heavier than the left.



A PLD accountant is only as good as its grid. At \(k = 1000\) on \(h = 10^{-3}\) the width is \(kh = 1\), and the upper bound, 2.3279, is worse than RDP’s 2.1014. Choose \(h\) for your largest \(k\), and check the width before trusting the upper bound.

title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
33.1 Why this matters
Amplification by subsampling showed that uncertainty is worth privacy: if an adversary cannot tell whether a step used your record, the step leaks far less than its noise alone suggests. Two other kinds matter in practice. In the shuffle model, \(n\) users randomize their own data and a trusted shuffler strips identities and mixes the order, so the analyst does not know which report is yours. Each report alone satisfies local differential privacy (DP) at a level \(\varepsilon_0\), usually large to keep reports useful, yet the bag of reports is central DP with an \(\varepsilon\) that falls like \(1/\sqrt n\). And when noisy gradient descent (GD) on a convex loss releases only its final model, the adversary does not see what happened inside training: later steps add fresh noise and pull the parameters together, hiding early records better than composition says.
One idea gives every result. Show that what the adversary sees can be generated from a much simpler pair of distributions by a procedure that does not depend on your record. Anything the adversary learns from the real output, it could then have learned from the simple pair, so that pair’s privacy carries over. For shuffling the simple pair is a pair of counts; for iteration, a pair of Gaussians. Throughout, neighbouring datasets differ by replacing one record. The shuffling results are about anonymous, locally randomized reports, not the shuffle-and-partition batching used to train models in the central model, where no comparable theorem applies (Amplification by subsampling).

title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
33.2 Shuffled randomized response, exactly
Start with the simplest randomizer, whose exact answer is the yardstick for every general bound. Each user reports a bit with binary randomized response: the true bit with probability \(\theta = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\), the flipped bit otherwise. Once the order is gone, a bag of bits can tell the analyst only how many of them are 1. Your report moves that count by at most one, while the other users’ random flips spread it over a range of about \(\sqrt{n\theta(1 - \theta)}\), and that spread is what hides you.
Let your bit be 0 in \(D\) and 1 in \(D'\), and let the others all hold 0, so their number of 1-reports is binomial, \(\mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, 1 - \theta)\), with probability mass function \(b\). A count of \(y\) arises either when your report is 0 and the others sent \(y\) ones, or when your report is 1 and they sent \(y - 1\), so \[P(y) = \theta\,b(y) + (1 - \theta)\,b(y - 1), \qquad Q(y) = (1 - \theta)\,b(y) + \theta\,b(y - 1). \tag{33.1}\] The exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the larger of the two hockey-stick divergences between \(P\) and \(Q\), one per order, which takes milliseconds to compute (Section 33.6). Strictly, this is exact for the case where all the others hold 0 and a lower bound on the worst case; the other configurations the full edition scans come within \(10^{-4}\) of it, so the book treats it as exact.
Why \(1/\sqrt n\)? The count is a sum of many independent bits, so it is nearly normal. Your report shifts its mean by \(2\theta - 1\), and its standard deviation is \(\sqrt{n\theta(1 - \theta)}\) under both datasets. A pair of normals is a Gaussian mechanism whose \(\mu\) is the shift divided by the standard deviation, and simplifying gives \[\mu \approx \frac{2\sinh(\varepsilon_0/2)}{\sqrt n}. \tag{33.2}\] More users mean more noise to hide one bit in, hence \(1/\sqrt n\); a larger \(\varepsilon_0\) means more faithful reports and a less noisy count, hence the growth like \(e^{\varepsilon_0/2}\). A company that asks 10,000 users whether they used a feature, with \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\), gets reports that are each the truth with probability 0.8808, a weak local guarantee; the shuffled bag is \((0.0870, 10^{-6})\)-DP.






Figure 33.1: Left: the number of 1-reports among \(n = 30\) shuffled randomized-response reports with \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\), when you hold 0 (blue) and 1 (orange); your report moves the count by at most one. Right: the exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for one unshuffled report and for \(n = 10, 100, 1000\) shuffled reports. Every curve reaches 0 only at \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\), but for large \(n\) it is negligible far earlier.



Shuffling never improves pure DP, as the count of zero shows. If nobody reports a 1, you most likely hold 0, and the likelihood ratio of that outcome is \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) whatever \(n\) is. What shuffling changes is how often it happens: rarely, for large \(n\). So amplification moves the bad outcomes into \(\delta\) (Figure 33.1), and a shuffled guarantee always needs \(\delta > 0\). The normal approximation fails for the same reason it works: it needs many 1-reports to hide among. At \(n = 1000\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\) the others send about 18 on average, the count is far from normal, and the approximation gives 0.9667 against the exact 1.6910.

title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
section: 33.3 The clone bound for any local randomizer
text:
33.3 The clone bound for any local randomizer
Users often send histograms or noisy vectors, so you need a bound for every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP local randomizer. The argument of Feldman, McMillan & Talwar (2021) finds a hidden randomized response inside any of them. Being \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP means no output is more than \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) times likelier for one input than for another. Read the other way, any user’s report keeps at least a fraction \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) of each output’s probability under your \(D\)-version, and likewise under your \(D'\)-version. So every other user’s report can be generated by a coin: with probability \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) it is a clone, a draw distributed exactly like your report could be, half the time like your \(D\)-version and half like your \(D'\)-version; otherwise it is a draw that depends only on that user’s own data.
After shuffling, nobody can tell a clone from your report, so the adversary can do no better than count how many reports look like each version of you. That count is the simple pair, and its exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the numeric clone bound, valid for every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP randomizer, even adaptively chosen ones. The clones supply the noise: about \(ne^{-\varepsilon_0}\) of them, whose split between the two versions has standard deviation \(\sqrt{ne^{-\varepsilon_0}}/2\). That again gives \(1/\sqrt n\) with a constant growing like \(e^{\varepsilon_0/2}\). The analytic form (their Theorem 3.1) bounds the count pair with Chernoff bounds: \[\varepsilon \le \ln\left(1 + \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}\left(\frac{8\sqrt{e^{\varepsilon_0}\ln(4/\delta)}}{\sqrt n} + \frac{8e^{\varepsilon_0}}{n}\right)\right), \qquad\text{valid when } \varepsilon_0 \le \ln\frac{n}{16\ln(2/\delta)}. \tag{33.3}\] The condition says there must be enough clones to hide among: it is \(ne^{-\varepsilon_0} \ge 16\ln(2/\delta)\). At \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) it caps \(\varepsilon_0\) at 1.460 for \(n = 1000\) and 6.066 for \(n = 10^5\).

Table 33.1 shows the cost of generality. The numeric clone bound is 1.44 to 2.36 times the exact value for randomized response, for a clear reason: in randomized response every other report is a bit that could be yours, while the clone argument counts only the \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) fraction guaranteed to look like yours. No general bound can beat the exact column, since randomized response is one of the randomizers it must cover. The closed form loses another factor of 3.10 to 4.75 to its Chernoff constants, so use it for scaling and the numeric bound to deploy.
The choice can decide whether a deployment is feasible. To collect a bit from \(10^5\) users with central \(\varepsilon \le 0.2\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), the closed form allows \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\) (0.1862), the numeric clone bound allows \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\) (0.1698), and the exact value at \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\) is 0.0847. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\) the noise adds only \(0.0190/n\) to the variance of the estimated proportion, against up to \(0.25/n\) from sampling alone. All of this rests on a uniformly random order the analyst cannot see: if the order leaks, the analyst knows which report is yours and the guarantee falls back to \(\varepsilon_0\).

title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
33.4 Amplification by iteration
Projected noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD) makes one pass over the data, using record \(x_t\) at step \(t\). If every iterate is released, \(x_t\) is protected only by the noise of its own step. If only the final model is released, the noise of every later step also covers it, and Feldman, Mironov, Talwar & Thakurta (2018) turned this into a guarantee.
The step that uses your record pushes the two runs apart. Each later noisy step can “pay off” part of that gap, and the price of paying an amount \(a\) is quadratic in \(a\), like the Rényi divergence of two Gaussians shifted by \(a\). Paying a gap \(s\) in \(m\) equal instalments costs \(m(s/m)^2 = s^2/m\), so spreading the payment over every remaining step is cheapest. This only works if the later steps never push points apart, if they are contractions; a gradient step on a convex, \(\beta\)-smooth loss with step size \(\eta \le 2/\beta\), followed by projection onto a convex set, is one. For convex, Lipschitz, smooth losses and noise multiplier \(\tilde\sigma\) (noise per unit of the gradient’s replace-one sensitivity), releasing only the last iterate gives the record used at step \(t\) of \(n\) the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve \[\varepsilon_t(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2\tilde\sigma^2}\cdot\frac{1}{n - t + 1}: \tag{33.4}\] one Gaussian step’s curve divided by the number of noisy steps from \(t\) to the end.
Take one pass over \(n = 10{,}000\) records with \(\tilde\sigma = 1\), converted to \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\) (Rényi DP). The first record gets \(\varepsilon = 0.0481\), the one in the middle 0.0707, and the one used 100 steps before the end 0.4849. The last record gets 5.2985, exactly what it would get if every iterate were released: no later step pays anything for it.






Figure 33.2: The \(\mu\) of the last iterate against the step \(t\) at which your record is used, for a one-pass run of \(T = 100\) steps with per-step shift equal to the noise standard deviation. Releasing all iterates gives \(\mu = 1\) for every record (dotted). The bound Equation 33.4 (red) is exact in the worst case; for typical contractions (blue, orange) the true value is smaller.



So a report must state the worst record’s value, which gets no amplification at all; randomizing the stopping time spreads the benefit across records. The bound is exact in the worst case, when the step that uses your record wipes out all earlier noise, and loose for typical runs, where earlier noise and strict contraction also help (Figure 33.2). It covers one pass in a fixed order; several passes or subsampling need other theorems (Altschuler & Talwar 2022). And it needs convexity, because a non-contractive step can stretch a small gap faster than the noise pays it off.
crumbs: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
section: 33.5 Hidden state: privacy that stops growing
text:
33.5 Hidden state: privacy that stops growing
Full-batch noisy GD uses every record at every step, and composition charges every step, so the privacy loss grows linearly in the number of steps \(T\), and amplification by iteration alone does not help: each step opens a fresh gap, and paying each one off as it comes is composition again. Two properties can change that when only the final model is released. If the parameters live in a bounded convex set, the two runs can never be further apart than its diameter, however long they run, so only the last stretch of steps has to hide that gap and the cost stops depending on \(T\). If the loss is strongly convex, each step is a strict contraction that shrinks the gap for free.
Altschuler & Talwar (2022) prove the bounded-domain version: the last iterate’s RDP grows like composition up to a number of steps proportional to the diameter, then stays flat, and their lower bound shows the shape is right. For a quadratic loss the answer is exact. With contraction factor \(c < 1\) per step, your record’s per-step shift \(s\) reaches the end damped, so the total signal saturates at \(s/(1 - c)\); the noise saturates the same way, at a standard deviation of \(\sigma/\sqrt{1 - c^2}\). Their ratio is the limiting Gaussian mechanism, \[\mu_\infty = \frac{s}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{1 + c}{1 - c}}, \tag{33.5}\] reached after about \(1/(1 - c)\) steps, the time it takes \(c^T\) to become small; for a gradient step of size \(1/\beta\) on a \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, \(\beta\)-smooth loss, that is the condition number \(\beta/\lambda\). With \(c = 1\) the signal grows like \(T\) and the noise only like \(\sqrt T\), so there is no plateau: without contraction, hiding the state buys nothing.
Run 10,000 steps of full-batch noisy GD with \(\sigma/s = 10\) on a quadratic with \(c = 0.99\). Releasing every iterate is a Gaussian mechanism with \(\mu = 10\), which is \(\varepsilon = 91.8173\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\): no guarantee at all. Releasing only the final model is at the plateau, \(\mu = 1.4107\), which is \(\varepsilon = 6.5534\), with the same noise. The bounded-domain bound is looser: for a linear loss on the unit interval (Figure 33.3, right), after 2000 steps composition charges an RDP of 20.0000 at \(\alpha = 2\) and the bound 4.0000, while a hard instance reaches 0.3786. The shape is right; the constant is loose.






Figure 33.3: Left: the exact \(\mu\) of the last iterate of one-dimensional full-batch noisy GD against the number of steps \(T\), for \(c = 1\) (on top of composition), \(c = 0.99\) and \(c = 0.9\); with contraction it plateaus. Right: the Rényi divergence of order 2 of the last iterate for a linear loss on \([0, 1]\): composition, the bounded-domain bound, and the exact value for two projected random walks.



Both conditions are load-bearing. The argument needs only the last iterate released, because the adversary must not see the run before it has forgotten: checkpoints, logged intermediate models, a model published after each epoch, or the best of several checkpoints put you back to composition. It also needs contractive steps, which require convexity. For non-convex losses, Annamalai (2024) built a loss for which the last iterate of DP-SGD leaks as much as all iterates together. That attacks seeing only the final model have fallen short of the DP-SGD bound (Nasr et al. 2021) is an observation about attacks, not a guarantee. Do not report a hidden-state \(\varepsilon\) for deep learning.

title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
33.6 Code
This standard-library snippet builds Equation 33.1 in log space, takes the larger hockey-stick divergence over both directions, and bisects for \(\varepsilon\):
from math import exp, lgamma, log


def log_binom_pmf(k: int, n: int, p: float) -> float:
    return lgamma(n + 1) - lgamma(k + 1) - lgamma(n - k + 1) + k * log(p) + (n - k) * log(1 - p)


def shuffled_rr_pair(n: int, eps0: float) -> tuple[list[float], list[float]]:
    """Distribution of the number of 1-reports when you hold 0 (P) or 1 (Q); the n - 1 others hold 0."""
    theta = exp(eps0) / (1 + exp(eps0))
    b = [exp(log_binom_pmf(y, n - 1, 1 - theta)) for y in range(n)] + [0.0]
    P = [theta * b[y] + (1 - theta) * (b[y - 1] if y else 0.0) for y in range(n + 1)]
    Q = [(1 - theta) * b[y] + theta * (b[y - 1] if y else 0.0) for y in range(n + 1)]
    return P, Q


def hockey_stick(P: list[float], Q: list[float], eps: float) -> float:
    return sum(max(p - exp(eps) * q, 0.0) for p, q in zip(P, Q))


def shuffled_rr_epsilon(n: int, eps0: float, delta: float) -> float:
    P, Q = shuffled_rr_pair(n, eps0)
    lo, hi = 0.0, eps0  # shuffling never does worse than the local eps0
    for _ in range(50):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        worst = max(hockey_stick(P, Q, mid), hockey_stick(Q, P, mid))
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if worst > delta else (lo, mid)
    return hi


print(f"{shuffled_rr_epsilon(10_000, 2.0, 1e-6):.4f}")  # 0.0870
print(f"{shuffled_rr_epsilon(100_000, 4.0, 1e-6):.4f}")  # 0.0847
print(f"{shuffled_rr_epsilon(1_000, 4.0, 1e-6):.4f}")  # 1.6910
It reproduces the exact column of Table 33.1. The full edition’s script, shuffling_iteration.py, also computes the numeric clone bound and every iteration result:
uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/shuffling_iteration.py

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.1 Why this matters
You train a model with differential privacy (DP) using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped per-example gradients and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD. You may want to stop when the validation loss stalls, lower the noise mid-run, or let well-fitted records keep training. Every composition theorem so far assumes the opposite: the per-step budgets \(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_k\) and the number of steps \(k\) are fixed before the run (Advanced and optimal composition). Once they depend on what the run released, they are random, and plugging the values you happened to use into a fixed-parameter theorem afterwards is not valid.
So the question splits in two. A privacy filter answers “may I run one more step without exceeding a budget fixed in advance?” A privacy odometer answers “how much have I spent so far?”, and since you may stop at any moment, its answer must hold at every step at once. Both rest on one fact about Rényi differential privacy (RDP): at an order fixed before the run, adding up the spends as you go is as safe as if they had been fixed. That makes a filter free, an odometer cheap, and per-record accounting possible.
crumbs: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
section: 34.2 Why plugging in the realized parameters fails
text:
34.2 Why plugging in the realized parameters fails
Advanced composition is a high-probability statement: at a time \(t\) fixed in advance, the total privacy loss exceeds a bound \(U_t\), its mean plus a spread growing like \(\sqrt t\), only with probability \(\delta\). It says nothing about a time chosen by watching the outputs. An analyst who stops when the loss happens to be high picks exactly the paths on which the bound fails, and so does stopping on anything correlated with it, such as “these answers look unusual”.
Ask randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) about one person’s bit at every step. Each report moves the privacy loss up or down by 0.1, so the loss is a random walk with a slight upward drift. At any single step up to 1,000, the plug-in bound at \(\delta = 0.01\) fails with probability at most 0.0016. Now stop at the first crossing and report \(U_T\). The bound is narrow early, when \(\sqrt t\) is small, so a few walks cross it early and are frozen there (Figure 34.1). By \(10^4\) steps a fraction 0.0318 of runs have crossed (Table 34.1): “\(\varepsilon = U_T\) with \(\delta = 0.01\)” is wrong 3.18 times as often as it claims. A smaller \(\delta\) does not save it (Table 34.1, last row).

Right: the probability that the bound is crossed by step \(n\), for \(\delta = 0.05\) and \(0.01\) (dashed lines); it passes \(\delta\) and keeps growing.



The probability keeps growing because a random walk eventually wanders further than any fixed multiple of \(\sqrt t\) (its reach grows like \(\sqrt{t\ln\ln t}\)), so given time it crosses with certainty. A valid running bound must be wider, and Rogers et al. (2016) showed that every odometer pays at least an extra \(\ln\ln n\) inside the logarithm for \(n\) steps.
Basic composition escapes the problem: the sum of the realized \(\varepsilon_t\) bounds the loss of every output, so there is no bad event for a stopping rule to select. A filter escapes it too, because it makes no running claim to catch at a bad moment; it only asks whether the next step fits a budget fixed in advance.
crumbs: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.3 The Rényi filter
RDP describes each step by a curve \(\varepsilon_t(\alpha)\) over orders \(\alpha > 1\), and with fixed parameters the curves of a run add (Rényi DP). This survives adaptivity at one fixed order. Fix an order \(\alpha\) and an RDP budget \(B\) before the run. Let step \(t\) be \((\alpha, \varepsilon_t(\alpha))\)-RDP whatever happened before it, with \(\varepsilon_t(\alpha)\) known before the step runs. Run step \(t\) only if the spends so far, its own included, fit: \[\sum_{j \le t}\varepsilon_j(\alpha) \le B. \tag{34.1}\] Then the stopped run is \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP, as if the spends had been fixed.
The reason is a betting argument. Treat \(e^{(\alpha - 1)(\text{loss} - \text{spend})}\) as your wealth in a game. RDP at order \(\alpha\) bounds the average of \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\times\text{loss}}\), so a step charged its RDP spend cannot make this wealth grow on average: the game is fair or tilted against you. In such a game no quitting rule raises your expected final wealth, as long as you decide whether to play each round before seeing its result. If the total spend is at most \(B\) on every path, the average of \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\times\text{loss}}\) at the end is at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)B}\), which is exactly what \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP says.
Each condition is a step of that argument. A step’s price must be known before it runs: a mechanism allowed to charge little on exactly the outputs that reveal most would make the game a winning one. The budget must hold on every path, not on average, because the paths that spend most may be those where the loss is high. And the order must be fixed in advance. You may track several orders and halt when any one is exhausted, since then each held on every path; continuing while some order still fits, chosen after seeing the spends, is not free (Section 34.5 prices it).
You train with full-batch noisy gradient descent towards \((5.299, 10^{-5})\) at order \(\alpha = 5.8\). Mironov’s conversion turns \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP into \((B + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1), \delta)\)-DP, so run backwards it sets \(B = 5.299 - \ln(10^5)/4.8 = 2.900\). A full-batch Gaussian step with noise multiplier \(\sigma_t\) spends \(\alpha/(2\sigma_t^2)\). With \(\sigma_t = 10\) each step spends \(5.8/200 = 0.0290\) and you get 100 steps. If training plateaus at step 60 and you drop to \(\sigma_t = 5\), each later step costs \(5.8/50 = 0.1160\), and the filter allows \((2.900 - 60\times0.0290)/0.1160 = 10\) more. Either way the run is \((5.8, 2.900)\)-RDP, whatever rule decided the switch.
At a fixed order the filter costs nothing. It can even beat fixed-curve composition, which charges every step its worst branch, while the filter charges what each path spent.

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.4 Filters for pure differential privacy
An interactive query system has a global budget \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\), and each query brings a pure-DP \(\varepsilon_t\) chosen after earlier answers. Summing the \(\varepsilon_t\) is valid but grows like the number of queries \(k\); you want advanced composition’s \(\sqrt k\) without the failure of Section 34.2.
The Rényi filter delivers it. An \(\varepsilon_t\)-DP step spends at most \(\alpha\varepsilon_t^2/2\) at every order \(\alpha\) (Concentrated differential privacy). So a rule that keeps \(\frac12\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2\) below a fixed level is a Rényi filter at every order at once, and because the rule does not mention the order, the conversion may pick the best one afterwards. Doing that conversion gives the Whitehouse filter (Whitehouse et al. 2023): continue while \[\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)\textstyle\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2} + \tfrac12\textstyle\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2 \le \varepsilon_g, \tag{34.2}\] with sums over every step so far. It reads like advanced composition, the first term the spread of the total loss and the second its mean, and the stopped run is \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\)-DP.
At \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) and \(\varepsilon_g = 1\), the filter allows 349 steps of 0.01, slightly more than the 337 of advanced composition with \(k\) fixed in advance (Table 34.2). It wins, despite allowing adaptivity, because its mean term, \(\varepsilon_t^2/2\) per step, is tighter than the \(\varepsilon_t(e^{\varepsilon_t} - 1)\) of the fixed-\(k\) form. From the budget side, 1,000 steps of 0.01 need 1.712 under the Whitehouse filter, 1.763 under fixed-\(k\) advanced composition and 10.000 under the basic filter \(\sum_t\varepsilon_t \le \varepsilon_g\).

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.5 Odometers
Early stopping and open-ended analyses need a running “how much have I spent?” that is true whenever the run stops. Return to the betting game of Section 34.3. Markov’s inequality says that the wealth, which starts at 1, reaches \(c\) at one given time with probability at most \(1/c\). Ville’s inequality extends this to reaching \(c\) at any time, because “stop the first time you reach \(c\)” is itself a quitting rule and cannot raise the mean. Unpacked, at one order fixed in advance, Mironov’s conversion of the running spend holds at every step at once, for free.
The cost comes from the order: the best order for 10 steps is not the best for 1,000. To choose it late, fix a grid \(\Lambda\) of \(|\Lambda|\) orders, track the spend \(S_t(\alpha) = \sum_{j\le t}\varepsilon_j(\alpha)\) at each, and give each order a share \(\delta/|\Lambda|\) of the failure probability. The Ville odometer reports the best order’s conversion, \[U_t = \min_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\Big[S_t(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(|\Lambda|/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\Big], \tag{34.3}\] and with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) the loss stays below \(U_t\) at every step. It is Mironov’s conversion with \(\delta\) replaced by \(\delta/|\Lambda|\); that union bound is the whole price.
For full-batch Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 10\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the part’s 154 orders raise \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.513\) to 16.550, and the odometer costs 15–19% over the fixed-time value: 6.253 against 5.299 at \(t = 100\) (Table 34.3). A single order chosen in advance, 5.8, is free at \(t = 100\), its design point, and poor elsewhere: 31.399 at \(t = 1000\). On the part’s running example (DP-SGD with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(10^4\) steps, \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)), the fixed-time RDP value is 7.43, and an odometer valid whenever the run stops costs 8.82 (Ville) or 9.08 (the slightly looser odometer of Lécuyer 2021).

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.6 Individual privacy accounting in DP-SGD
DP-SGD’s usual analysis charges every record at every step as if its clipped gradient had norm \(C\), the clipping norm. But once the model fits a record, its gradient shrinks and it moves the noisy sum less, so the same noise hides it better.
That cost is exact. With full-batch steps and noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) on the summed clipped gradients, removing record \(i\) shifts the output by its clipped gradient \(\bar g_{i,t}\), so its spend is the Gaussian RDP for that shift: \[\varepsilon_{i,t}(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha\|\bar g_{i,t}\|^2}{2\sigma^2C^2} \le \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{34.4}\] It depends only on the record and the current model, which depends only on earlier releases, so it is known before the step: what the Rényi filter needs. The individual filter (Feldman & Zrnic 2021) runs one Rényi filter per record. Record \(i\) joins the sum only while its own spends total at most \(B\); once dropped, it no longer changes the output and spends nothing. Neighbouring datasets differ in one record, whose filter held, so the run is \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP. No step costs more than the worst case, so every record trains at least as long as in the worst-case run.
The full edition simulates 10,000 records (\(C = 1\), \(\sigma = 10\), full batch): 90% typical records whose gradients shrink as the model fits them, 10% hard records it never fits. The worst-case run has 100 steps and \(\varepsilon = 5.299\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), best at order 5.8, where \(B = 2.900\). Converting each record’s own spend after 100 steps (Table 34.4) gives a typical median of 3.17 and a hard median of 5.02, near the worst case. Run the individual filter for 300 steps and hard records reach the budget and are dropped from step 101 (the median one at step 111), while no typical record ever is: their median spend at step 300 is 0.778, a quarter of the budget (Figure 34.4).

The filter certifies one guarantee for everyone, \((5.8, 2.900)\)-RDP. The per-record values in the table are estimates: each is a fixed-time conversion of a random spend, the mistake of Section 34.2, and at a fixed order none can fall below the conversion’s toll \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1) = 2.399\). They are also sensitive, since a small spend says “the model fits this record well”: show a value to the record’s owner, never publish them all. There is a fairness cost too: records the model fits worst, often from under-represented groups, keep large gradients, exhaust their budget first and are dropped first, so the model sees even less of them. With Poisson subsampling the argument still works, using the subsampled Gaussian at noise multiplier \(\sigma C/\|\bar g_{i,t}\|\) (Amplification by subsampling), but you need every record’s gradient norm at every step, sampled or not.

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.7 Code
Filters and odometers are a sum of spends and a comparison. This snippet implements the Whitehouse filter, the Rényi filter for a noise schedule and the Ville odometer for full-batch Gaussian steps, and reproduces the numbers above.
from math import log, sqrt


def whitehouse_statistic(eps_steps: list[float], delta: float) -> float:
    """Advanced composition of pure-DP budgets with mean term eps^2 / 2: valid under adaptivity."""
    v = sum(e * e for e in eps_steps)
    return sqrt(2 * log(1 / delta) * v) + v / 2


def steps_allowed(eps_step: float, eps_global: float, delta: float) -> int:
    """Run steps of eps_step while the Whitehouse filter, checked before each step, says continue."""
    spent: list[float] = []
    while whitehouse_statistic([*spent, eps_step], delta) <= eps_global:
        spent.append(eps_step)
    return len(spent)


def gaussian_rdp(alpha: float, sigma: float) -> float:
    """RDP at order alpha of one full-batch Gaussian step with noise multiplier sigma."""
    return alpha / (2 * sigma**2)


def renyi_filter(sigmas: list[float], alpha: float, budget: float) -> int:
    """Number of steps of a noise schedule that a Renyi filter at order alpha lets through."""
    spent, steps = 0.0, 0
    for sigma in sigmas:
        cost = gaussian_rdp(alpha, sigma)
        if spent + cost > budget + 1e-12:  # tolerance for floating-point sums
            break
        spent, steps = spent + cost, steps + 1
    return steps


ORDERS = [1 + x / 10 for x in range(1, 100)] + [float(x) for x in range(12, 64)] + [128.0, 256.0, 512.0]


def ville_odometer(t: int, sigma: float, delta: float, orders: list[float]) -> float:
    """Running epsilon after t full-batch Gaussian steps, valid whenever the run stops."""
    return min(t * gaussian_rdp(a, sigma) + log(len(orders) / delta) / (a - 1) for a in orders)


print(f"{whitehouse_statistic([0.01] * 1000, 1e-6):.3f}")  # 1.712
print(steps_allowed(0.01, 1.0, 1e-6))  # 349
alpha, budget = 5.8, 2.9
print(renyi_filter([10.0] * 1000, alpha, budget))  # 100
print(renyi_filter([10.0] * 60 + [5.0] * 1000, alpha, budget) - 60)  # 10
print(f"{budget + log(1 / 1e-5) / (alpha - 1):.3f}")  # 5.299
print(len(ORDERS))  # 154
print(f"{ville_odometer(100, 10.0, 1e-5, ORDERS):.3f}")  # 6.253
print(f"{ville_odometer(100, 10.0, 1e-5, [alpha]):.3f}")  # 5.299
print(f"{ville_odometer(1000, 10.0, 1e-5, [alpha]):.3f}")  # 31.399
ORDERS is the part’s grid of orders. The full edition’s script, adaptive_composition.py, also computes the plug-in failure exactly, checks the Rényi filter by simulation and runs the individual-accounting experiment:
uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/adaptive_composition.py

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
text:
35.1 Why this matters
You trained a model with differential privacy (DP), using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipping and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD: each record joined each batch independently with probability \(q = 0.01\) (Poisson sampling), gradients were clipped to norm \(C\), and noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) was added to their sum, with noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\), for \(k = 10{,}000\) steps. Now you must write “the model is \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP” in a model card. The procedure that bounds or estimates \(\varepsilon\) is an accountant. On this run, composing per-step guarantees gives 11296.93, Rényi differential privacy (RDP) gives 7.4287 or 6.7127 depending on the conversion, the Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) central limit theorem (CLT) gives 6.0071, and a privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant gives the interval \([6.1377, 6.2377]\). Which do you report, and what else must you say?
The numbers differ because they are different kinds of statement. An upper bound comes with a proof that the run is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP; it may be loose, but it is true. An approximation has no proof, and if it lands below the truth, the claim it supports is false. A certified lower bound says the true \(\varepsilon\) is at least this large: not a guarantee, but a referee for every other number. Hence the rule this chapter unpacks: report the tightest upper bound whose assumptions hold for the code you ran, with enough detail that someone else can recompute it.

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
text:
35.2 Every accountant on one run
Every accountant starts from what one step reveals about one record. Along that record’s clipped gradient, in units of \(C\), the output is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) without the record. With it, the record is sampled with probability \(q\) and then shifts the output by 1, giving the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). Accountants differ in how much of this pair they keep before combining \(k\) copies, and whatever they throw away must be replaced by a worst case. So the more they keep, the tighter they are.
The crudest keeps two numbers per step, an amplified \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair (Amplification by subsampling), and composes them. That is a valid bound, but composition must assume every step leaks its worst case, while in reality the losses of different steps mostly cancel. It is right at \(k = 1\) and over a thousand times too large at \(k = 10{,}000\) (Table 35.1); advanced composition is even worse here.
RDP keeps a whole curve, the Rényi divergence of the pair at every order \(\alpha\) (Rényi DP). Curves add exactly under composition, and a conversion then turns \(k\) times the curve into one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair (From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests). Mironov’s, the improved and the optimal conversion are each proved for every pair of distributions with that curve, so all three are upper bounds, ordered Mironov \(\ge\) improved \(\ge\) optimal \(\ge\) true \(\varepsilon\). The improved conversion beats Mironov’s at every order, so never use the older one.
RDP’s excess has two sources, and the run’s length decides which dominates. One is the conversion’s toll, \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), about \(11.5/(\alpha - 1)\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), paid however small the curve is. After one step the curve is tiny, the toll is most of the answer, and RDP with the improved conversion overstates the PLD by 379.1%. In a long run the toll is negligible, but the curve itself keeps only moments of the privacy loss, not its distribution: that costs the last 7.6% at \(k = 10{,}000\), and no conversion can remove it.
The GDP CLT treats the run as \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = q\sqrt{k(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\) (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy), since a sum of many small losses should be nearly Gaussian. But that is a large-\(k\) limit with no error bound, and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is read far in the tail, where a Gaussian approximation is least reliable. On this run it falls below the certified lower bound at every \(k\).
The PLD accountant keeps everything: the whole distribution of the privacy loss on a grid of width \(h\), composed numerically (Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions). Rounding every loss up describes a pair that leaks at least as much as the real one, which stays true through composition, so the result is an upper bound; rounding down gives a lower bound. Each step’s rounding moves the loss by less than \(h\), so after \(k\) steps the two are at most \(kh\) apart: 0.1 here, with \(h = 10^{-5}\).

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
section: 35.3 Calibrating the noise for a target ε
text:
35.3 Calibrating the noise for a target ε
In practice you fix the budget, the steps and the batch size, and ask how much noise to add. Then a loose accountant costs utility: it overstates \(\varepsilon\) at every \(\sigma\), so it asks for more noise to meet the same target. The averaged gradient’s noise has standard deviation \(\sigma C/(qn)\) for \(n\) records, so every percent of \(\sigma\) is a percent of gradient noise.
The noise accountant \(A\) requires for a target \(\varepsilon^*\) is the smallest \(\sigma\) at which its reported \(\varepsilon_A(\sigma)\) meets the target: \[\sigma_A(\varepsilon^*) = \min\{\sigma > 0 : \varepsilon_A(\sigma) \le \varepsilon^*\}. \tag{35.1}\] More noise never raises a correct accountant’s \(\varepsilon\): a noisier run can be made from a less noisy one by adding independent noise, without looking at the data, and that cannot reveal more. So this is where a decreasing function crosses a level, and bisection finds it. Return the end of the final bracket where \(\varepsilon_A \le \varepsilon^*\) was actually checked, never the midpoint, which may miss the target.

At \(\varepsilon = 8\), RDP with the improved conversion sets \(\sigma = 0.917\) and the PLD \(\sigma = 0.885\): 3.6% more noise for the same certified budget (Table 35.2). Across the targets the improved conversion costs 3.4 to 4.9% more noise, less than its 7.6% excess in \(\varepsilon\), because in this range a small rise in \(\sigma\) buys a larger fall in \(\varepsilon\). Mironov’s conversion costs 8.6 to 24.7% more, most at the strictest target, where its toll weighs most.






Figure 35.2: Each accountant’s noise multiplier for a target \(\varepsilon\) (\(k = 10{,}000\), \(q = 0.01\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)), divided by the one the PLD upper bound requires. The CLT and the PLD lower bound fall in the shaded region: less noise than any certified accountant can justify.



Calibrate with the accountant you will report, and never with the CLT. It asks for 2.0 to 4.8% less noise than the certified bound needs, and at \(\varepsilon = 8\) that is provably too little: at its \(\sigma = 0.8676\) the optimistic PLD already gives 8.2594. At small targets the PLD’s fixed width \(kh\) is a large fraction of \(\varepsilon\): at \(\varepsilon = 1\) it brackets \(\sigma\) only to \([3.654, 3.988]\), so refine \(h\).

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
text:
35.4 Where each accountant is tight
The ranking changes with the mechanism, by the principle above: an accountant is tight when its summary describes the mechanism’s privacy loss exactly.
For the plain Gaussian mechanism, with no subsampling, the composed pair is exactly Gaussian, and GDP describes it with one number, \(\mu\), whose squares add. GDP is then exact. A team that releases 100 noisy counts at \(\sigma = 10\) has exactly \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\); an old RDP accountant with Mironov’s conversion reports 5.2985, 21.0% too high, and the improved conversion 4.7285, because RDP keeps this curve exactly but still pays in the conversion.
For pure-DP steps such as randomized response, the privacy loss takes only a few values, so the PLD needs no rounding and is exact. For 100 steps of randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), the exact PLD gives 4.3068, RDP 4.6154, zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) 4.7263, advanced composition 5.8502 and basic composition 10.0000: each summary that keeps less pays more.
For DP-SGD, subsampling makes each step a mixture that no closed form describes exactly, and only the PLD is both certified and tight. zCDP is the wrong tool here: its single line \(\rho\alpha\) must lie above the RDP curve at every order, and at high orders the subsampled curve’s slope approaches the unsubsampled one, so the line cannot express the gain from subsampling. When the noise, the stopping time or per-record budgets are chosen during training, the per-step pair is no longer fixed in advance as the PLD accountant assumes; an RDP filter at a fixed order loses nothing to that adaptivity (Adaptive composition).

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
section: 35.5 Matching the accountant to the code
text:
35.5 Matching the accountant to the code
An accountant takes \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(k\) and trusts that the code does what its theorem assumes. A mismatch makes the number a statement about a different algorithm.
The sampling scheme is the most expensive mismatch, for a mechanical reason. With fixed-size random batches, adding a record must push another one out, so the batch sum can move by up to \(2C\) instead of \(C\), and such a run is covered by the Poisson accountant only at noise multiplier \(\sigma/2\) (Lebeda et al. 2024). With shuffle and partition, each record is used exactly once per epoch, in a batch fixed by the shuffle, and no amplification theorem holds for every dataset. What remains certain is one unamplified Gaussian step per epoch, for zero-out neighbours (one record’s gradient replaced by zero).
In a code review: a script uses a data loader with shuffle=True and batch_size=500 on 50,000 records for 100 epochs, and calls an RDP accountant with sample_rate=0.01, which reports 6.71. That sampler is shuffle and partition, so what holds is 100 unamplified steps at \(\sigma = 1\): \(\mu = 10\) GDP and \(\varepsilon = 91.8173\), or 284.39 under replace-one, where the sum moves by \(2C\). Fixed-size random batches, accounted correctly, would give 47.42 (RDP) and 43.42 (PLD). Switching to Poisson sampling makes the PLD’s 6.24 honest. The factor of 6.96 from fixed-size batches dwarfs the factor of at most 1.19 between RDP and PLD at 10,000 steps: check the sampler before arguing about accountants.
Other assumptions fail quietly. If you tune 10 configurations on the private data and release the best, which one is best depends on all 10 runs, so the release costs all 10 composed: \(\varepsilon = 27.23\) with RDP. The guarantee protects whatever differs between neighbours, so example-level DP protects each example, not a person who contributed many. And the theorems assume exact real-valued Gaussian noise; floating-point sampling can break a mechanism that is correct on paper (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
text:
35.6 What to report
An \(\varepsilon\) without its assumptions cannot be checked or compared. NIST SP 800-226 (2025) and Ponomareva et al. (2023) ask for the setting (who is trusted), what is covered (one run, or tuning too), the unit of privacy, the neighbouring relation, the accountant and whether its assumptions hold, and, for DP-SGD, everything needed to recompute \(\varepsilon\): sampling scheme, \(q\), \(k\), \(\sigma\), \(C\), and the accountant’s version and discretization.
Choose \(\delta\) with its meaning in mind: it is the probability with which the promise may fail. A mechanism that publishes one randomly chosen record in full meets a \(\delta\) of about \(1/n\) with \(\varepsilon = 0\), while exposing someone completely. So \(\delta\) must be much smaller than \(1/n\) for \(n\) units of privacy (The definition of differential privacy): Ponomareva et al. suggest \(n^{-1.1}\), and NIST gives \(1/n^2\) as a common recommendation and calls values above \(10^{-5}\) suspicious. For \(n = 50{,}000\), \(1/n = 2.0\times10^{-5}\), so the customary \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is only half of it.
Report \(\varepsilon\) at several \(\delta\), not one pair. Many different mechanisms share a single \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair and behave differently at smaller \(\delta\), so a reader cannot convert your pair to the \(\delta\) they care about. One composed PLD gives the whole profile cheaply (Table 35.5). For the same reason, give the parameters behind any conversion: the RDP accountant’s is its curve, \(\varepsilon(4.1) = 3.7336\) at the best order 4.1, which the improved conversion turns into 6.7127.

A filled-in statement:

Privacy guarantee. The model was trained with DP-SGD in the central model: the training server is trusted to run the code below, and the guarantee covers every intermediate noisy gradient, hence every checkpoint and the final model. Unit of privacy: one training example; each person contributes at most one example. Neighbouring relation: add or remove one example. Training: Poisson sampling with rate \(q = 0.01\) (\(n = 50{,}000\) examples, expected batch size 500), \(k = 10{,}000\) steps (100 epochs), per-example clipping norm \(C = 1\), Gaussian noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\). Accountant: privacy loss distributions, pessimistic discretization on the grid \(h = 10^{-5}\), both add and remove directions. Guarantee: \((6.24, 10^{-5})\)-DP and \((9.06, 4.0\times10^{-10})\)-DP. The optimistic discretization gives 6.1377 and 8.9378, so the accountant’s own error is at most 0.1000 and 0.1124. For comparison, the RDP accountant with the improved conversion gives 6.7127 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Not covered: hyperparameters were tuned on a public proxy dataset; no tuning on the private data was performed. If the sampling assumption failed (for example, shuffled fixed-size batches), the guarantee without amplification is \((91.82, 10^{-5})\)-DP for zero-out neighbours.

Three habits in it follow from what an upper bound is. It is rounded up: 9.0502 becomes 9.06, because 9.05 would be a claim the accountant has not certified. The optimistic value is its error bar, which an RDP number cannot have, since RDP has no matching lower bound. And where an assumption is in doubt, the statement gives the fallback guarantee that does not rely on it.

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
text:
35.7 Checking an accountant
Test an accountant on cases whose answers you know. With \(q = 1\) there is no subsampling, so \(k\) steps are exactly \(\sqrt k/\sigma\)-GDP, and every upper bound must lie above that closed form. For \(\sigma = 1\) and \(k = 10\) the exact \(\varepsilon\) is 17.8566, and the RDP accountant gives 19.0536, above it as it must be. The CLT formula at \(q = 1\) gives \(\mu = 4.1452\) instead of 3.1623 and \(\varepsilon = 25.5853\): it fails, because its derivation assumes small \(q\). The PLD bracket for the plain Gaussian must contain the same closed form, and it does: \([17.8516, 17.8616]\) at \(h = 10^{-3}\).
Two properties hold for every correct accountant, so a violation is a bug, not slack. The orderings of Section 35.2 must hold at every \(k\), with no reported upper bound below the optimistic PLD. And \(\varepsilon\) must never decrease with \(k\), because what the first \(k\) steps release is part of what \(k + 1\) steps release.
Then compare against an independent library: Google’s dp_accounting (RDP and PLD), Opacus (RDP, GDP, and a privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant, its default), or Microsoft’s prv_accountant. When two RDP accountants disagree, the size of the gap says why: the improved conversion beats Mironov’s by \(\frac{\ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1} + \ln\frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\) at order \(\alpha\) (0.3612 at order 10); on the running example it is what separates Mironov’s 7.43 from the improved 6.71. Certified PLD and PRV brackets from different libraries each contain the truth, so they must overlap; if they do not, one has a bug.
