text:
35.10 Further reading

Ponomareva et al., “How to DP-fy ML: A Practical Guide to Machine Learning with Differential Privacy” (JAIR 2023): matching accounting to the data pipeline, setting \(\delta\), and what to report.
Near, Darais, Lefkovitz & Howarth, “Guidelines for Evaluating Differential Privacy Guarantees” (NIST SP 800-226, 2025): what an evaluator will ask of your claim.
Lebeda, Regehr, Kamath & Steinke, “Avoiding Pitfalls for Privacy Accounting of Subsampled Mechanisms under Composition” (IEEE SaTML 2025): fixed-size batches versus Poisson sampling.
Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz, “Numerical Composition of Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2021): the PRV accountant with certified error bounds, and where the CLT under-reports.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
The common thread
The previous parts built the guarantee and the tools to account for it. This part trains models with it, and asks the questions that decide whether a private model is worth deploying: how do you train with differential privacy (DP), how much accuracy does it cost, which knobs move that cost, and how do you check that the trained model is as private as the accountant claims? The answers are mostly about one algorithm, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD, and about everything around it.
Read this part if you train, review or sign off on a model that claims an \(\varepsilon\). It assumes the Gaussian mechanism and clipping from Differential privacy foundations, and amplification by subsampling and the accountant for DP-SGD from Privacy accounting. Each chapter restates what it uses.
A private training algorithm has two halves. The privacy half says which quantity has bounded sensitivity, meaning how far one record can move it, and how much noise covers that move; it is a theorem, and the accountants of Part 4 turn it into a number. The utility half says how much the noise and the bounding cost in accuracy; it is mostly measured, rarely proved. Every chapter moves one of the two, and keeping them apart is the most useful habit here: a choice that only affects accuracy can be tuned freely, one that touches the privacy half must be accounted for.
The first two chapters build the algorithm. Private empirical risk minimization compares three places to put the noise, on the final weights, inside the objective and on every gradient, and shows that only noise on the gradients survives non-convex models, because it needs nothing but a bound on each record’s gradient. DP-SGD supplies that bound by clipping, adds random minibatches and an accountant, and works out what each knob does. Every later chapter uses it, so these two come first.
The next three ask what else spends the budget, or could spend it better. Hyperparameter tuning shows that picking the best of several private runs is itself a computation on the data, and how to pay for it honestly. Mechanisms built on the follow the regularized leader (FTRL) algorithm, DP-FTRL and matrix factorization, replace the random batches that DP-SGD’s amplification relies on with correlated noise, for settings where sampling cannot be trusted or controlled. Private prediction privatizes answers instead of weights, which can be cheaper when you only need a limited number of predictions.
The next three change the setting rather than the algorithm. Public data and private fine-tuning explains why a public pretrained model helps so much: the noise grows with the number of parameters you train, so fine-tuning fewer of them can be more accurate. User-level differential privacy changes the unit of protection from one record to one person, which is usually what you meant to promise. Disparate impact asks who pays for the noise and the clipping, and finds that small groups and hard examples pay most.
The last two close the loop between theory and practice. Choosing ε turns a budget into what it means for an attacker and asks how to justify one. Auditing private training runs attacks with planted records against a trained model and turns their success into an empirical lower bound on \(\varepsilon\), which catches implementations that do not deliver what the accountant says. It comes last because it checks what the others claim.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
The running examples
Two models recur. The first is ridge-regularized logistic regression in ten dimensions on synthetic data, where the exact minimizer can be computed, so every private method can be compared with the non-private optimum. The second is a small neural network trained with DP-SGD on synthetic data, small enough that every experiment runs on a laptop in seconds, yet non-convex, so clipping and noise behave as they do in deep learning. It runs exactly the configuration whose \(\varepsilon\) Part 4 computed, so you can see what that number costs in accuracy.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
How to read this part
Read the first two chapters in order. Hyperparameter tuning and DP-FTRL change how the algorithm is run and can be read in either order. The chapters on private prediction, public data, user-level privacy and disparate impact are independent of each other. Read choosing \(\varepsilon\) after them, and auditing last. The derivations are in the full edition.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do
By the end of this part you will be able to train a convex model privately and predict what it costs, and run DP-SGD knowing which knobs set \(\varepsilon\) and which only set accuracy. You will be able to check an implementation for the details that silently break its guarantee, account for tuning, decide when correlated noise, private prediction or a public pretrained model is the better route, and state the privacy unit you protect. And you will be able to say who pays for the noise, choose an \(\varepsilon\) you can defend, and audit a trained model to test whether it is as private as claimed.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.1 Why this matters
Most of machine learning is empirical risk minimization (ERM): choose the weights \(w\) that minimize the average loss on the training data, usually plus a ridge penalty \(\frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\). The trained weights are a function of every record, and Membership inference showed that they give some of those records away. Differential privacy (DP) promises that the distribution of whatever you release changes by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), plus a slack \(\delta\), when one record changes. To keep that promise for a trained model, randomness has to enter somewhere between the data and the released weights, and there are three natural places: on the final weights (output perturbation), inside the objective (objective perturbation), or on every gradient during training (gradient perturbation).
The one idea that organizes all three is that privacy needs a bound on how far one record can move what you release. That bound is the sensitivity, and the noise is sized to hide a move of that length. The three methods differ only in which quantity they bound, and each step back toward the data needs fewer assumptions. Output perturbation needs an exact, unique minimizer of a strongly convex objective. Objective perturbation needs that and a loss with bounded curvature. Gradient perturbation, for its privacy, needs only that each record’s gradient is bounded, with no convexity and no exact solution, which is why it is the one that survives in deep learning, as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD.
Throughout, neighbouring datasets differ by replacing one record, so both have \(n\) records; \(L\) bounds the length of every record’s loss gradient. The running example is ridge-regularized logistic regression in \(d = 10\) dimensions with \(\lambda = 0.01\), features on the unit sphere (so \(L = 1\)), and a target of \(\varepsilon = 1\), with \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for the methods that need one. Quality is measured by the excess risk, how much worse the private weights fit the training objective than the exact minimizer.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.2 Output perturbation
The simplest private trainer treats training as a black box: compute the exact minimizer \(w^*\), then add noise. For that you need the minimizer’s sensitivity. Replacing one record changes the average loss by one term in and one out, so the objective’s gradient changes by at most \(2L/n\) anywhere. The ridge makes the objective \(\lambda\)-strongly convex: its gradient grows by at least \(\lambda\) per unit of distance, so a point where the gradient is \(g\) long lies within \(g/\lambda\) of the minimizer. At the new minimizer, the old objective’s gradient is at most \(2L/n\), hence the minimizer moves by at most \[\|w^*(D) - w^*(D')\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{36.1}\] Add Gaussian noise to that, and you have the Gaussian mechanism (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Its privacy depends only on the ratio \(\mu\) of the sensitivity to the noise standard deviation, and the exact calibration (Balle & Wang 2018) gives the largest admissible ratio \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), \(\mu = 0.2681\), so the noise must be \(\sigma = 3.7306\) times the sensitivity. The classic formula \(\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}/\varepsilon\) asks for 4.8448 times, 30% more noise for the same guarantee, so always calibrate exactly.
The noise must hide the worst case, not the actual move. In one dimension with \(n = 20\) records and \(\lambda = 0.5\), replacing one record moves the minimizer by 0.0832, but the bound is \(2/(0.5 \times 20) = 0.2\), and the noise is sized for 0.2 (Figure 36.1).






Figure 36.1: Left: two neighbouring regularized logistic objectives in one dimension (\(n = 20\), \(\lambda = 0.5\)), their minimizers (vertical lines) 0.083 apart, below the bound \(2L/(\lambda n) = 0.2\). Right: the released weight’s density under each dataset with Gaussian noise for \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\); the noise must hide a shift as large as the bound, not the actual shift.



What does the noise cost? Near the minimizer the objective is a bowl whose curvature is the Hessian \(H\), so a random displacement \(Z\) raises it by about \(\frac12 Z^\top HZ\), and for Gaussian noise that averages to \[\mathbb E\big[J(\tilde w) - J(w^*)\big] \approx \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\operatorname{tr}H. \tag{36.2}\] Notice the mismatch: the noise is calibrated to the curvature the ridge guarantees, \(\lambda\), but the damage is weighed by the actual curvature \(H\), data included. A small ridge buys a better non-private fit and costs a lot of noise, since \(\sigma \propto 1/\lambda\). In the running example at \(n = 10{,}000\), the sensitivity is \(2/(0.01 \times 10{,}000) = 0.02\), so \(\sigma = 0.07461\) per coordinate, next to a minimizer of length 2.886. The Hessian has trace 0.3129, and Equation 36.2 predicts an excess risk of \(8.711 \times 10^{-4}\); 20 simulated releases average \(9.274 \times 10^{-4}\). Because the noise falls like \(1/n\), the excess risk falls like \(1/n^2\), faster than the \(1/n\) statistical error of the non-private model, so in this convex, low-dimensional setting privacy eventually costs less than sampling does.
The weak point is that the sensitivity bound holds for the exact minimizer. If the optimizer stops at a point whose gradient has length \(g\), each output may sit \(g/\lambda\) from its exact minimizer, and the sensitivity becomes \(2L/(\lambda n) + 2g/\lambda\). In the running example a tolerance of \(g = 10^{-3}\), which looks tight, gives a sensitivity of 0.22 instead of 0.02: eleven times the noise and roughly 121 times the excess risk. To keep the extra term small you need \(g\) well below \(L/n\), which shrinks with the dataset. And the stopping rule must be a gradient check, not a step count: the privacy proof needs the bound on every pair of datasets, and “50 Newton steps” only guarantees it on datasets where 50 steps happen to be enough.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.3 Objective perturbation
Output perturbation wastes the data’s curvature: it pays for the worst case \(\lambda\) and is judged on the actual \(H\). Chaudhuri, Monteleoni & Sarwate (2011) put the noise inside the optimization instead. They add a random linear term \(\frac1n\langle b, w\rangle\) to the objective and minimize exactly. A linear term acts like a constant force pushing the minimizer, and all of the objective’s curvature resists it, so where the data add curvature the minimizer moves less.
The privacy argument is subtler, because the output is no longer “something fixed plus noise”, and its result says where the budget goes. Each noise vector \(b\) produces exactly one output, so the output’s density is the noise density at the matching \(b\) times a stretching factor from the change of variables. Both factors differ between neighbours, and each consumes part of \(\varepsilon\). The stretching factor is governed by how much one record can change the objective’s curvature, which needs a loss of the form \(g(y\langle w, x\rangle)\) with \(|g'| \le 1\), curvature \(0 \le g'' \le c\) and \(\|x\| \le 1\); logistic regression qualifies with \(c = \frac14\). What is left for the noise is \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon - 2\ln\Big(1 + \frac{c}{n\lambda}\Big), \tag{36.3}\] and \(b\) is drawn with density proportional to \(e^{-\varepsilon'\|b\|/2}\). The result is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The stretching share shrinks as \(n\lambda\) grows: at \(n = 10{,}000\) in the running example it is 0.0050, so \(\varepsilon' = 0.9950\), while at \(n = 100\) the noise would get only \(\varepsilon' = 0.5537\). If \(\varepsilon'\) comes out non-positive, the method raises the ridge until the stretching takes only half the budget.
The benefit shows in the excess risk. To first order the minimizer moves by \(-H^{-1}b/n\), so the damage is weighed by \(H^{-1}\) rather than \(H\). If every eigenvalue of \(H\) is close to some \(h\), objective perturbation beats output perturbation by about \((h/\lambda)^2\). When the ridge supplies all the curvature the two are the same; when the data add curvature, objective perturbation wins quadratically. In the running example the curvature lies between 0.0263 and 0.0330, about three times the ridge, and the measured excess risk at \(n = 10{,}000\) is \(8.156 \times 10^{-5}\), against \(8.321 \times 10^{-4}\) for pure-DP output perturbation at the same \(\varepsilon\): ten times better, close to the \(3^2 = 9\) the rule of thumb predicts.
The analysis is safe, not tight. In one dimension the output densities can be computed exactly, and over 500 random datasets of 5 records with \(\lambda = 0.1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), the largest log ratio is 0.3779 (Figure 36.2). The noise part never exceeds 0.0992 of its budget of 0.1891, and the stretching part never exceeds 0.3395 of its budget of 0.8109, because the worst cases each factor assumes cannot happen together for logistic loss. The bound has to cover every dataset, so you cannot spend that slack, but for logistic loss the guarantee is conservative.






Figure 36.2: Objective perturbation in one dimension, \(n = 5\), \(\lambda = 0.1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\). Left: the exact densities of the released weight under a dataset and its neighbour, computed by change of variables. Right: their log ratio, the privacy loss, which stays well inside \(\pm\varepsilon\).



The price is in the requirements: exact minimization (the change of variables needs a unique minimizer), a twice-differentiable loss (a support vector machine’s hinge loss must be smoothed first) and a known curvature bound. Kifer, Smith & Thakurta (2012) extend it to Gaussian noise and constraints, and Iyengar et al. (2019) give a version that tolerates approximate solvers by adding a little output noise on top.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.4 Gradient perturbation: noisy gradient descent
Real training is iterative and stops early. Gradient perturbation, analysed by Song, Chaudhuri & Sarwate (2013) and Bassily, Smith & Thakurta (2014), makes each step of the optimizer private and composes the steps. Its simplest form is full-batch gradient descent with Gaussian noise added to the mean gradient at each of \(T\) steps.
Each step is a Gaussian mechanism. Given the current weights, which are public at that moment because they were computed from earlier noisy outputs, replacing one record moves the mean gradient by at most \(2L/n\), whatever the weights are. Gaussian steps compose exactly: \(T\) steps, each with ratio \(\mu_{\text{step}}\), are as private as one Gaussian mechanism with ratio \(\sqrt T\,\mu_{\text{step}}\) (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy). Setting that equal to \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) gives the noise on the mean gradient, \[\sigma = \frac{2L}{n}\cdot\frac{\sqrt T}{\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)}. \tag{36.4}\] Releasing every iterate is covered. Nothing in this argument used convexity, a minimizer or smoothness: only the gradient bound at the points the algorithm visits.
The consequence for practice is that the step count is a privacy parameter. Every step spends budget, so the per-step noise grows like \(\sqrt T\). For a strongly convex objective, the excess risk is an optimization error that shrinks geometrically with \(T\) plus a noise floor, roughly \(d\sigma^2/(4\beta)\) for a step size \(1/\beta\) set by the largest curvature \(\beta\), that grows in proportion to \(T\). Too few steps leave optimization error; too many drown the solution in noise (Figure 36.3).






Figure 36.3: Excess risk of noisy gradient descent at \(n = 10{,}000\), \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (1, 10^{-5})\), against the number of steps \(T\), averaged over datasets, with the same steps without noise (dashed). The noiseless error falls geometrically and reaches machine precision; the noisy run is limited by noise that grows with \(T\), so its error is smallest near \(T = 50\).



You cannot pick \(T\) by trying several and keeping the best validation score for free: that choice is itself a computation on the data (Hyperparameter tuning). One honest option is a rule that uses only public quantities, the ridge, a curvature bound, the dimension, \(n\) and the budget, and minimizes the predicted excess risk. For \(n = 10{,}000\) it picks \(T = 218\), with per-step noise \(\sigma = 0.01102\) and a predicted excess risk of \(1.301 \times 10^{-3}\); simulated runs average \(1.384 \times 10^{-3}\). The rule is pessimistic, because it only knows that the curvature is at least \(\lambda\). With the data’s actual curvature the best \(T\) is near 50, with \(2.875 \times 10^{-4}\), five times less, but you may only use that knowledge if you obtained it privately or from similar public data.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.5 Which to use
Each method is private by its own argument, so the choice is about accuracy. Theory says that for strongly convex problems the best achievable excess risk under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP falls like \[\frac{L^2\,d\,\ln(1/\delta)}{\lambda\,(n\varepsilon)^2}, \tag{36.5}\] up to logarithmic factors in \(n\) (Bassily, Smith & Thakurta 2014), and that a version of noisy gradient descent attains it; no method can do better, by the fingerprinting lower bounds of Lower bounds. Two practical readings follow. The cost grows with the dimension \(d\), so more parameters cost more privacy. And \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\) appear only as the product \(n\varepsilon\), because every sensitivity is proportional to \(1/n\) and every noise to sensitivity over \(\varepsilon\): to keep the same accuracy at half the budget, you need twice the data.
All methods share the rate; the constants differ, and the constant is what you choose by. Table 36.1 measures them on the running example.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
section: 36.6 When the model is not convex
text:
36.6 When the model is not convex
A neural network’s loss is not convex, and that breaks the first two methods outright. Without strong convexity the minimizer need not be unique or move continuously with the data. Take a one-dimensional loss with two wells near \(\pm1\), where the empirical minimizer sits in the well favoured by the majority label: with 501 labels of one kind and 500 of the other, changing one label flips the majority and moves the minimizer by 2.0010. No \(1/n\) appears, so output perturbation would need \(\sigma = 7.465\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), more than three times the distance between the wells, whatever the dataset size. Objective perturbation fails at its first step, since the map from noise to output is no longer invertible.
Gradient perturbation keeps its guarantee, because its argument only used the gradient bound at the visited points. What it loses is the accuracy guarantee: whether it learns anything becomes an empirical question. For a neural network there is no bound \(L\) either, since gradients can be arbitrarily long, but you can force one by clipping: rescale each record’s gradient to length at most \(C\) before averaging, as Beyond global sensitivity clips a value before averaging it. The mean of clipped gradients moves by at most \(2C/n\), and the privacy argument goes through with \(L = C\). Clipping has a cost of its own: the mean of clipped gradients is no longer the gradient of the objective, so the algorithm optimizes something slightly different.
Full-batch steps are also too slow for large datasets. Using a random minibatch at each step makes steps cheap and, by amplification by subsampling, more private, since each record is used only with a small probability. Clipping, noise, minibatches and a subsampled-Gaussian accountant together are DP-SGD.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.7 Code
The calibrations of this chapter take a few lines: find the largest admissible Gaussian ratio by bisection on the exact \(\delta\), then size the noise for each method.
from math import erfc, exp, log, sqrt


def phi(x: float) -> float:
    """Standard normal cumulative distribution function."""
    return 0.5 * erfc(-x / sqrt(2))


def gaussian_delta(eps: float, mu: float) -> float:
    """Exact delta of a Gaussian mechanism with sensitivity-to-noise ratio mu."""
    return phi(mu / 2 - eps / mu) - exp(eps) * phi(-mu / 2 - eps / mu)


def gaussian_mu(eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Largest ratio mu for which the Gaussian mechanism is (eps, delta)-DP."""
    lo, hi = 1e-6, 50.0
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (lo, mid) if gaussian_delta(eps, mid) > delta else (mid, hi)
    return lo


mu = gaussian_mu(1.0, 1e-5)
print(f"{mu:.4f} {1 / mu:.4f}")  # 0.2681 3.7306
print(f"{sqrt(2 * log(1.25 / 1e-5)):.4f}")  # 4.8448
# Output perturbation: sensitivity 2L/(lambda n), L = 1, lambda = 0.01, n = 10,000.
print(f"{2 / (0.01 * 10_000) / mu:.5f}")  # 0.07461
# Objective perturbation: the share of eps left for the noise, c = 1/4.
print(f"{1 - 2 * log(1 + 0.25 / (10_000 * 0.01)):.4f}")  # 0.9950
# Noisy gradient descent: noise on the mean gradient for T = 218 steps.
print(f"{2 / 10_000 * sqrt(218) / mu:.5f}")  # 0.01102
The full edition’s script implements the three methods for logistic regression with exact Newton solves, computes the exact one-dimensional densities of objective perturbation, and runs the comparison:

text:
36.9 Further reading

Chaudhuri, Monteleoni & Sarwate, “Differentially Private Empirical Risk Minimization” (JMLR 2011): output and objective perturbation with their excess-risk bounds.
Bassily, Smith & Thakurta, “Private Empirical Risk Minimization: Efficient Algorithms and Tight Error Bounds” (FOCS 2014): noisy gradient methods that attain the optimal rates, and the matching lower bounds.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 37  DP-SGD
text:
37.1 Why this matters
Private empirical risk minimization ended with one method left standing for non-convex models: gradient descent with Gaussian noise on every step, made safe for any model by clipping each record’s gradient. Two more changes make it practical for differential privacy (DP) at scale. Each step uses a random minibatch, which makes steps cheap and, by amplification, more private. And an accountant composes thousands of such steps into one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). The result is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD (Abadi et al. 2016), which nearly every private deep-learning system runs. Privacy accounting computed its \(\varepsilon\) without running it; this chapter runs it, and asks what the noise and the clipping cost and how to set the knobs that control them.
The one idea is that the privacy analysis never looks inside the model. Each step releases a noisy sum of clipped per-example gradients. Clipping caps each record’s contribution at length \(C\), so adding or removing one record moves the sum by at most \(C\), whatever the network, the loss or the current weights, and the proof stops there. That splits the knobs in two. The noise multiplier \(\sigma\), the sampling rate \(q\) and the number of steps \(T\) set \(\varepsilon\), and nothing else does. The clipping norm \(C\) and the step size \(\eta\) do not change \(\varepsilon\) at all; they decide how much of the gradient survives and how far the noise pushes the weights. The cost of privacy then comes in two forms: a bias from clipping, which changes the direction of the average gradient, and a variance from the noise.
The running example is a network with one hidden layer of 64 units, \(p = 3{,}329\) weights, trained on \(n = 10{,}000\) synthetic records and tested on 20,000 more, with \(q = 0.01\) (expected batch \(B = 100\)), \(C = 0.5\), \(\eta = 0.5\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\) steps: Part 4’s running example, now actually trained.

title: 37  DP-SGD
section: 37.2 The algorithm and what its guarantee assumes
text:
37.2 The algorithm and what its guarantee assumes
Each step of DP-SGD does five things, and each is an assumption of the proof:

Sample: put each record in the batch independently with probability \(q\) (Poisson sampling).
Per-example gradients: compute each sampled record’s gradient \(g_i\) separately.
Clip: rescale each to length at most \(C\), \(\bar g_i = g_i\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\).
Noisy sum: add Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to each coordinate of \(\sum_i\bar g_i\).
Step: divide by the expected batch size \(B = qn\), a public constant, and take a gradient step.

Why is this private? With the weights and the other records fixed, the record in question adds at most one term of length \(C\) to the sum, so a step on which it is drawn is a Gaussian mechanism with shift \(C\) and noise \(\sigma C\), so its ratio of shift to noise is \(1/\sigma\); the clipping norm cancels. Under Poisson sampling it is drawn with probability \(q\) independently of everyone else, so its effect on a step is a mixture of “shifted” and “not there”, which is the subsampled Gaussian of Amplification by subsampling. Dividing by a public \(B\) is post-processing. The steps depend on earlier outputs only through the weights, and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curves add even for such adaptive sequences (Rényi DP), so the accountant adds the \(T\) per-step curves and converts once (From Rényi DP to (ε, δ)). Neighbours differ by adding or removing a record, which is the relation Poisson sampling pairs with. For the running example the accountant gives \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), attained at order \(\alpha = 4.1\), and Table 37.1 gives the noise multiplier other budgets need with the same \(q\) and \(T\).

Because the proof rests on these steps, an implementation can break the guarantee by changing a detail, with no visible symptom. Batch normalization computes statistics over the batch, so one record changes every other record’s gradient and the sum can move by much more than \(C\); private models use normalizations that act on one example at a time, such as group or layer normalization. Choosing \(C\) from the current batch, say as its median gradient norm, makes the noise scale depend on the data; fix \(C\) in advance, from public data or a private estimate. Shuffling the data and cutting it into fixed batches is a different mechanism, which can be much less private than the Poisson accountant reports. Dividing by the actual batch size \(|S_t|\) reveals how many records were drawn, which changes when one is added, so it is not post-processing; divide by \(B\). The accountant must see every step, including the steps of runs discarded during tuning (Hyperparameter tuning). And the guarantee is per record: a person with many records needs user-level privacy, and preprocessing that uses the data, such as normalizing features by their mean, must itself be private or use public statistics.
How large is the noise in practice? The averaged update carries noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C/B = 1 \times 0.5/100 = 0.005\) per coordinate. A Gaussian vector of \(p\) such coordinates has length close to \(0.005\sqrt p\), which is about 0.288 for 3,329 weights. The averaged clipped gradient is 0.070 long at the first step and between 0.015 and 0.027 from step 1,000 on, so every step’s noise is about ten times longer than its signal. Training works anyway because the signal points in roughly the same direction from step to step while the noise is independent: over \(k\) steps the signals add to about \(k\) times their length and the noise to about \(\sqrt k\) times, since independent vectors add in squares. Signal overtakes noise when \(k \cdot 0.026 > \sqrt k \cdot 0.288\), after about 123 steps. The final model reaches test accuracy 0.9589, against 0.9627 for non-private SGD.

title: 37  DP-SGD
section: 37.3 Clipping: bias, noise and the choice of C
text:
37.3 Clipping: bias, noise and the choice of C
The clipping norm does not affect privacy, but it controls both forms of cost. Averaged over the sampling and the noise, the update direction is \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|g_i\|}\Big)g_i, \tag{37.1}\] the average gradient with each record weighted by \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\). Each record is in the batch with probability \(q\) and the noise has mean zero, so dividing the noisy sum by \(B = qn\) cancels the \(q\) exactly; that is why the denominator is the expected batch size. The weights are where the bias lives. Records the model fits badly, such as rare examples, members of small groups or mislabelled points, have large gradients and are down-weighted, while well-fitted records keep their full weight. So DP-SGD follows the gradient of a reweighted loss whose weights change during training, and Disparate impact measures who pays for this.
Two regimes follow from the formula. When \(C\) is below every per-example gradient norm, every gradient is clipped to exactly length \(C\), so the clipped sum is \(C\) times a sum of unit vectors, and the noise is \(C\) times \(\sigma\) times a standard normal vector. The whole update is then \(\eta C/B\) times something that does not depend on \(C\): DP-SGD becomes normalized SGD plus noise, and depends on \(\eta\) and \(C\) only through their product \(\eta C\). Lowering \(C\) further changes nothing once \(\eta\) is scaled up to match, which is why practitioners often clip aggressively and tune only the step size (De et al. 2022 report that small clipping norms work well). When \(C\) is above most gradient norms, the clipped average stops growing with \(C\) but the noise \(\sigma C/B\) keeps growing, so the signal-to-noise ratio falls like \(1/C\). A large \(C\) is never better than the smallest \(C\) that clips almost nothing.
Table 37.2 shows both regimes on the running example at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\), once with \(\eta\) fixed and once with \(\eta C\) fixed at 0.25.

title: 37  DP-SGD
section: 37.4 Batch size at a fixed budget
text:
37.4 Batch size at a fixed budget
Suppose the budget \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) and the number of epochs \(E\) are fixed. Each epoch is \(1/q\) steps, so should you take many small steps or few large ones? Recall from Amplification by subsampling that for small \(q\) a step’s RDP is about \(\frac\alpha2q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), close to \(\alpha q^2/(2\sigma^2)\) when \(\sigma\) is well above 1. Over \(E/q\) steps that adds up to about \(\alpha Eq/(2\sigma^2)\), so \(\varepsilon\) stays fixed when \(q/\sigma^2\) does: the noise multiplier must grow like \(\sqrt q\). The noise on the averaged gradient, \(\sigma C/B\) with \(B = qn\), then falls like \(1/\sqrt B\). Larger batches give cleaner gradients.
Small batches are worse than that law says. They need small \(\sigma\), and when \(\sigma\) is near or below 1, \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\) is much larger than \(1/\sigma^2\), so each step costs more than the approximation assumes, by the factor \(\sigma^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\). Steps with little noise are expensive per unit of signal because sampling buys little in the tail of the privacy loss. title: 37  DP-SGD
section: 37.5 Per-example gradient norms without per-example gradients
text:
37.5 Per-example gradient norms without per-example gradients
Ordinary backpropagation computes the gradient of the batch’s summed loss, never each record’s. Forming all \(B\) per-example gradients costs \(B\) times the model’s gradient memory, which is prohibitive for large models. Ghost clipping avoids it for dense layers. A dense layer’s gradient for one record is an outer product \(\delta_ia_i^\top\) of the error flowing back into the layer and the layer’s input, and the length of an outer product is the product of the lengths, \(\|\delta_i\|\,\|a_i\|\). So one backward pass gives every record’s gradient norm, layer by layer, without forming any gradient; the clipped sum then comes from rescaling each record’s error by its clipping factor and doing the usual batch product. For a sequence of \(T\) tokens, the squared norm is a sum over pairs of tokens of input dot products times error dot products, which costs two \(T \times T\) Gram matrices per record. That beats forming the gradient only when \(2T^2 < p_{\text{in}}p_{\text{out}}\), so long sequences in narrow layers favour explicit gradients, and Bu, Mao & Xu (2022) choose per layer.

The whole loss comes from the noise, and it is steeply non-linear in \(\varepsilon\): from 8 to 4 the accuracy drops by half a point, from 2 to 1 by 2.7 points, and from 1 to 0.5 by almost 10 (Figure 37.3).






Figure 37.3: Test accuracy of DP-SGD on the running example at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) against \(\varepsilon\) (log scale), with the non-private model dashed. Accuracy is close to non-private above \(\varepsilon = 4\) and falls steeply below \(\varepsilon = 1\).



The signal-against-noise argument of Section 37.2 explains the collapse. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the noise on the averaged gradient is about 1.19 long against a signal of about 0.026, so signal overtakes noise only after about 2,100 steps, and the 10,000 steps hold only a few independent useful moves. With \(\sigma = 4\) the model reaches its accuracy early and then wanders (Figure 37.4). Before promising a budget, locate where that collapse happens for your task.






Figure 37.4: Left: test accuracy during training with clipping alone, with \(\sigma = 1\) (\(\varepsilon = 6.71\)) and with \(\sigma = 4\). Right: the length of the averaged clipped gradient at each step (solid, log scale) against the length of the noise on it (dotted). The noise is about ten times longer than the signal at \(\sigma = 1\), and about forty times at \(\sigma = 4\).



Run-to-run variation grows with the noise too: the standard deviation over runs is 0.0019 at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and 0.018 at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\). A single private run is one sample from a wide distribution, so comparing two configurations by one run each is reliable only for differences well above that spread. For Part 4’s configuration, \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) costs 0.4 points of accuracy here; reaching \(\varepsilon = 1\) would cost about four. Choosing ε asks which trade is worth making, and Auditing private training checks whether the trained model is as private as the accountant says.

title: 37  DP-SGD
text:
37.7 Code
Before a long run, check how the noise compares with the signal. This snippet computes the noise on the averaged gradient and the number of steps after which a steady signal overtakes it, for the running example at \(\sigma = 1\) and at \(\sigma = 4.13\) (\(\varepsilon = 1\)), using the signal length of about 0.026 measured in the run:
from math import sqrt


def noise_length(sigma: float, clip: float, batch: float, params: int) -> float:
    """Approximate length of the noise on the averaged clipped gradient."""
    return sigma * clip / batch * sqrt(params)


def break_even_steps(noise: float, signal: float) -> float:
    """Steps after which a steady signal (adds like k) overtakes independent noise (adds like sqrt k)."""
    return (noise / signal) ** 2


print(f"{1.0 * 0.5 / 100:.3f}")  # 0.005
print(f"{noise_length(1.0, 0.5, 100, 3329):.3f}")  # 0.288
print(f"{break_even_steps(0.288, 0.026):.0f}")  # 123
print(f"{noise_length(4.13, 0.5, 100, 3329):.2f}")  # 1.19
print(f"{break_even_steps(1.19, 0.026):.0f}")  # 2095

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.1 Why this matters
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, run once with a fixed step size, clipping norm, batch size and number of steps, satisfies differential privacy (DP) with the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) its accountant reports; this is DP-SGD, and its guarantee covers one training run. Nobody trains once. You try a grid of step sizes, score each model on a validation set and ship the best, and every run and every score touched private data. How much does the search leak, and how do you pay for it honestly?
Releasing the best of \(k\) private runs can cost as much as releasing all \(k\), and composition, which charges for every run, turns a grid of 10 DP-SGD runs of this part’s running example from \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) into 27.23. But one change to the procedure changes the answer: draw the number of runs at random, from a suitable distribution, before the search starts. Then the best-of release costs a constant multiple of one run plus a term that grows only with the logarithm of the expected number of runs. For 10 runs in expectation, the cost falls from 27.23 to between 10.08 and 13.67, depending on the distribution, and for 1,000 runs from 1,035.93 to 13.46.
The one idea: the model you ship depends on every run, and a fixed number of runs lets an attacker test for the event “every run came out badly”, whose likelihood ratio is the product of the per-run ratios. A random number of runs explains that event mostly by “there happened to be few runs”, which does not depend on the data.

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 38.2 The best of k runs costs k runs
text:
38.2 The best of k runs costs k runs
A choice among eight step sizes carries at most three bits, so why charge for it? Because the released model is not just the choice: it is a whole private run, picked because of how it came out. The worst case is easy to build. Let one run be randomized response on two outcomes, “good” and “bad”: on a dataset \(D\) it comes out good with probability \(1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), on its neighbour \(D'\) with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), so one run is exactly \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The best of \(k\) runs is bad only if every run is bad. The runs are independent, so the probability of that event is a product of \(k\) per-run probabilities on each dataset, and its likelihood ratio is the product of \(k\) ratios of \(e^\varepsilon\) each: \[\frac{P_D[\text{best of } k \text{ is bad}]}{P_{D'}[\text{best of } k \text{ is bad}]} = e^{k\varepsilon}. \tag{38.1}\] Here the best of \(k\) is exactly \(k\varepsilon\)-DP, no better than releasing all \(k\) runs. With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(k = 10\), the whole loss sits on one rare event: the privacy loss is \(-0.0446\) with probability 0.9564 and 10 with probability 0.0436 (Figure 38.1, right). An attacker who checks whether the released model is bad gets a likelihood ratio of \(e^{10}\) whenever the test fires.






Figure 38.1: Left: the exact \(\varepsilon\) of releasing the best of \(K\) randomized-response runs, each \(1\)-DP, against the expected number of runs, for a fixed number of runs, a Poisson, a geometric and a logarithmic number. A fixed number grows linearly; the geometric and logarithmic numbers stay below their bounds \(3\varepsilon\) and \(2\varepsilon\). Right: the privacy loss of the released outcome under \(D\) for one run, the best of 10 runs and the best of a Poisson number with mean 10; the best of 10 puts a loss of 10 on an event of probability 0.0436.



This is not a contrived corner: a DP-SGD run that sometimes diverges is a run with a “bad” outcome whose probability depends a little on the data, and best-of-\(k\) multiplies those small dependences. A particular search may leak much less, but no analysis that knows only each run’s guarantee can promise it, so a cheaper guarantee needs a different procedure.
Tuning without noise and then training once privately does not help: the winning hyperparameters are a non-private function of the data, which the final run’s \(\varepsilon\) does not cover. Papernot & Steinke (2022) build a model whose best regularization weight alone reveals whether a few outliers were in the training set.
The safe baseline is composition: charge every run. For DP-SGD this is simple, because the accountant charges each step the same whatever weights it is applied to, so \(k\) runs of \(T\) steps cost exactly one run of \(kT\) steps. Table 38.1 applies it to the running example (\(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), 10,000 steps, one run at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)).

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.3 Random stopping
Liu & Talwar (2019) found the change that breaks the \(k\varepsilon\) barrier. After each run, flip a coin and stop with probability \(\gamma\); then release the best run seen. The number of runs is geometric with mean \(1/\gamma\), and if each run is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, the release is \(3\varepsilon\)-DP whatever \(\gamma\) is.
Why a constant, and why 3? Write \(p\) for the probability that one run produces outcome \(y\), \(p_>\) for the probability that it produces something strictly better, and \(p_\ge = p_> + p\). Averaging the best-of-\(k\) probabilities over the geometric number of runs gives \[P[\text{release} = y] = \frac{\gamma\,p}{\big(\gamma + (1 - \gamma)p_>\big)\big(\gamma + (1 - \gamma)p_\ge\big)}. \tag{38.2}\] Each of \(p\), \(p_>\) and \(p_\ge\) is the probability of an event about one run, so each moves by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) between neighbours. The constant \(\gamma\), which does not depend on the data, cannot amplify those moves. Three factors, each moving by at most \(e^\varepsilon\): the ratio is at most \(e^{3\varepsilon}\). Compare the fixed-\(k\) case, where the ratio was a \(k\)-th power. The event “every run was bad” is now mostly the event “the coin stopped early”.
The 3 can be approached: on a three-outcome mechanism that is exactly 1-DP, the release reaches 2.9987. With two outcomes, as in randomized response, nothing is better than the best outcome, so only two factors move: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the exact value rises from 1.7957 at \(\gamma = 0.1\) to 1.9977 at \(\gamma = 0.001\) (Figure 38.1, left).
The price is paid in runs. The release misses the top fraction \(\pi\) of a single run’s outcomes with probability at most \(\gamma/\pi\). With a grid of 8 and \(\gamma = 1/8\), a mean of 8 runs, the chance of never trying the best eighth is 0.4667; it takes \(\gamma = 1/80\), a mean of 80 runs, to bring it to 0.0805. The geometric distribution is spread out, stopping after one run with probability 1/8 at \(\gamma = 1/8\), and that spread is what buys the privacy.

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.4 Rényi bounds for DP-SGD
DP-SGD is not usefully \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any small \(\varepsilon\). Its guarantee is a curve in Rényi differential privacy (RDP): a bound \(\varepsilon(\lambda)\) on the Rényi divergence of order \(\lambda\) between its outputs on neighbours, where curves add under composition and are converted to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, at the best order (Rényi differential privacy). Papernot & Steinke (2022) extended random stopping to RDP and to a family of distributions for the number of runs \(K\), the truncated negative binomial with a shape parameter \(\eta > -1\). The geometric distribution is \(\eta = 1\); \(\eta = 0\) is the logarithmic distribution. For a run with RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\lambda)\), the best of \(K\) runs has curve at most \[\varepsilon(\lambda) + (1 + \eta)\Big(1 - \frac1{\hat\lambda}\Big)\varepsilon(\hat\lambda) + \frac{(1 + \eta)\ln(1/\gamma)}{\hat\lambda} + \frac{\ln\mathbb E[K]}{\lambda - 1}, \tag{38.3}\] for any second order \(\hat\lambda \ge 1\) you choose, where \(\gamma\) is the distribution’s other parameter, set by the mean.
Each term pays for something. The first is one run, the floor, since the release is a run. The last is the number of runs, and it is logarithmic: ten times more runs adds \(\ln 10/(\lambda - 1)\). The middle terms pay for the tail of \(K\), how well an attacker can tell “many runs, all bad” from “few runs”, as a constant multiple of the run’s own privacy at another order. For a pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP run the bound becomes \((2 + \eta)\varepsilon\): \(3\varepsilon\) for the geometric, as before, and \(2\varepsilon\) for the logarithmic.
For a Poisson number of runs with mean \(\mu\), the bound is \[\varepsilon(\lambda) + \mu\hat\delta + \frac{\ln\mu}{\lambda - 1}, \tag{38.4}\] where the run must be \((\hat\varepsilon, \hat\delta)\)-DP with \(e^{\hat\varepsilon} \le 1 + 1/(\lambda - 1)\). The tail term \(\mu\hat\delta\) is linear in \(\mu\), but it is multiplied by the run’s \(\hat\delta\) at a small \(\hat\varepsilon\), so it is small only when one run is very private.
On the running example (Table 38.2, Figure 38.2), the logarithmic distribution costs 10.08 for 10 runs in expectation, 1.5 times one run, and going to 1,000 runs adds only 3.38. The Poisson bound starts well but grows nearly linearly, because one run at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) is far from private enough at the small \(\hat\varepsilon\) the condition demands.

Smaller \(\eta\) gives a cheaper bound but a more skewed \(K\), which often runs only a few candidates. With mean 10, the logarithmic distribution stops after one run with probability 0.2692, against 0.1000 for the geometric; the Poisson is concentrated near its mean, with \(P[K \le 1] = 4.99 \times 10^{-4}\) (Figure 38.3). They also have conditions. Each run must draw its candidate independently from a distribution fixed in advance, typically uniform on the grid: this is random search. Adaptive methods that choose the next candidate from the scores so far, such as Bayesian optimization, are not covered and need adaptive composition. And the score that ranks the runs must itself be part of each run’s private output.

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 38.5 The validation score, and selecting among fixed candidates
text:
38.5 The validation score, and selecting among fixed candidates
That last condition is easy to miss: ranked by an exact validation accuracy, the validation records are not protected at all. Score each run instead by its count of correct predictions on a held-out validation set, plus Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma_{\text{val}}\). The count is the right score because adding or removing one validation record changes it by at most 1, while an accuracy divides by the number of records, itself private. The noisy count is a Gaussian mechanism with RDP curve \(\lambda/(2\sigma_{\text{val}}^2)\).
It also need not add to the cost. Each record sits in exactly one of the training and validation sets, and a pair of neighbours differs in one record, so the procedure’s cost is the larger of the cost in training records and the cost in validation records, not their sum, and the scores add nothing as long as their cost stays below the training cost. With \(\sigma_{\text{val}} = 20\) correct predictions, one noisy count alone has \(\varepsilon = 0.182\) and eight composed \(0.546\). In the experiment below, eight DP-SGD runs at \(\sigma = 2.07\) cost 1.994 together, and adding the eight noisy counts leaves the total at 1.994, because the counts’ curve stays below the training curve at the orders that matter.
When the candidates do not depend on the private training data, such as public pretrained checkpoints, only the choice is private. That is a pure selection problem, and the exponential mechanism of Selection solves it: pick candidate \(r\) with probability proportional to \(e^{\varepsilon u(r)/2}\), where \(u(r)\) is its count of correct predictions. It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and its expected shortfall from the best count among \(k\) candidates is at most \(2(\ln k + 1)/\varepsilon\) correct predictions, logarithmic in \(k\) with no linear privacy cost. Table 38.3 runs it on eight trained models whose counts out of 5,000 range from 4,123 to 4,694, the best beating the second by 13.

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 38.7 What to do and what to report
text:
38.7 What to do and what to report
The cheapest fix is upstream. In Table 38.4, the two strategies that spend the whole budget on one private run beat every honest search. That will not always hold, since a poor guess can be far worse than a noisy search, but it says where to start: get hyperparameters from public data, proxy data or similar tasks, and shrink what is left. Below the typical gradient norm only the product of step size and clipping norm matters (DP-SGD), so one of the two need not be searched.
Search the rest privately, and fix the search before touching the data: candidates, distribution of the number of runs, score, validation set. The random-\(K\) theorems are about a procedure, and an engineer who looks at the first results and decides to “try a few more” has changed it. Then account for the whole search: compose for a few candidates; for more, use random search with Equation 38.4 when each run is already very private and the search is moderate, or Equation 38.3 for many runs. Every run on the private data counts, including crashed runs, debugging runs and evaluations used for early stopping.
Finally, report two numbers: the \(\varepsilon\) of the released run, and the \(\varepsilon\) of the whole procedure with how it was computed. For the Poisson row of Table 38.4 a complete report reads: “DP-SGD with Poisson sampling rate 0.01, clipping norm 0.5, noise multiplier 1.53, 1,000 steps; one run satisfies \((0.98, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The step size was selected by random search over \(\{0.0625, 0.125, \dots, 8\}\) with a Poisson number of runs with mean 8, scored by correct predictions on a disjoint validation set of 5,000 records with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 20; the whole procedure satisfies \((1.99, 10^{-5})\)-DP by the Rényi bound of Papernot & Steinke (2022, Theorem 6), add/remove neighbours, record level.”
An audit will not catch a missing tuning charge: it tests the released model, not how it was chosen.

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.8 Code
The best-of-\(K\) formula is one line once you have the generating function \(f(x) = \mathbb E[x^K]\) of the number of runs: the best of \(K\) runs is bad exactly when all runs are bad, with probability \(f(P[\text{bad}])\). This snippet computes the exact \(\varepsilon\) for randomized response with a fixed and a geometric number of runs:
from collections.abc import Callable
from math import exp, log


def best_of_rr_epsilon(eps: float, f: Callable[[float], float]) -> float:
    """Exact epsilon of releasing the best of K randomized-response runs, f(x) = E[x^K]."""
    bad_d = exp(eps) / (1 + exp(eps))  # one run comes out bad on D
    bad_d2 = 1 / (1 + exp(eps))  # ... and on its neighbour D'
    # The best is bad only if every run is bad: probability f(P[bad]).
    out_d = [f(bad_d), 1 - f(bad_d)]
    out_d2 = [f(bad_d2), 1 - f(bad_d2)]
    return max(abs(log(a / b)) for a, b in zip(out_d, out_d2))


def fixed(k: int) -> Callable[[float], float]:
    return lambda x: x**k


def geometric(gamma: float) -> Callable[[float], float]:
    """Stop after each run with probability gamma; the mean number of runs is 1/gamma."""
    return lambda x: gamma * x / (1 - (1 - gamma) * x)


print(f"{best_of_rr_epsilon(1.0, fixed(10)):.4f}")  # 10.0000
print(f"{best_of_rr_epsilon(1.0, geometric(0.1)):.4f}")  # 1.7957
print(f"{best_of_rr_epsilon(1.0, geometric(0.001)):.4f}")  # 1.9977
For DP-SGD, the full edition’s script, hyperparameter_tuning.py, has the bounds: tuned_epsilon(q, sigma, steps, strategy) gives the total \(\varepsilon\) of a search, with strategy one of ("fixed", k), ("poisson", mean) or ("tnb<η>", mean), and sigma_for_tuning(q, steps, eps, strategy) the noise multiplier for a budget. title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.1 Why this matters
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP), the DP-SGD of this part, gets much of its privacy from Poisson sampling: each record enters a batch only with probability \(q\), and the accountant credits the run for the attacker’s uncertainty about whether the record was used at all (Amplification by subsampling). Many pipelines cannot honestly claim it: data loaders shuffle and cut fixed batches, streams arrive in order, and a federated server cannot choose which phones check in. The Poisson accountant can then understate \(\varepsilon\) considerably, and giving up amplification is expensive: on this part’s running example, for \(\varepsilon = 2\) over five passes through the data, the noise multiplier has to grow from 0.928 to 4.458, and test accuracy falls from 0.9460 to 0.8941.
How do you train privately without random batches, and can correlated noise beat independent noise? It can, by a lot. The first algorithm to show it ran the follow the regularized leader (FTRL) optimizer on noisy gradient sums released through a binary tree, and is called DP-FTRL. Its modern form, the matrix factorization mechanism, contains the tree as a special case, and on the running example it closes nearly all of the gap to amplified DP-SGD without any sampling.
The one idea: training releases running sums of gradients, so put the noise where the running sums need it. Noise added at one step may partly cancel the noise added before it; the price is that each record’s gradient then has to be hidden in several noisy quantities at once.

title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
section: 39.2 Training is a stream of prefix sums
text:
39.2 Training is a stream of prefix sums
Plain gradient descent, without momentum, adds up its steps. If \(x_t\) is the sum of the clipped gradients of the batch at step \(t\), each of length at most the clipping norm \(C\), and \(\hat x_t\) is its noisy version, then after \(t\) steps with step size \(\eta\) and batch size \(B\) \[w_{t+1} = w_0 - \frac\eta B\hat S_t, \qquad \hat S_t = \hat x_1 + \dots + \hat x_t. \tag{39.1}\] Every model along the way is a fixed function of the noisy prefix sums \(\hat S_t\), so releasing those privately makes every model private, and the noise in a model is the noise in its prefix sum. FTRL with a quadratic regularizer produces the same weights. All \(T\) prefix sums must be released, not just the last, because training is adaptive: the gradient at step \(t\) is computed at \(w_t\), which depends on the earlier sums.
Two mechanisms suggest themselves. Independent noise on each step, which is DP-SGD without amplification, hides a record’s single gradient with noise of the size of one gradient, but the noise in \(\hat S_t\) is a sum of \(t\) independent terms, a random walk whose standard deviation grows like \(\sqrt t\). Independent noise on each prefix sum keeps every error the same size, but a record at step 1 appears in all \(T\) sums, so the noise must be \(\sqrt T\) times larger to hide it, and every sum is as bad as the worst sum of the first mechanism. Neither uses the structure of the problem.
Take one epoch of the running example, \(T = 100\) steps, at \(\varepsilon = 2\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Independent noise needs a noise scale of 1.994 per step, in units of \(C\), so the final prefix sum carries noise of standard deviation 19.94. DP-SGD with Poisson sampling at \(q = 0.01\) and the same \(\varepsilon\) needs only \(\sigma = 0.827\), and its final prefix sum carries 8.27: amplification buys a factor of 2.4. The rest of the chapter shows that correlated noise can beat even that without sampling.

title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.3 The matrix mechanism
Releasing all prefix sums is a linear map, \(S = Ax\), where \(A\) is the \(T \times T\) lower-triangular matrix of ones and \(x\) stacks the \(x_t\) as rows. The matrix mechanism splits \(A\) into two factors, \(A = LR\), adds Gaussian noise \(z\) in the middle, and releases \[\hat S = L(Rx + z) = Ax + Lz, \tag{39.2}\] where \(z\) has independent entries with standard deviation \(sC\), and \(s\) is the noise scale, the analogue of DP-SGD’s noise multiplier. The encoder \(R\) decides what gets noised; the decoder \(L\) recovers the prefix sums from it.
Privacy lives in the columns of \(R\). A record that takes part in step \(\tau\) changes row \(\tau\) of \(x\) by a gradient \(g\) of length at most \(C\), which moves \(Rx\) by column \(\tau\) of \(R\) times \(g\). Recall that the privacy of a Gaussian mechanism depends only on one ratio, the sensitivity divided by the noise standard deviation, called \(\mu\) (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). So the mechanism has \[\mu = \frac{\operatorname{sens}(R)}{s}, \qquad \operatorname{sens}(R) = \max_j\|r_j\|, \tag{39.3}\] the length of the longest column \(r_j\). To meet an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) target, find the largest admissible ratio \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) from the exact Gaussian calibration, for example \(\mu(2, 10^{-5}) = 0.502\) and \(\mu(8, 10^{-5}) = 1.666\), and set \(s = \operatorname{sens}(R)/\mu\).
Error lives in the rows of \(L\). The error in \(\hat S_t\) is row \(t\) of \(L\), written \(\ell_t\), times the noise, a weighted sum of independent normals, so its standard deviation in each coordinate is \(sC\|\ell_t\|\). At a fixed privacy level that is \((C/\mu)\,e_t\), with \[e_t = \operatorname{sens}(R)\,\|\ell_t\| \tag{39.4}\] the error per unit of privacy. Multiplying \(R\) by 2 and dividing \(L\) by 2 changes nothing, so only the product matters, and the best factorization balances short columns against short rows. Independent noise on each step is \(R = I\), \(L = A\): columns of length 1, rows of length \(\sqrt t\). Noise on each prefix sum is \(R = A\), \(L = I\), the opposite extreme.
Does this survive adaptive training, where later gradients depend on earlier outputs? Yes, if both factors are lower-triangular (Denisov et al. 2022, Theorem 2.1). Then row \(j\) of \(Rx + z\) depends only on steps up to \(j\) and can be released at step \(j\). Before the record’s step the outputs have the same distribution on both datasets, and from then on the record shifts the remaining rows by column \(\tau\) times \(g\), so the accounting is the same as for inputs fixed in advance. A factor with entries above the diagonal would need noise or data from future steps.
When \(R\) is square and invertible, the mechanism is noisy SGD with correlated noise: it adds \(\zeta = R^{-1}z\) to the gradients, each step’s noise a fixed combination of the noise drawn so far. Neighbours here leave the record’s slot in the public data order empty; if they replace the record instead, every sensitivity doubles.
How good can a factorization be? No factorization can push the root-mean-square of \(e_t\) over a run below the trace norm of \(A\) (the sum of its singular values) divided by \(T\): 2.18 at \(T = 100\) and 3.63 at \(T = 10{,}000\). title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.4 Tree aggregation and DP-FTRL
The first mechanism with error far below \(\sqrt T\) was the binary tree, from the theory of private running counts (Dwork, Naor, Pitassi & Rothblum 2010; Chan, Shi & Song 2010). Build a tree over the steps: each leaf is one step, each node above covers a block of \(2, 4, 8, \dots\) consecutive steps. Release every node’s gradient sum with independent noise. Any prefix \(1, \dots, t\) is the union of one node for each 1 in the binary expansion of \(t\): \(7 = 4 + 2 + 1\) uses the nodes covering steps 1 to 4, 5 and 6, and 7. So a prefix sum collects at most \(\log_2 t + 1\) noise terms instead of \(t\). The price is that each step sits in one node per level, so its column in \(R\) has length \(\sqrt{L_T}\), with \(L_T = \lceil\log_2 T\rceil + 1\) levels, and the noise must be that much larger.
That trade is a large win for long runs: at \(T = 10{,}000\) the root-mean-square error is 9.84 against 70.71 for independent noise. But the error jumps around: the prefix \(127 = 1111111_2\) uses seven nodes and \(128\) uses one (Figure 39.2, left). And the encoder is wasteful: few prefixes use the top nodes, yet every step pays for being in them.
Kairouz et al. (2021) ran FTRL on prefix sums released by the tree, with momentum and periodic restarts, and called it DP-FTRL. They report that it compares favourably with amplified DP-SGD in their experiments while allowing much more flexible data access, and Xu et al. (2023) used it to train production keyboard language models in federated learning.

title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.5 The square-root factorization
A natural symmetric choice is \(L = R\), a lower-triangular matrix whose square is \(A\). It exists and has a closed form, because lower-triangular matrices that are constant along each diagonal multiply like power series in a variable \(x\), coefficient by coefficient. \(A\), all ones, is the series \(1 + x + x^2 + \dots = 1/(1 - x)\), so its square root is the series \((1 - x)^{-1/2}\), whose coefficients are \[r_k = \binom{2k}k4^{-k}: \qquad r = 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac38, \tfrac5{16}, \tfrac{35}{128}, \dots, \tag{39.5}\] computed by \(r_0 = 1\), \(r_k = r_{k-1}(2k - 1)/(2k)\). The first column of \(R\) is the longest and the last row of \(L = R\) the longest, both with squared length \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2\), so that sum is both \(\operatorname{sens}(R)^2\) and the largest error per unit of privacy. It grows like \(\ln(T)/\pi\): logarithmic, like the tree’s error, but much smaller than the tree’s at both horizons of Table 39.1, and far below \(\sqrt T\). At \(T = 100\), \(\sum r_k^2 = 2.531\), so \(\operatorname{sens}(R) = 1.591\) and the final prefix sum’s error is 2.53, a quarter of independent noise’s 10.
Seen as noisy SGD, the noise added to step \(t\)’s gradient comes from \(R^{-1}\), the series \((1 - x)^{1/2} = 1 - \frac12x - \frac18x^2 - \frac1{16}x^3 - \dots\): \[\zeta_t = z_t - \tfrac12z_{t-1} - \tfrac18z_{t-2} - \tfrac1{16}z_{t-3} - \dots, \tag{39.6}\] fresh noise minus a decaying share of the noise already injected. Each step’s noise is slightly larger than independent noise, with standard deviation tending to \(\sqrt{4/\pi} = 1.128\) times the noise scale, but the negative coefficients pull the accumulated noise back towards zero, so the running sums no longer drift like a random walk (Figure 39.1).






Figure 39.1: Left: one coordinate of the noise added to each of the first 60 steps’ gradients, independent (identity factorization) and square-root correlated, both calibrated to \(\mu = 1\) for one participation. Right: the noise in the prefix sums over 1,000 steps, for independent noise, the binary tree and the square root, with bands of two standard deviations. Independent noise drifts like a random walk; the square root’s stays within a narrow band.



The square root is close to optimal: its root-mean-square error, 2.37 at \(T = 100\) and 3.84 at \(T = 10{,}000\), is within 9% and 6% of the lower bound. The best factorization, computed by a fixed-point iteration (Denisov et al. 2022), reaches 2.24 at \(T = 100\), but each iteration costs cubic time in \(T\), so the square root, free and nearly as good, is the usual default for long runs (Figure 39.2). The two even look alike (Figure 39.3).






Figure 39.2: Left: standard deviation of the error of each released prefix sum \(S_t\) for \(T = 256\), one participation, at \(\mu = 1\) and \(C = 1\), for five factorizations. Right: the root-mean-square error over a run against its length \(T\), with the trace-norm lower bound dotted; the optimal factorization is computed up to \(T = 256\).

The tree’s encoder has one row per node (31 rows), and its decoder picks the nodes of each prefix. The square root uses the same matrix for both; the optimal factorization’s encoder has columns of length exactly 1.

title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.6 Several participations
Training for \(E\) epochs puts a record’s gradient into \(E\) steps, each through a different column of \(R\), and the shifts add before the norm is taken. When all inner products between columns are nonnegative (as for any \(R\) with nonnegative entries: the identity, the tree, the square root), the worst case is the same gradient every time, and the sensitivity is the length of the sum of the record’s columns, maximized over the possible participation patterns.
For independent noise the columns are orthogonal, so \(E\) participations cost \(\sqrt E\), the usual composition of Gaussian mechanisms. For the square root, columns of nearby steps overlap and point in similar directions, so a record that appears again lands on top of its earlier contribution and the sensitivity grows faster than \(\sqrt E\). The tree is worse still: a node covering many steps holds several participations of the same record, and their contributions add inside it.
Banding fixes this. Keep only the first \(b\) diagonals of the square-root encoder, and make sure any two participations of a record are at least \(b\) steps apart (\(b\)-min-separation). Then the columns of different participations do not overlap at all, the cross terms vanish, and the sensitivity is back to at most \(\sqrt E\) times the longest column. The banded decoder, \(L = AR^{-1}\), is less accurate than the square root’s for a single participation, because the band no longer spreads the noise across the whole run, but with many participations the sensitivity saving dominates. Table 39.2 uses the running example’s order: 100 steps per epoch, each record exactly 100 steps apart, band \(b = 100\).

At 20 epochs the banded sensitivity is \(\sqrt{20} \times 1.591 = 7.115\), while the full square root’s is 17.191, more than twice as large. The final errors are closer, 29.85 against 32.09, because the banded decoder is less accurate; both are between a sixth and a seventh of independent noise’s 200.
So the data order is part of the mechanism. A fixed permutation, drawn independently of the data and repeated every epoch, guarantees a separation of exactly \(n/B\) steps; reshuffling every epoch can put a record at the end of one epoch and the start of the next, one step apart, which breaks the banded bound. The order must be fixed in the analysis, but need not be random. Banded factorizations can also use amplification by sampling when it is available (Choquette-Choo et al. 2023).

Without amplification, correlated noise is essential. At \(\varepsilon = 2\), independent noise loses 2.8 points to DP-SGD after one epoch and 8.5 points after ten, and gets worse with more epochs, because its per-step noise grows like \(\sqrt E\) and then accumulates like a random walk. The tree recovers between a quarter and a half of the gap. The square root and the banded square root recover nearly all of it: at ten epochs the banded encoder reaches 0.9491, within 0.0002 of DP-SGD.
For short runs and large \(\varepsilon\), matrix mechanisms can beat amplified DP-SGD outright, because amplification gains little there. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) and one epoch, DP-SGD needs \(\sigma = 0.501\) and independent noise without sampling 0.600, barely more, while the square root’s final prefix sum carries 1.52 against DP-SGD’s 5.01, and it reaches 0.9461 against 0.9371. DP-SGD keeps its lead at small \(\varepsilon\) over many epochs, where amplification is strongest: at \(\varepsilon = 2\) its per-step noise grows only from 0.827 to 1.03 between one and ten epochs, while every fixed-order mechanism pays for ten participations. There the full square root falls behind, 0.9398 against 0.9493, because its overlapping columns make repeated participation expensive, and only banding keeps up. Across the table, the method with the least final-prefix noise is the most accurate, or within the run-to-run spread of the most accurate, in every row: that number is a good guide when choosing.






Figure 39.4: Test accuracy of the running example after 5 epochs (500 steps of batch 100) at step size 1, against \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), one run per point. DP-SGD uses Poisson sampling; the other four use a fixed data order and differ only in how their noise is correlated.



Three caveats. The RDP accountant overstates DP-SGD’s \(\varepsilon\) somewhat compared with a numerical accountant (Choosing an accountant), so a tighter one would lower its noise somewhat. The step size was picked per method by test accuracy, a leak that Hyperparameter tuning charges for; here it only compares methods at their best. And the runs are short, at most 1,000 steps; the noise gaps of Table 39.2 keep widening with epochs, so longer runs should separate the methods more, not less. Figure 39.4 shows the same pattern across budgets at five epochs.
This is what makes matrix mechanisms the tool for federated learning. The server cannot sample devices independently with a known rate, so the Poisson accountant does not apply, but it can enforce that a device contributes at most once every \(b\) rounds. With that min-separation, a banded mechanism has a provable guarantee, and on the running example’s scale it is as accurate as DP-SGD with sampling would be. That is why production federated training of language models uses DP-FTRL (Xu et al. 2023); the privacy unit there is a user, not an example, which User-level differential privacy treats.

title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.8 Code
A correlated-noise mechanism is a few lines on top of noisy SGD; what takes care is the sensitivity, which depends on the data order and must be computed for the order you actually use. This snippet computes the square root’s coefficients, its single-participation errors, the multi-epoch sensitivities of Table 39.2 and the resulting noise scale:
from math import ceil, erfc, exp, log2, sqrt


def sqrt_coeffs(t: int) -> list[float]:
    """r_k = C(2k, k)/4^k: the first column of the lower-triangular square root of A."""
    r = [1.0]
    for k in range(1, t):
        r.append(r[-1] * (2 * k - 1) / (2 * k))
    return r


def toeplitz_sensitivity(c: list[float], t: int, sep: int, epochs: int) -> float:
    """Length of the sum of the encoder columns a record touches, worst slot (entries of c >= 0)."""
    best = 0.0
    for offset in range(sep):
        steps = range(offset, t, sep)[:epochs]
        col = [sum(c[i - p] for p in steps if 0 <= i - p < len(c)) for i in range(t)]
        best = max(best, sqrt(sum(v * v for v in col)))
    return best


def tree_sensitivity(t: int, sep: int, epochs: int) -> float:
    """A record's contributions to one tree node add up before the norm is taken."""
    best = 0.0
    for offset in range(sep):
        steps = range(offset, t, sep)[:epochs]
        total = 0
        for level in range(ceil(log2(t)) + 1):
            counts: dict[int, int] = {}
            for p in steps:
                counts[p >> level] = counts.get(p >> level, 0) + 1
            total += sum(n * n for n in counts.values())
        best = max(best, sqrt(total))
    return best


def phi(x: float) -> float:
    return 0.5 * erfc(-x / sqrt(2))


def gaussian_mu(eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Largest sensitivity-to-noise ratio for which a Gaussian mechanism is (eps, delta)-DP."""
    lo, hi = 1e-9, 100.0
    for _ in range(200):
        mu = (lo + hi) / 2
        if phi(mu / 2 - eps / mu) - exp(eps) * phi(-mu / 2 - eps / mu) > delta:
            hi = mu
        else:
            lo = mu
    return lo


T = 100
r = sqrt_coeffs(T)
sens = sqrt(sum(v * v for v in r))  # the first column is the longest
rows = [sqrt(sum(v * v for v in r[:t])) for t in range(1, T + 1)]  # row t of L = R
print(f"{sens:.3f} {sens * rows[-1]:.2f}")  # 1.591 2.53
print(f"{sens * sqrt(sum(x * x for x in rows) / T):.2f}")  # 2.37
print(f"{sqrt(sum(range(1, T + 1)) / T):.2f}")  # 7.11

E = 20  # epochs of 100 steps, each record exactly 100 steps apart
print(f"{toeplitz_sensitivity(sqrt_coeffs(T * E), T * E, T, E):.3f}")  # 17.191
print(f"{toeplitz_sensitivity(r, T * E, T, E):.3f}")  # 7.115
print(f"{tree_sensitivity(T * E, T, E):.3f}")  # 30.430
print(f"{toeplitz_sensitivity(r, T * 10, T, 10) / gaussian_mu(2.0, 1e-5):.3f}")  # 10.031
The banded encoder is the square root cut to its first 100 coefficients, which is why it reuses r; the last line is its noise scale for \(\varepsilon = 2\) over ten epochs, as in Table 39.3. title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
40.1 Why this matters
Training with differential privacy (DP) by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped, noisy gradients, called DP-SGD (DP-SGD), makes the weights private, and after that every use of the model is free: answering a query is post-processing of the weights. But you pay during training, and you must own the training loop. Sometimes you cannot. The model may be a large language model (LLM) you can prompt but not train, a model without gradients such as a decision forest, or a tool that will answer a few dozen questions in its whole life, for which a private training run is overkill.
The alternative is to train ordinary models, never release them, and make each answer private instead. The idea that makes this work is one record, one vote. Split the private records into \(k\) disjoint shards and train one model, a teacher, on each. To answer a query, let every teacher vote for a label, add noise to the vote counts, and release only the winning label. A record lives in one shard, so it can change one teacher and so one vote, however that teacher was trained and however badly it overfits. That is the whole privacy argument. The accuracy argument is about the gap between the top two vote counts against the noise, and the noise must grow with the number of answers. Private prediction is therefore cheap for a few queries on which the teachers agree, and expensive otherwise. The method that turns those answers into a releasable model is private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE), due to Papernot et al. (2017).

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 40.2 The noisy vote and its cost
text:
40.2 The noisy vote and its cost
Fix the partition before looking at the data, by a hash of a record identifier rather than by position. Then adding or removing a record changes exactly one shard and one teacher, and that teacher’s vote can move from one label to another: one count goes down by 1 and another goes up by 1. The vote histogram moves by at most \(\sqrt2\) in Euclidean length. If shards were cut by position, inserting one record at the front would shift every later record into the next shard and could change every teacher; the guarantee would be gone.
Two mechanisms release the label. LNMax adds Laplace noise of scale \(b\) to each count and releases the index of the largest noisy count. It is report-noisy-max (Selection) on scores that one record moves by at most 1 each, in opposite directions, so each answer is \((2/b)\)-DP. GNMax adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) to each count instead. Adding the noise is the Gaussian mechanism on a vector of sensitivity \(\sqrt2\), and taking the argmax is post-processing, so in Rényi differential privacy (RDP), the accounting whose curves simply add under composition (Rényi DP), each answer costs \(\alpha/\sigma^2\) at order \(\alpha\) (Papernot et al. 2018). \(Q\) answers cost \(Q\alpha/\sigma^2\), even when each query is chosen after seeing the earlier answers. That curve is a line whose slope is \(Q/\sigma^2\), and a line converts to an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) that depends only on its slope. Call \(\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)\) the largest slope that still converts to your budget; then the noise you need is \[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{Q}{\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)}}. \tag{40.1}\] At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), \(\rho = 0.0306\) for \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(0.3731\) for \(\varepsilon = 4\).
Three consequences follow from this formula. First, the noise grows like \(\sqrt Q\): a hundred times more answers need ten times more noise. Second, neither \(k\) nor anything about the teachers appears in it. A teacher can be a network trained without noise, a decision forest or a human annotator who saw one shard; only the noise and the number of answers set the cost. The noise can be large in absolute terms because the counts are large: with 250 teachers, noise of standard deviation 40 is noticeable but not overwhelming. Third, release only the label. Publishing the noisy counts too would release a whole vector, and the data-dependent analysis below needs the label alone.

But the Gaussian’s privacy loss is itself Gaussian and composes without slack, so from 100 answers on GNMax needs about half the noise.
