title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 40.3 When a noisy vote is accurate
text:
40.3 When a noisy vote is accurate
On two labels, GNMax returns the plurality label when the noise difference between the two counts does not overturn the gap \(g\). The difference of two independent Gaussians of standard deviation \(\sigma\) is a Gaussian of standard deviation \(\sqrt2\sigma\), so the plurality wins with probability \(\Phi(g/(\sqrt2\sigma))\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. With more labels, the probability of losing to any competitor is at most the sum of the probabilities of losing to each, a union bound that is exact on two labels and loose when several labels are nearly tied with the winner.
The part’s running example makes this concrete: 50-dimensional Gaussian inputs labelled \(\pm1\) by a fixed random network, 10,000 private records, teachers that are regularized logistic regressions on one shard each. With \(k = 100\) teachers and the noise for 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 4\), \(\sigma = 51.8\), a query on which 98 teachers vote one way, a gap of 96, gets the plurality label with probability 0.9051. One split 70 to 30 gets it with probability 0.7076, and one split 52 to 48 with probability 0.5218, barely better than a coin (Figure 40.1).






Figure 40.1: Left three panels: the votes of 100 teachers on three public queries, with bars of one noise standard deviation (\(\sigma = 51.8\), the GNMax noise for 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 4\)); the title gives the probability that the noisy vote returns the plurality label. Right: across all 10,000 public queries, the fraction of the 100 teachers voting \(+1\).



How many teachers? More teachers multiply the gap by \(k\) while the noise stays fixed, but each teacher sees fewer records and agrees less with the others. On the running example the second effect is weaker than you might fear. Going from 25 teachers of 400 records to 500 teachers of 20, each teacher’s accuracy falls from 0.8954 to 0.6459, but the noiseless plurality vote hardly moves, staying between 0.9336 and 0.9403: a majority of many weak, nearly independent voters is right far more often than any one of them. The median gap grows in absolute terms, from 25 to 138, and since the noise does not depend on \(k\), more teachers win. With 100 answers at \(\varepsilon = 4\), 500 teachers answer with accuracy 0.9237, about a point below their noiseless vote. With 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 1\), even 500 teachers fall to 0.6987. Note the ceiling: noise can only pull answers towards a coin flip, so no private answer beats the noiseless vote, and on queries the teachers find hard any noise makes the answer close to random.

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 40.4 Private answers against a private model
text:
40.4 Private answers against a private model
You have one budget. Spend it on DP-SGD, and the model’s accuracy is fixed however many queries it answers. Spend it on answers, and accuracy starts near the noiseless ensemble and, on this task, falls towards a coin flip as \(Q\) grows, because \(\sigma\) grows like \(\sqrt Q\). A falling curve crosses a constant at most once, so there is a break-even number of queries \(Q^*\) below which private answers win.

On the running example (Table 40.2), at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), where DP-SGD reaches only 0.8164, 500 teachers answer up to 58 queries more accurately than the private model, and at \(\varepsilon = 1\) up to 18. From \(\varepsilon = 2\) on, DP-SGD beats even a single noiseless vote, because the ensemble’s ceiling is below DP-SGD’s 0.9438 (Figure 40.2). The pattern is general: private prediction wins at small budgets, where DP-SGD loses much, and for few queries. Two things the comparison leaves out cut the other way. If you cannot run DP-SGD at all, because the model is behind an interface or the data cannot be pooled, the comparison is with nothing. And private prediction runs \(k\) models on every query, while DP-SGD trains once.

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 40.5 PATE: from answers to a model
text:
40.5 PATE: from answers to a model
Answers cost budget forever; a model costs it once. PATE spends the budget on labelling \(Q\) public, unlabelled inputs with GNMax, then trains a student on them and releases only the student. The student’s training reads public inputs and the \(Q\) noisy labels and nothing else, so it is post-processing: its weights and every prediction it ever makes cost exactly the \(Q\) answers, whatever its size, training algorithm or number of predictions. The student may choose which inputs to have labelled after seeing earlier labels, since the composition allows adaptive queries.
Three things limit the student: it learns from \(Q\) examples rather than \(n\), some of its labels are wrong, and the plurality vote has its ceiling. More labels mean more noise per label, so for each \(\varepsilon\) there is a best \(Q\). On the running example, with 250 teachers and the part’s network as student, the best student reaches 0.8238 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 0.8898 at \(\varepsilon = 4\), against 0.9128 and 0.9573 for DP-SGD, which wins at every budget. The best \(Q\) was chosen by looking at test accuracy, itself a leak that Hyperparameter tuning shows how to pay for. The reasons PATE loses here are the conditions under which it wins elsewhere: the task is binary, so a wrong label is as damaging as it can be; the teachers are weak and often disagree; the student needs thousands of labels; and DP-SGD does well even at \(\varepsilon = 1\). On a handwritten-digit benchmark (MNIST), where teachers agree on most inputs, Papernot et al. (2018) report a student with 98.5% accuracy against a non-private 99.2%, at \(\varepsilon = 1.97\) with 286 answered queries.
PATE needs public inputs from the same distribution as the private data, which are plentiful for images or text and absent for medical records, and they must really be public: an input that is someone else’s private record is protected by nothing. And the teachers are non-private models that must stay secret. An attacker who steals one can attack its shard directly, so PATE moves the trust from the training algorithm to the server that holds the teachers.
crumbs: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 40.6 Paying less when the teachers agree
text:
40.6 Paying less when the teachers agree
The cost \(\alpha/\sigma^2\) is a worst case over vote histograms, including ties that one teacher decides. When 249 of 250 teachers agree, one record cannot realistically change the answer, and the data-dependent analysis of Papernot et al. charges such a query less: its cost is roughly proportional to the probability that the noise overturns the plurality. Figure 40.3 shows it for one answer with \(\sigma = 40\) at order 8. Up to a gap of about 100 the bound is no better than the data-independent 0.005; then it falls steeply, to \(1.23 \times 10^{-3}\) at a gap of 150. The bound is valid but not tight: the exact cost on two labels is five times lower at that gap.






Figure 40.3: The RDP cost at order 8 of one GNMax answer with \(\sigma = 40\), against the gap between the two vote counts, on a log scale: the data-independent \(\alpha/\sigma^2\), the data-dependent bound of Papernot et al. (2018), and the exact data-dependent cost on two labels.



The total saving depends on how many queries have large gaps. On the running example only 0.2879 of the public queries have a gap of at least 150 with 250 teachers, so 1,000 answers with \(\sigma = 40\) cost \(\varepsilon = 4.37\) instead of 5.38 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), about 20% less. On tasks where nearly every teacher agrees on nearly every input, almost every answer is nearly free. Confident-GNMax exploits this by design: it first checks, with a noisy maximum count of large noise \(\sigma_1\), whether the consensus clears a threshold, and answers with GNMax only if it does. The check costs a little on every query, the answer only on the confident ones, which are also the ones more likely to be right. The price is that the student never sees labels near the decision boundary. On the running example it answered 459 of 1,000 queries and trained a student to 0.8894 at a data-independent \(\varepsilon = 3.59\), about what plain GNMax reached at \(\varepsilon = 4\).
There is a trap. The data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) is computed from the votes, so it is itself private information, and its sensitivity is large: one record changes one teacher, whose votes may change on every query. Papernot et al. publish it only after adding noise calibrated to its smooth sensitivity, and pay for that release; on MNIST their data-dependent \(\varepsilon = 2.00\) becomes \(2.52 \pm 0.385\) once sanitized. Until it is sanitized, a data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) is a measurement, not a guarantee. Report the data-independent value, or pay for the release.
crumbs: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
40.7 Private in-context learning
An LLM learns a task from a few labelled examples, the exemplars, placed in its prompt. If the exemplars are private, every answer is computed from them. Duan et al. (2023) showed a membership inference attack (MIA) on GPT-3 prompted with one private example: the model’s probability for the correct label is markedly higher on the example in the prompt. The script’s stand-in learner shows the same: the attack’s area under the curve (AUC), the chance a member scores above a non-member, is 1.000 against a 1-shot learner and 0.889 against a 16-shot one. Putting private exemplars in a prompt that answers users directly protects nothing.
The fix is PATE with prompts as teachers (Wu et al. 2024; Duan et al. 2023). Split the exemplars into disjoint groups by a fixed rule, prompt the model once per group with the query, and release the GNMax label. One exemplar changes one prompt and so one vote, whatever the LLM computes, and the cost is exactly that of GNMax. Wu et al. also draw a fresh Poisson sample of the exemplars for each query, each record kept with probability \(r\); a record is then absent from most queries, and the cost is that of the subsampled Gaussian of Amplification by subsampling with rate \(r\) and noise multiplier \(\sigma/\sqrt2\), the same accountant DP-SGD uses. The \(\sqrt2\) is the vote histogram’s sensitivity. Within one query the groups must still be disjoint, or a record in two groups moves two votes. PromptPATE (Duan et al.) instead labels a few public inputs this way and deploys them as the exemplars of one public prompt, the student in prompt form, free to use forever.
This is where private prediction is strongest. A prompted LLM knows most of the task from pretraining, so its votes with different exemplars agree far more than independently trained small models do, and high agreement is exactly what makes answers accurate and data-dependent costs small. The papers report, on a movie-review sentiment task with GPT-3 models, 92.7% accuracy at \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (0.147, 10^{-6})\) with PromptPATE against 95.2% without privacy (Duan et al.), and 91.97% at \(\varepsilon = 1\) for 10,000 queries each answered by ten 4-shot prompts, against 91.89% for one non-private 4-shot prompt (Wu et al.). The script’s stand-in learner has no pretraining at all, so it shows the accounting, not the accuracy. Subsampling makes its noise small: 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 1\) need \(\sigma = 7.39\) with \(r = 0.04\), against 181 without, yet with only 25 voters its accuracy still falls from 0.8090 to 0.6800 (Figure 40.4).






Figure 40.4: Accuracy of private answers from the stand-in in-context learner against the number of queries answered at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 4\) (\(\delta = 10^{-5}\)), with 25 groups of about 16 exemplars drawn per query at rate 0.04. The dashed line is the vote without noise and the dotted line a single 16-shot learner.

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
40.8 Code
This snippet answers the two questions to ask before deploying a noisy vote: how much noise \(Q\) answers need (Equation 40.1, with \(\rho\) found by searching the RDP conversion over orders), and how often a vote with a given gap survives it.
from math import erfc, log, sqrt


def eps_of_line(rho: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """(eps, delta) of the RDP line rho * alpha, by the improved conversion at the best order."""
    orders = [1 + j / 100 for j in range(1, 6_000)]
    return min(rho * a + log((a - 1) / a) - (log(delta) + log(a)) / (a - 1) for a in orders)


def largest_slope(eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """The largest rho whose RDP line rho * alpha converts to (eps, delta), by bisection."""
    lo, hi = 1e-6, 10.0
    for _ in range(60):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if eps_of_line(mid, delta) <= eps else (lo, mid)
    return lo


def gnmax_sigma(answers: int, eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Noise per vote count so that `answers` GNMax answers cost (eps, delta) in total."""
    return sqrt(answers / largest_slope(eps, delta))


def p_plurality(gap: float, sigma: float) -> float:
    """Probability that a two-label GNMax vote returns the plurality label."""
    return 1 - 0.5 * erfc(gap / (2 * sigma))


print(f"{largest_slope(1.0, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 0.0306
print(f"{gnmax_sigma(100, 1.0, 1e-5):.1f}")  # 57.2
print(f"{gnmax_sigma(10_000, 1.0, 1e-5):.0f}")  # 572
sigma = gnmax_sigma(1000, 4.0, 1e-5)
print(f"{sigma:.1f}")  # 51.8
print(f"{p_plurality(96, sigma):.4f}")  # 0.9051
print(f"{p_plurality(4, sigma):.4f}")  # 0.5218

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.1 Why this matters
Training with differential privacy (DP) from random weights, by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD (DP-SGD), costs little on the part’s running example at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and a great deal at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and below. The most accurate private models are not trained that way. They start from a model pretrained non-privately on a large public dataset and only fine-tune it privately on the sensitive data, and at the same \(\varepsilon\) they are far more accurate than the same models trained privately from scratch (Tramèr & Boneh 2021; Yu et al. 2022; Li et al. 2022; De et al. 2022). A second practice helps on top of that: fine-tuning only a small part of the model often beats fine-tuning all of it under DP, although without privacy it would usually be the other way round.
Both follow from one idea: the noise is paid per trainable direction, the signal is not. DP-SGD adds noise of the same size to every coordinate it updates, while the useful part of the gradient is bounded in length however many coordinates there are, and usually concentrated in a few directions. A coordinate the task does not need only collects noise. Public data helps twice: it moves the starting point close to a good model, so little remains to be learned privately, and it tells you, for free, which few directions that remainder lies in. What it does not do is protect the people in the public data.
crumbs: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 41.2 Why dimension costs, and when it does not
text:
41.2 Why dimension costs, and when it does not
Each step of DP-SGD adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to a sum of per-example gradients clipped to length \(C\), where \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier, and divides by the expected batch size \(B\). Nothing in the privacy proof depends on which weights the gradient is taken with respect to, so whatever you train, the accountant gives the same \(\varepsilon\). What changes is the noise. Over \(k\) trainable coordinates, a Gaussian vector with standard deviation \(s = \sigma C/B\) in each coordinate has length about \(s\sqrt k\), because its squared length is a sum of \(k\) terms of mean \(s^2\): \[\text{noise length} \approx \frac{\sigma C\sqrt k}{B}. \tag{41.1}\]
The signal, the average clipped gradient, is at most \(C\) long whatever \(k\) is, and it can be longer when \(k\) is smaller, because each record’s gradient restricted to fewer coordinates is shorter and less often clipped. The part’s running example shows both effects: 50-dimensional Gaussian inputs labelled by a fixed random network, \(n = 10{,}000\) private records, a student network with 3,329 weights pretrained on a related public task (Section 41.6), and DP-SGD with sampling rate \(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\) and 10,000 steps, which needs \(\sigma = 4.13\) for \(\varepsilon = 1\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). From the pretrained weights, the signal is 0.0130 long when all weights are trained, 0.0207 for a rank-4 adapter with the last layer, and 0.0250 for the last layer alone. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the noise is 92.0 times the signal for all weights, 22.9 times for the adapter and 6.7 times for the last layer (Table 41.1, Figure 41.1). A signal of constant direction outgrows a random walk of noise after about \((\text{noise}/\text{signal})^2\) steps: 8,455, 523 and 44 steps.

Yet large language models with hundreds of millions of weights are fine-tuned privately with good results, so the count \(k\) cannot be the whole price. It is not, because noise only hurts in directions the loss cares about. Model the loss near the starting point as a quadratic. In a direction with curvature \(h\), noise kicks the weights around and the curvature pulls them back. A curved direction reaches a steady state and charges a fixed amount for it; a nearly flat direction keeps accumulating kicks but charges almost nothing for them, because moving along it barely changes the loss. Adding this up over \(T\) steps of step size \(\eta\) gives a loss increase of about \[\Delta \approx \frac{\eta s^2}{4}\,d_{\text{eff}}, \qquad d_{\text{eff}} = \sum_{j=1}^k\Big(1 - (1 - \eta h_j)^{2T}\Big), \tag{41.2}\] where \(h_j\) are the curvatures of the trainable directions. Each term is close to 1 for a direction whose curvature is above about \(1/(2\eta T)\) and close to 0 below it. So the effective dimension \(d_{\text{eff}}\) roughly counts the directions the noise has time to fill, and it is at most \(k\). Li, Liu et al. (2022) give this kind of explanation for why private fine-tuning of large models does not suffer from their size.
On the running example, at the pretrained weights with \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\), only 406 of the 3,329 directions have curvature above \(1/(2\eta T) = 5 \times 10^{-4}\), and \(d_{\text{eff}} = 451\); for the last layer, \(d_{\text{eff}} = 60.2\) of 65. Full fine-tuning’s noise is 7.2 times longer than the last layer’s, and by Equation 41.2 it costs only about 7.5 times more, not the 51 times that the ratio of weight counts suggests. Freezing weights can only lower \(d_{\text{eff}}\), but it adds bias: a frozen direction the task needs can never be learned. And \(d_{\text{eff}}\) grows with \(\eta T\), so a larger step size fills more flat directions with noise, one reason private fine-tuning wants smaller step sizes than training from scratch. The quadratic is a local model and loss is not accuracy, so use Equation 41.2 to compare strategies, not to predict accuracy.

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.3 The last layer: linear probing
The simplest strategy freezes everything except the last layer and trains a linear classifier on the frozen features, linear probing. Since the features come from public data, they are a fixed transformation of each record, and the problem becomes private convex empirical risk minimization (ERM) in \(k\) dimensions, where the methods and rates are known (Private ERM). Tramèr & Boneh (2021) showed that this beats end-to-end private training on standard image benchmarks at moderate budgets, even with handcrafted features.
A probe’s error splits in two. The feature gap is the distance from the best linear model on these features to the best model of any kind; it is paid even with infinite data and no privacy. The privacy cost is private convex ERM’s, which falls like \(\sqrt k/(n\varepsilon)\) up to logarithmic factors (Bassily, Smith & Thakurta 2014). So features cap the accuracy, and privacy only decides how close you get to the cap. On the running example, the pretrained network labels 0.9035 of the private test inputs correctly without any private data. Fitting its last layer exactly and non-privately on the 10,000 private records raises this to 0.9536, the probe’s ceiling, against 0.9606 for a network trained non-privately from scratch, a feature gap of 0.007. The private probe reaches 0.9478 at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and 0.9514 at \(\varepsilon = 8\): within 0.006 of its ceiling at every budget, and unable to pass it at any.
That makes the probe the safe first baseline: convex, with few hyperparameters, and if it meets your accuracy target there is little reason to train more.
crumbs: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.4 Low-rank adapters
When the features are not quite right for the new task, the probe stops at its ceiling, and training all weights pays for every weight. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al. 2022) sits in between. It freezes each pretrained matrix \(W_0\), of size \(d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}\), and learns a correction \(W = W_0 + UV^\top\) with \(U\) of size \(d_{\text{out}} \times r\) and \(V\) of size \(d_{\text{in}} \times r\), starting from \(U = 0\) so that training begins exactly at the pretrained model. It trains \[k = r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}) \tag{41.3}\] weights instead of \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\). A rank-8 adapter on a \(768 \times 768\) projection of a transformer trains 12,288 weights instead of 589,824, 48 times fewer, so its noise is 6.9 times shorter. Its per-example gradients are outer products of short vectors, so their norms can be computed without forming them, the ghost clipping of DP-SGD; on the running example the ghost norms agree with explicitly formed gradients to a relative difference of \(3.3 \times 10^{-16}\). The privacy guarantee is DP-SGD’s with the same \(q\), \(\sigma\) and number of steps.
What the restriction costs is direction. At the start, with \(U = 0\) and \(V\) random, the update projects the true gradient onto a random \(r\)-dimensional subspace of the layer’s inputs, which captures little of it. As training proceeds \(V\) moves and the subspace aligns with the useful directions. Adapters work when the change the new task needs is itself close to low rank, and the rank trades bias against noise. Yu et al. (2022) found that private fine-tuning of language models with LoRA matches or beats private full fine-tuning; Li, Tramèr, Liang & Hashimoto (2022) found full fine-tuning matching or beating the parameter-efficient methods once it had large batches and a tuned step size, which Equation 41.2 allows, since full fine-tuning pays \(d_{\text{eff}}\), not \(k\). The published evidence goes both ways. The adapter’s other advantages are certain: it stores only \(k\) numbers per task and clips much smaller gradients.
crumbs: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.5 Gradients near a public subspace
If noise costs little in directions the loss does not use, you could add noise only in the directions it does use, if you knew them. Public data gives an estimate: compute per-example gradients on public records, find their top principal directions, and project the private clipped gradient sum and its noise onto those \(m\) directions. Projection never lengthens a vector, so the sensitivity is still \(C\), and because the subspace is fixed before any private data are read, the guarantee is unchanged. This is projected DP-SGD (Zhou, Wu & Banerjee 2021).
The trade is between noise and bias. The noise falls by \(\sqrt{p/m}\), where \(p\) is the number of weights. The signal keeps only the fraction \(f_m\) of its energy that lies in the subspace, and the lost part is a bias that no number of steps recovers. If the public data resemble the private task, \(f_m\) is close to 1 for small \(m\) and the trade is excellent. If they do not, the subspace is no better than a random one, \(f_m \approx m/p\), and the projection removes as much signal as noise. On the running example, a single direction of 500 public per-example gradients holds 60% of the private gradient’s energy, and 64 directions, 2% of the dimensions, hold 73%, against 2.2% for 64 random directions. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the kept signal outgrows the noise after 222 steps in the 64-dimensional subspace, against 8,455 for all weights; the price is the 27% outside it, which a fixed projection never learns, so methods recompute the subspace as training proceeds. The same concentration is what makes \(d_{\text{eff}}\) small for full fine-tuning (Figure 41.2).






Figure 41.2: Left: eigenvalues of the Gauss–Newton curvature of the private loss at the pretrained weights, estimated from 2,000 private records, on log scales, with the thresholds \(1/(2\eta T)\) for \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(0.5\) and \(T = 10{,}000\); directions below a threshold contribute little noise cost. Right: the fraction of the energy of the private average clipped gradient that lies in the top \(m\) principal directions of 500 public per-example gradients (solid), and in \(m\) random directions (dashed).

41.6 Pretraining and fine-tuning the running example
The public task labels 50,000 inputs from the private input distribution with a related teacher: the private teacher’s hidden units, each slightly perturbed, read out with weights turned partly towards a random vector. It agrees with the private teacher on 0.9004 of the private test inputs, so pretraining helps without solving the private task. On this task pretraining is worth about a factor of eight in \(\varepsilon\) (Table 41.2). Which weights to train depends on the budget, as the noise lengths and the ceiling explain together. At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the last layer is best: its noise is 7.2 times shorter than full fine-tuning’s, and its ceiling, 0.9536, is not yet binding. From \(\varepsilon = 1\) on it is stuck near that ceiling, while the adapter and full fine-tuning keep improving, because they can correct the features and the noise is now small enough to let them. title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 41.7 What public data does not buy
text:
41.7 What public data does not buy
The guarantee treats the public data as a fixed input. For every fixed public dataset, the map from the private dataset to the fine-tuned model is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, because the DP-SGD proof holds for any starting weights chosen independently of the private data. With respect to the public data there is no guarantee at all: non-private pretraining can memorize individual records (Memorization and extraction), and the fine-tuned model inherits whatever the pretrained weights encode.
This matters most for a person whose record is in both datasets. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), any test of whether a record was in the private set that has a false positive rate of 0.01 has a true positive rate of at most \(e \times 0.01 + 10^{-5} = 0.0272\). If the same record is also in the public set, a membership test against the pretrained model, such as the likelihood-ratio attack of Membership inference, is bounded by nothing; it may fail in practice, but no theorem says it will. Compare a record that appears twice in the private set: group privacy gives the two copies \((2\varepsilon, 2e^\varepsilon\delta) = (2, 5.44 \times 10^{-5})\), weaker but real. A copy in the public set is worse than a duplicate in the private set. Web-scale “public” data contain posts, profiles and leaked documents, so overlap with private medical notes or emails is a real risk, and Tramèr, Kamath & Carlini (2024) argue that “differentially private” should be used with care for such models. Deduplication against the private set is the minimum check, and exact matching protects copies, not people: paraphrases and other records about the same person survive it.
Two further caveats. Benchmarks whose “private” set resembles curated public data can overstate what the method does on genuinely sensitive data, which is often unlike anything public. And any choice made by looking at private data, such as which public model to start from or the step size, is part of the private computation and must be paid for; choosing on public validation data is free. When you report \(\varepsilon\), say what the public data are, how they were obtained, whether overlap was checked, and that the guarantee covers the private data given the pretrained model.

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.8 Code
Before choosing what to fine-tune, count: the noise length for each candidate set of trainable weights, at the \(\sigma\) your accountant gives, is the first number to compare with the signal.
from math import sqrt


def noise_length(sigma: float, clip: float, batch: float, trainable: int) -> float:
    """Length of DP-SGD's noise on the averaged gradient over `trainable` coordinates."""
    return sigma * clip * sqrt(trainable) / batch


def lora_weights(rank: int, d_in: int, d_out: int) -> int:
    """Trainable weights of a rank-r adapter W0 + U V^T on a d_out x d_in matrix."""
    return rank * (d_in + d_out)


adapter = lora_weights(4, 51, 64) + 65  # first-layer adapter plus the 65-weight last layer
print(adapter)  # 525
print(f"{noise_length(4.13, 0.5, 100, 3329):.3f}")  # 1.191
print(f"{noise_length(4.13, 0.5, 100, adapter):.3f}")  # 0.473
print(f"{noise_length(4.13, 0.5, 100, 65):.3f}")  # 0.166
big = lora_weights(8, 768, 768)
print(big, 768 * 768 // big)  # 12288 48
print(f"{sqrt(768 * 768 / big):.1f}")  # 6.9

uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/public_data.py

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.1 Why this matters
Every differential privacy (DP) guarantee in this part so far protects one record. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, reports \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for the part’s running example, and that number says an adversary who sees the model learns little about whether any single training example was used. But people do not contribute one record each. A user of a messaging app writes hundreds of messages, a patient has dozens of visits, a photographer uploads thousands of photos. Each record is protected; the person behind all of them is not, because what an adversary learns from all of a person’s records together can be far more than what they learn from one.
The one idea: the neighbouring relation is the privacy unit. DP compares outputs on two datasets that differ in one unit, and whatever differs between them is what is protected. If neighbours differ in one record, records are protected; if they differ in all of one person’s records, people are. Nothing else in the definition changes. So there are two ways to protect a person. You can keep the record as the unit and pay for the person afterwards, which is cheap to build and expensive in privacy. Or you can make the person the unit from the start: sample people, bound each person’s total contribution, and run the usual accountant with people in place of records. On the running example the first route gives a useless model at any reasonable budget, and the second a model within a few points of the non-private one.

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.2 The privacy unit
A mechanism is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if the definition of DP holds for every pair of datasets that differ by adding or removing all the records of one user; it is example-level DP if it holds for datasets that differ in one record. User-level DP is not a new privacy notion, only a coarser neighbouring relation, so post-processing, composition and every accountant of Part 4 hold for it unchanged. What changes is the sensitivity: how far one unit can move the computation. Records, users, households, devices and organizations are all possible units, and the right one answers the question “whose participation do I want to hide?” A guarantee that does not name its unit leaves that question open.
What does an example-level guarantee promise a person with \(k\) records? Adding that person’s records one at a time walks from one dataset to the other in \(k\) example-level steps. Group privacy applies the one-record guarantee at each step (Post-processing, group privacy and composition): each step multiplies the probability bound by \(e^\varepsilon\), so the person gets \(k\varepsilon\), and each step’s slack \(\delta\) is multiplied by the \(e^\varepsilon\) of every later step, \[\delta_k = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}. \tag{42.1}\] Some mechanisms attain this bound, so nothing better holds for a mechanism known only to be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. The \(\varepsilon\) part is linear in \(k\), already weak: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) per record, a person with 10 records gets \(\varepsilon = 10\). The \(\delta\) part is worse, because it grows exponentially in \(k\varepsilon\).
Read naively, the running example’s \((6.71, 10^{-5})\) gives a user with two records \(\varepsilon = 13.42\) and \(\delta_2 = 10^{-5}(1 + e^{6.71}) = 0.0082\): a chance of almost one in a hundred that the guarantee fails outright, which is no guarantee. You can do better for DP-SGD, because its accountant converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at any \(\delta\): pick the per-record \(\delta\) that makes \(\delta_2 = 10^{-5}\) exactly. That gives a per-record \(\varepsilon\) of 9.30 and a user-level \((18.61, 10^{-5})\). For five records the same procedure gives a user-level \(\varepsilon\) of 118.12. For ten it gives nothing at all. Shrinking the per-record \(\delta\) raises the per-record \(\varepsilon\), and \(\delta_k\) is a race between a falling \(\delta\) and a rising \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\); beyond a few records the rising term wins at every \(\delta\), and no choice brings \(\delta_{10}\) down to \(10^{-5}\). In the running example’s population of 1,000 users, 244 have at least ten records.

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
section: 42.3 What a record-level model gives a heavy user
text:
42.3 What a record-level model gives a heavy user
Group privacy treats DP-SGD as a black box, and it is not one: you know exactly how a user’s records enter each step. Recall that DP-SGD draws each record into the batch independently with probability \(q\) (Poisson sampling), clips each record’s gradient to norm \(C\), sums them and adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\), where \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier. A user with \(k\) records therefore has a random number of them in each batch, between 0 and \(k\), binomially distributed, and the worst case is that all the drawn ones push the sum by the full \(C\) in the same direction. So, in units of \(C\), one step compares the noise alone, \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), with a mixture of Gaussians shifted by \(m = 0, 1, \dots, k\), each weighted by the probability that \(m\) of the user’s records were drawn. Charles et al. (2024, Theorem 3) prove that this pair, composed over the steps, bounds the user’s privacy loss, and that some loss function, one that aligns the user’s gradients, attains it. An accountant built on the pair computes the user’s guarantee directly, the same way the subsampling accountant does for one record.
The result has a simple reading while \(kq\) is small: a user with \(k\) records looks like one record sampled at rate \(kq\). Amplification by subsampling works because the unit is usually absent from the batch, and what matters is the probability that some record of the user is present, about \(kq\). Halving the sampling rate exactly compensates doubling the user’s records. So the quick estimate is to rerun the record-level accountant with \(q\) replaced by \(kq\). It errs on the low side, because it drops the steps in which several of the user’s records are drawn together, and those steps shift the sum by several clipping norms at once, a mechanism with noise multiplier \(\sigma/m\) whose tail no amount of rarity can hide at high orders.

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.4 User-level DP-SGD
Accounting for users after the fact charges a heavy user for every one of their records. The alternative, due to McMahan, Ramage, Talwar & Zhang (2018), who used it for federated learning of a language model, changes what DP-SGD samples and clips. At each step, put each user in the batch independently with probability \(q\). For each sampled user, compute one vector from that user’s records alone, for example their average gradient, or the change in weights after a few local SGD steps on their data. Clip that vector to norm \(C\), sum over the sampled users, add Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\), and divide by the expected number of sampled users, \(qU\) for \(U\) users.
The guarantee follows because each property the DP-SGD proof used still holds with users in place of records. Adding a user adds one clipped vector to the sum and changes no other, so one user moves the sum by at most \(C\) however many records they have. The user is in the batch with probability \(q\), independently of the others, so each step is the same subsampled Gaussian mechanism as before. The result is user-level DP with exactly the accountant of example-level DP-SGD, with \(q\) now the user sampling rate.
Two consequences follow, one bad and one good. The bad one: you pay for the number of units. There are fewer people than records, so to keep the same expected batch you must sample at a higher rate, and amplification is weaker. On the running example, with 1,000 steps and an expected batch of 100 units, a record-level \(\varepsilon = 4\) needs \(\sigma = 0.778\) at \(q = 0.01\), while a user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\) needs \(\sigma = 3.78\) at \(q = 0.1\). The noise on the averaged update is about five times larger, 0.0189 against 0.00389. That is the honest price of protecting people: there are ten times fewer of them than records, and DP’s cost per unit is fixed. The good one: records inside a user are free. The guarantee does not depend on how many records a user has, so they can be averaged, used for several local steps or subsampled without changing \(\varepsilon\). More records make each user’s vector a better estimate of their gradient, so the signal improves while the noise stays put.
A common variant keeps per-record clipping: keep at most \(k\) records per user, clip each to \(C\), and sum them, with users still sampled whole. One user then moves the sum by up to \(kC\), and the guarantee is that of noise multiplier \(\sigma/k\), a factor \(k\) in noise that averaging before clipping avoids. Summing all of a user’s records and then clipping the sum is also valid, with sensitivity \(C\).
The proof assumes two things that implementations can break. Each user’s vector must be computed from that user’s data alone, which rules out normalizing across users and requires that one person is not spread over several “users”; if one person has several accounts, the unit is the account and the person is again a group. And users must be Poisson-sampled; iterating over users in a fixed shuffled order is a different mechanism, exactly as for records.

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.5 Contribution bounding
User-level DP-SGD needs a pipeline that groups records by user and computes one vector per user. Many pipelines are built around records instead: shuffled files of examples, per-example gradient code, fixed-length batches. You can keep such a pipeline and still protect users with contribution bounding: keep at most \(k\) records of each user, chosen without looking at other users’ data (for example at random), discard the rest, and run example-level DP-SGD on what remains. Adding a user then adds at most \(k\) records, all theirs, so the user accountant of Section 42.3 with \(k\) records gives the user-level guarantee. The selection must look only at the user’s own records; a rule that kept, say, the records most similar to the rest of the dataset could change which records other users keep when one user is added.
The cap is a bias–variance trade-off (Amin, Kulesza, Muñoz Medina & Vassilvitskii 2019). A larger cap keeps more data but, since the user looks like a record sampled at rate \(kq\), it needs noise growing roughly in proportion to \(k\) at a fixed sampling rate. A smaller cap needs less noise but throws away data, all of it from heavy users, so what remains is both smaller and reweighted toward light users. Table 42.2 shows the trade-off at a user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\) on the running example, with 1,000 steps and an expected batch of 100 records.

And the two techniques combine: cap records to bound compute, then compute one clipped vector per user, so the cap costs data but no longer noise.

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.6 Heavy users and the objective
User sizes are rarely equal. In the running example’s population the mean user has 10 records, the median 4, and the largest 348; the 30 users with at least 50 records hold 30.6% of all records (Figure 42.2).






Figure 42.2: Left: the number of records per user in the running example’s population of 1,000 users, on log–log axes; 193 users have one record and the largest has 348. Right: the share of all records held by the largest users. The largest 10 users hold 17.9% of the records and the smallest half of the users 10.3%.



Example-level training gives each user a weight proportional to their records, so those 30 users carry 30.6% of the expected update. User-level DP-SGD with averaged, clipped vectors gives each user at most \(1/U\), because each clipped vector is at most \(C\) long and the sum is divided by the number of users; the same 30 users carry at most 3.0%. So user-level training changes the objective, not only the noise: it minimizes roughly the average over users of each user’s average loss, not the average over records. Whether that is what you want depends on the application. For a keyboard model, weighting people equally keeps a few very active users from defining everyone’s suggestions. For a model meant to fit the overall distribution of records, it under-weights heavy users’ content, which matters when heavy users differ from light ones in language, topic or device. Summing a user’s gradients before clipping sits in between: it weights records until a user’s sum reaches \(C\), and users beyond that.
On the running example the reweighting costs nothing measurable. At user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\), user-level DP-SGD reaches 0.9361 on test points whose nearest training record belongs to a heavy user and 0.9319 on the others, against 0.9607 and 0.9622 for the non-private model. That is because one teacher network labels every record, so light users’ records teach the same function. On data where heavy users follow their own patterns, the same reweighting would cost accuracy on those patterns, and clipping adds to it: a heavy user whose data are unusual has a long average gradient, which is clipped to the same \(C\) as everyone else’s, the user-level version of what clipping does to small groups in Disparate impact.

Keeping the record as the unit fails: strategy (a) stays near chance at every budget up to \(\varepsilon = 8\). The heaviest user has on average \(348 \times 0.01 = 3.48\) records in every batch, so subsampling hardly hides them, and the noise must cover a shift of several clipping norms in nearly every step, which takes \(\sigma\) in the hundreds and drowns every gradient. Removing that user would not help much either, since the next-largest has 258 records.
Changing the unit wins. User-level DP-SGD is the best strategy at every budget, 0.9347 at \(\varepsilon = 4\) against 0.9612 non-private, with its largest advantage at small budgets: 9.8 points ahead of the cap at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 1.1 points at \(\varepsilon = 8\). It needs a little less noise than the cap and, unlike the cap, uses every record through the per-user average. Its cost is compute: each step processes all the records of about 100 users, about 1,000 records, ten times what the record-based strategies process. Bounding is the fallback when the pipeline must stay record-based; it comes close at \(\varepsilon = 8\), where the discarded data, not the noise, limits accuracy. Single runs vary by about a point at these budgets, so read the large gaps, not the small ones (Figure 42.3).






Figure 42.3: Test accuracy of the running example against the user-level \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), for the three strategies (1,000 steps, expected batch 100, one run each; the runs differ from Table 42.3 in their random seeds). User-level DP-SGD is best at every budget; example-level DP-SGD on all records, accounted for its heaviest user, stays near chance.



Published comparisons on language models, with different data, models and accountants, point the same way. Chua et al. (2024) find that user-level DP-SGD with per-user averaging generally beats contribution bounding, especially at small budgets, though they account for the cap with generic group privacy, which costs them more noise than the direct accountant would. Charles et al. (2024) report that sampling users usually does better when each user’s data are varied and when strong privacy is required, and that sampling examples sometimes wins.
At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the user-level model is 2.7 points below the non-private one (0.9347 against 0.9612). The record-level model of DP-SGD at the same \(\varepsilon\), trained for 10,000 steps, reached 0.9548; the difference is the price of the unit, and the user-level model protects 1,000 people instead of 10,000 records, including the person with 348 records as well as the one with a single record.

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.10 Further reading

McMahan, Ramage, Talwar & Zhang, “Learning Differentially Private Recurrent Language Models” (ICLR 2018): user-level DP-SGD in federated learning, the algorithm of Section 42.4.
Charles, Ganesh, McKenna, McMahan, Mitchell, Pillutla & Rush, “Fine-Tuning Large Language Models with User-Level Differential Privacy” (arXiv 2407.07737, 2024): the tight accountant for a user under example-level sampling, and an empirical comparison of sampling examples against sampling users.
Chua, Ghazi, Huang, Kamath, Kumar, Liu, Manurangsi, Sinha & Zhang, “Mind the Privacy Unit! User-Level Differential Privacy for Language Model Fine-Tuning” (Conference on Language Modeling 2024): contribution bounding against user-wise DP-SGD, with rules for which records to keep.
Amin, Kulesza, Muñoz Medina & Vassilvitskii, “Bounding User Contributions: A Bias-Variance Trade-off in Differential Privacy” (ICML 2019): how to think about the cap, and how the best one depends on the distribution of user sizes.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.1 Why this matters
Training the part’s running example with differential privacy (DP) at \(\varepsilon = 4\) costs less than one point of test accuracy: 0.9548 against 0.9610 without privacy (private gradient descent). That number is an average over the test set, and it says nothing about who loses the point. Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov (2019) asked, and found that when a network is trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, the lost accuracy is concentrated on the classes and subgroups that are under-represented in the training data, and existing gaps between groups grow. They called this the disparate impact of DP on model accuracy. A model that is “less than a point worse” can be ten points worse for a group of people, and the groups that pay are often the ones privacy is meant to protect: small populations, rare conditions, unusual records.
The one idea: every record gets the same budget of influence, and every group gets the same noise. DP-SGD caps each record’s pull on the update at the clipping norm \(C\), then adds noise whose size depends only on \(C\) and the noise multiplier \(\sigma\), not on the data. Both rules are blind to groups, and that is exactly why they are not neutral. Clipping cuts back hardest the groups whose gradients are long, which are the groups the model fits badly. And the noise is the same for everyone while a group’s signal is proportional to its size, so a small group’s signal-to-noise ratio is smaller by its share of the data. Small groups that the model finds hard suffer from both, and the two compound.

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.2 Disparate impact, measured
An accuracy gap between groups in a private model is not enough to blame DP, because the non-private model may have the gap already. What privacy adds is measured by each group’s privacy cost: the accuracy the group loses when the same training recipe is made private, \[\pi_g = \mathrm{acc}_g(\text{non-private}) - \mathbb E\big[\mathrm{acc}_g(\text{private})\big], \tag{43.1}\] averaged over the randomness of private training (Esipova et al. 2023). DP has disparate impact when groups’ privacy costs differ.
The running example shows it. Of its 10,000 training records, 9,500 are the usual ones and 500, a 5% minority, come from a different region of input space, have larger inputs, and follow their own labelling rule, which the majority does not teach. The non-private model learns both: 0.9529 on the majority and 0.9411 on the minority, a gap of 1.2 points, so any large gap in a private model is caused by privacy. Each group is tested on 20,000 fresh records, so test error is small next to the effects, and each row of Table 43.1 averages three training runs.

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.3 Clipping reweights the groups
How does a rule that treats every record the same end up treating groups differently? Recall what DP-SGD’s expected update is: each record’s gradient, multiplied by its clipping weight \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\), averaged over all records. Group those records. Each group then pulls with its share of the records, \(s_g\), times its average clipped gradient, and since every clipped gradient is at most \(C\) long, a group’s pull is never longer than \(s_g C\), however badly the model fits it. A group of large-gradient records is cut back much more than a group whose gradients are already short.
When a group’s gradients point roughly the same way, the effect is a reweighting. Clipping keeps a fraction \(c_g\) of the group’s average gradient (its average clipping weight, when the group’s norms are equal), and the update becomes the gradient of a mixture in which group \(g\) has effective share \[\tilde s_g = \frac{s_g\,c_g}{\sum_h s_h\,c_h} \tag{43.2}\] instead of its true share \(s_g\). This splits clipping’s damage in two. The denominator shortens the whole update, which a larger step size undoes. The effective shares change which mixture of groups is being descended, and no step size undoes that. Esipova et al. (2023) find this direction error far more harmful than the length error, especially to the under-represented class.
A two-dimensional example makes it concrete. Take 95 majority records with gradient \((0.2, 0)\), already short, and 5 minority records with gradient \((0, 4)\), long because the model fits them badly. Without clipping the average is \((0.19, 0.2)\): the five minority records pull as hard as the ninety-five others. Clip at \(C = 0.5\). The majority’s gradients are untouched, the minority’s shrink eightfold, and the average becomes \((0.19, 0.025)\). The minority’s part of the update falls from 0.513 to 0.116, the update turns by 39.0 degrees toward the majority, and the minority’s effective share falls from 0.05 to 0.0065. Scaling every gradient by the same factor, \(1/8\), instead would shorten the update eightfold but keep its direction (Figure 43.2).






Figure 43.2: The clipping example in two dimensions: 95 majority records with gradient (0.2, 0) and 5 minority records with gradient (0, 4). Without clipping the two groups pull about equally hard (black); clipping at C = 0.5 cuts the minority’s pull eightfold and turns the update toward the majority (red). Scaling every gradient by the same factor 1/8 instead keeps the direction (blue).



Gradients are long for two reasons, and a small group the model has not learned has both. The model fits the group badly, so the loss’s derivative is large; and the group’s inputs are large, since a dense layer’s per-example gradient grows with the length of its input. Tran, Dinh & Fioretto (2021) identify both factors as the source of clipping’s part of disparate impact. That sets up a feedback loop during training. At the start every record is clipped and every group has a similar weight. As the majority is learned, its gradients shrink below \(C\) and its weight rises toward 1, while the minority, not yet learned, keeps long gradients and a low weight. Its effective share falls below its true share, so it is learned more slowly, so its gradients stay long. In the running example with clipping and no noise, the minority’s effective share starts at its true 0.0495, falls to 0.0251 at step 2,500, half its share exactly when it most needs to be learned, and recovers only to 0.0387 by the end. With the noise of \(\varepsilon = 4\) it is 0.0261 at step 2,500 and 0.0358 at the end: the noise keeps the minority’s gradients long, so clipping keeps cutting them back.

title: 43  Disparate impact
section: 43.4 The noise floor of a small group
text:
43.4 The noise floor of a small group
The noise is added to the sum, the same for everyone, so why should it hurt a small group more? Because what the noise competes with is each group’s signal, and a group’s signal in the sum is proportional to its size.
Two arguments make this quantitative. The first is about learning at all. A signal that keeps pointing the same way grows linearly with the number of steps, while independent noise grows only like its square root, so a signal beats the noise after about \((\ell_{\text{noise}}/\ell_{\text{sig}})^2\) steps, the squared ratio of the noise’s length to the signal’s per step. If the part of the update that serves a group is a fraction \(s_g\) of the population’s signal, that count is multiplied by \(1/s_g^2\). In the running example at \(\varepsilon = 4\), the averaged clipped gradient has length about 0.026 and the noise 0.392, so a signal shared by the whole population emerges after 228 steps. A signal that is 20% of it needs 5,693 steps; one that is 5% needs 91,085, nine times the entire run. A group whose rule the rest of the data does not teach is in this position. Running longer does not help, because at a fixed budget more steps mean more noise per step, and the break-even count grows about as fast as the run.
The second argument is about where training settles. In a simple model where each group’s loss is a quadratic bowl in its own weights, the training pull on a group’s weights is proportional to its share, while the noise is not. Noisy gradient descent then settles at an excess loss for the group of roughly \[\mathbb E[L_g] \approx \frac{k\,\eta\,\tau^2}{4\,s_g}, \tag{43.3}\] where \(k\) is the number of the group’s weights, \(\eta\) the step size and \(\tau = \sigma C/B\) the noise per coordinate on the averaged update, with \(B\) the expected batch size. The floor scales like one over the share: a group with a twentieth of the data sits at about twenty times the excess loss. The bowl’s curvature cancels, because a sharper loss pulls back harder but also charges more for each displacement. In a simulation with the noise of \(\varepsilon = 4\), the formula and the simulation agree within 1%, and the floor grows from \(4.07 \times 10^{-4}\) for a group with 95% of the data to \(2.96 \times 10^{-2}\) for a group with 1%, a factor of 73. With clipping, the share is replaced by the clipped share \(s_g c_g\), so the two mechanisms compound: a 5% group whose gradients clipping halves pays the floor of a 2.5% group. A network is not a set of bowls, and where a minority’s task overlaps the majority’s, the majority’s gradient does part of its work and the penalty is smaller; the model’s value is that it makes the role of the share explicit.
The network bears this out. Table 43.2 varies the minority’s share with everything else fixed.

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.5 Measuring per-group accuracy
Every number so far used 20,000 test records per group. Real evaluations are not so generous: a 2,000-record test split with a 5% minority holds 100 minority records. Each test record is classified right or wrong, so a group’s measured accuracy is a binomial proportion, and the Clopper–Pearson interval inverts the binomial exactly, covering the true accuracy with probability at least 95% (Hypothesis testing). Its width falls only like one over the square root of the number of records. For the gap between two groups measured on disjoint test records, the two errors are independent and their variances add, so an approximate 95% interval is \[(\hat p_a - \hat p_b) \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_a(1 - \hat p_a)}{m_a} + \frac{\hat p_b(1 - \hat p_b)}{m_b}}, \tag{43.4}\] with \(\hat p_g\) the measured accuracies and \(m_g\) the numbers of test records.
Take one model trained at \(\varepsilon = 4\), whose accuracy on all 20,000 minority test records is 0.8641. On 100 of them it gets 88 right, an estimate of 0.880 with interval \([0.800, 0.936]\), 13.6 points wide. The non-private model’s 0.9411 lies just above that interval, so on this test set alone the minority’s privacy cost could be anywhere from about half a point to fourteen. On 1,900 majority records the model gets 0.954, and the gap of 0.074 has the interval 0.010 to 0.138: real, but anywhere from one point to fourteen (Figure 43.4).






Figure 43.4: Width of the 95% Clopper–Pearson interval for a group’s accuracy against the number of test records in the group, for observed accuracies 0.95 and 0.7, on log scales. The width falls like one over the square root of the number of records.



Training is a second, separate source of variation, and a larger test set does nothing about it: it pins down the model you have, but another run gives another model. In Table 43.1 the run-to-run standard deviation at \(\varepsilon = 4\) is 0.0211 for the minority against 0.0037 for the majority, almost six times as large, so a comparison of two recipes on one run each can easily be reversed for the small group. Report each group’s interval and the spread over several runs. And per-group accuracies computed on private test data are statistics of that data: if you publish them, they need their own privacy analysis (Choosing ε).

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.6 Mitigations and what they cost
Both mechanisms come from DP-SGD’s two knobs, clipping and noise. The tempting fixes move the cost around rather than remove it, and it pays to know where to.
Changing the clipping norm trades one mechanism for the other. A smaller \(C\) clips more, so the minority’s effective share falls. A larger \(C\) clips less, so the update points in the right direction, but the noise \(\sigma C\) grows with \(C\) while short gradients do not, so it is larger relative to their signal. In the limit, scaling every gradient by the same factor \(C/Z\), with no gradient longer than \(Z\), is exactly DP-SGD with clipping norm \(Z\) and a smaller step: the right direction, the most noise. Table 43.3 shows both failures on the running example, keeping \(\eta C\) fixed.

Neither clipping norm helps the minority: the smaller one costs it 1.64 points through clipping, the larger one 3.44 points through noise. These differences are of the size of the run-to-run spread, so only their direction is clear. Esipova et al. (2023) propose a variant of global scaling that clips the rare gradients above \(Z\) and adapts \(Z\) from a privately estimated count, and report that it reduces the privacy cost gap on their datasets; it needs no group labels. Group-aware methods, such as giving more-clipped groups a larger clipping bound (Xu, Du & Wu 2021), need each training record’s group, which is itself sensitive, and their per-group statistics must be computed privately. Choosing \(C\) from the largest gradient observed in the data is not allowed at all: the clipping norm must be fixed in advance or chosen privately.
Upweighting a group’s loss does not work either, because clipping undoes it: the gradients grow and are then rescaled back to \(C\). Oversampling the group does raise its pull, but each record’s privacy depends on its own sampling rate, so the minority’s records sampled four times as often need \(\sigma = 4.71\) instead of 1.36 to stay at \(\varepsilon = 4\). The minority’s pull grows by 4 and the noise by 3.46, so its signal-to-noise ratio improves by only 1.16, while the majority’s falls by 3.46 and its records end up at \(\varepsilon = 0.86\), budget wasted. The gap narrows from 9.93 to 3.99 points, but by levelling down: the minority’s accuracy is 2.07 points lower than without oversampling and the majority’s 8.01 lower. A smaller gap is not by itself a fairer model, so report both groups’ accuracy and privacy cost, never the gap alone. And oversampling without raising \(\sigma\) would silently give the minority \(\varepsilon = 20.96\): the group already disadvantaged in accuracy would get the weakest privacy too.
Some of the cost is unavoidable. Learning a group’s own rule privately is partly a private estimation problem on that group’s records, and Lower bounds shows that private estimation has a price no algorithm avoids: the error that \(n_g\) records allow shrinks only like \(1/(n_g\varepsilon)\). Feldman (2020) argues more broadly that fitting a long tail of small subpopulations well requires memorizing their few examples, which is what DP forbids. What helps is more data from the group, a larger \(\varepsilon\) with its own costs, or a starting point that already serves the group, such as a public pretrained model (Public data and private fine-tuning).

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.7 Code
This snippet reproduces the two-dimensional clipping example and the interval for the accuracy gap measured on 1,900 majority and 100 minority test records:
from math import acos, degrees, hypot, sqrt


def clipped_mean(groups: list[tuple[float, tuple[float, float]]], c: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Expected DP-SGD update: each group's share times its gradient, clipped to norm c."""
    x = y = 0.0
    for share, (gx, gy) in groups:
        scale = min(1.0, c / hypot(gx, gy))
        x, y = x + share * scale * gx, y + share * scale * gy
    return x, y


def angle(u: tuple[float, float], v: tuple[float, float]) -> float:
    """Angle between two vectors, in degrees."""
    return degrees(acos((u[0] * v[0] + u[1] * v[1]) / (hypot(*u) * hypot(*v))))


def effective_share(share: float, weight: float, other_weight: float) -> float:
    """A group's share of the update after clipping, against one other group."""
    return share * weight / (share * weight + (1 - share) * other_weight)


def gap_interval(pa: float, ma: int, pb: float, mb: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Approximate 95% interval for the accuracy gap pa - pb, measured on disjoint test sets."""
    se = sqrt(pa * (1 - pa) / ma + pb * (1 - pb) / mb)
    return pa - pb - 1.96 * se, pa - pb + 1.96 * se


groups = [(0.95, (0.2, 0.0)), (0.05, (0.0, 4.0))]
true, clipped = clipped_mean(groups, float("inf")), clipped_mean(groups, 0.5)
print(f"{true[1] / (true[0] + true[1]):.3f} {clipped[1] / (clipped[0] + clipped[1]):.3f}")  # 0.513 0.116
print(f"{angle(true, clipped):.1f}")  # 39.0
print(f"{effective_share(0.05, 0.125, 1.0):.4f}")  # 0.0065
print("%.3f %.3f" % gap_interval(0.954, 1_900, 0.880, 100))  # 0.010 0.138
The full edition’s script trains the running example with a minority group, logs per-group gradient statistics, and checks every number in this chapter:

title: 43  Disparate impact
text:
43.9 Further reading

Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov, “Differential Privacy Has Disparate Impact on Model Accuracy” (NeurIPS 2019): the observation this chapter explains.
Esipova, Ghomi, Luo & Cresswell, “Disparate Impact in Differential Privacy from Gradient Misalignment” (ICLR 2023): separates clipping’s direction error from its length error, and proposes global scaling with an adaptive threshold.
Tran, Dinh & Fioretto, “Differentially Private Empirical Risk Minimization under the Fairness Lens” (NeurIPS 2021): a group’s excess risk split into clipping and noise terms, and the role of gradient and input norms.
Feldman, “Does Learning Require Memorization? A Short Tale about a Long Tail” (STOC 2020): why fitting small subpopulations well conflicts with privacy.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 44  Choosing ε
text:
44.1 Why this matters
Every model trained with differential privacy (DP) ships with a budget \(\varepsilon\), and someone has to pick it. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, makes the accuracy side of that choice easy to measure. On this part’s running example, a small neural network trained on 10,000 records at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), test accuracy is 0.9175 at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 0.9441 at \(\varepsilon = 2\), 0.9548 at \(\varepsilon = 4\) and 0.9604 at \(\varepsilon = 8\), against 0.9610 without privacy (DP-SGD). That is half of the decision. The other half is what each budget allows an attacker to learn about one person in the data. Without it, \(\varepsilon\) gets chosen by habit (“everyone uses 8”) or by the accuracy curve alone, and neither answer holds up when a reviewer asks what the number promises.
The idea that organizes the chapter is that \(\varepsilon\) is one line under a curve. An attacker deciding whether a record was used runs a test, and the test has a false positive rate and a true positive rate. A pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) draws one straight line that caps those rates. A training algorithm actually has a whole curve, the best true positive rate at every false positive rate, and that curve can lie far below the line. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) the line allows a test that catches nearly every member while almost never accusing a non-member. The curve of DP-SGD at the same \(\varepsilon\) caps the true positive rate at 0.0589 when the false positive rate is \(10^{-3}\). Choosing \(\varepsilon\) well means computing the curve, reading it at the error rates your threat cares about, and reporting it.

title: 44  Choosing ε
text:
44.2 What one (ε, δ) pair promises
Start with what “trained with \((8, 10^{-5})\)” forbids on its own, which is all you can say about a model whose training algorithm you have not seen. A membership attacker sees the model and says “member” on some set of outputs. Its true positive rate (TPR) is how often it says “member” when the target was in the training set, and its false positive rate (FPR) is how often it says so when the target was not. Both are probabilities of the same event in the two worlds, and DP bounds exactly that (The definition of differential privacy). Applied to the “member” event it gives the first line below; applied the other way round to the “non-member” event, it gives the second: \[\mathrm{TPR} \le \min\big\{1,\ e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta,\ 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\big\}. \tag{44.1}\]
Attacks are judged by their TPR at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) or below (Membership inference), because an attack that flags members while almost never flagging non-members is one that identifies people with confidence. There the first line binds. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) it caps the TPR at \(e \times 10^{-3} + 10^{-5} = 0.002728\), a real constraint. At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the cap is 0.05461. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) the line reaches 1 from an FPR of \(3.35\times10^{-4}\) on, so the pair says nothing at all at the false positive rates where attacks are usually evaluated.
The advantage, TPR minus FPR, is often quoted instead. The pair bounds it by \((e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\): 0.4621 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 0.9640 at \(\varepsilon = 4\), numbers that make \(\varepsilon = 4\) sound hopeless. But the bound is tight only for the worst mechanism with this \(\varepsilon\), randomized response, whose curve is exactly the two lines, and DP-SGD is not that mechanism. Read through the pair alone, \(\varepsilon \le 2\) is strong everywhere, \(\varepsilon = 4\) is meaningful only at very low FPR, and \(\varepsilon \ge 8\) is no guarantee against membership inference. For DP-SGD, the second and third of these conclusions are far too pessimistic.

title: 44  Choosing ε
text:
44.3 The whole curve of DP-SGD
The accountant that reported \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) could just as well have reported it at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) or \(10^{-3}\). The mechanism has a whole privacy profile \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), and every point of it is another line that every test must satisfy. The best TPR an attacker can reach at each FPR is the lower envelope of all those lines, the trade-off curve. Each line touches the curve at one point, and the line the accountant reports at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) touches it only at a false positive rate below \(10^{-4}\) for every run here. Everywhere else the reported line is a loose summary.
For DP-SGD the curve can be computed. The best test thresholds the privacy loss, the log of how much more likely the run’s output is with the record than without (the Neyman–Pearson lemma). Each step adds fresh noise, so the losses of the steps add up. The distribution of the total, the privacy loss distribution (PLD), is what a numerical accountant already computes, rounded up and down on a grid so that it brackets the truth (Numerical accounting). Two cheaper answers sit around it. The Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve that set the noise gives a valid but looser bound for free. The Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) approximation replaces the run by two unit normals at distance \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\), for sampling rate \(q\), noise multiplier \(\sigma\) and \(T\) steps (f-DP and Gaussian DP); it is an approximation, not a bound.

The advantage tells the same story, since the pair allows 0.9640 at \(\varepsilon = 4\) and DP-SGD at most 0.3429. The grey diagonal is an attacker with no information.



The curve is the best test of a strong attacker: one who knows every other record and every hyperparameter, sees every intermediate model, and targets a record whose clipped gradient is as large as clipping allows at every step. Nasr et al. (2021) showed that such an attacker, choosing the target’s gradient, does reach the accountant’s guarantee. A typical record attacked through the final model is much safer. On the running example, a loss-threshold attack has its TPR within 0.004 of its FPR at every budget, nearly at chance even against the non-private model. That describes this attack on this task, not a guarantee. Auditing private training builds the attacks that come close to the curve.

title: 44  Choosing ε
text:
44.4 What an attacker can believe
People who are not statisticians ask a different question: if someone sees the model, how sure can they be that I was in the data? Bayes’ rule answers it. The attacker’s odds that you are a member, after seeing an output, are its odds before times \(e^L\), where \(L\) is that output’s privacy loss. If no output has loss above \(\varepsilon\), a prior belief \(p\) can rise to at most \[\frac{p\,e^\varepsilon}{p\,e^\varepsilon + 1 - p}. \tag{44.2}\] DP bounds the change of belief, not the belief. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) an attacker who starts at 1% can reach at most 2.67%. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) it can reach 96.79%, so read through this bound, \(\varepsilon = 8\) permits near certainty.
That bound treats every output as the worst one. For DP-SGD the loss is a random variable, and the PLD says how it is spread (Figure 44.2). For a worst-case member of the \(\varepsilon = 8\) run, the median total loss is 1.136, which moves a 1% prior to 0.0305, and the loss exceeds 5.971, which moves it to 0.7984, only with probability \(10^{-3}\). At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the same two points give 0.0149 and 0.1771. The probability that the loss exceeds the reported \(\varepsilon\) at all is of the order of \(\delta\), between \(3.78\times10^{-6}\) and \(1.10\times10^{-4}\) across the runs.






Figure 44.2: Left: the largest posterior probability of membership against the prior, from Equation 44.2, for the six budgets (log axes). Right: for the \(\varepsilon = 8\) run, the bound (dotted) and the posterior of a member whose total privacy loss is the median of the PLD, or is exceeded with probability \(10^{-3}\) or \(10^{-5}\).



Base rates matter just as much. An attacker who acts on a flag is right with probability \(p\,\mathrm{TPR}/(p\,\mathrm{TPR} + (1 - p)\,\mathrm{FPR})\), and at a small prior even a large ratio TPR/FPR leaves most flags wrong. At \(\varepsilon = 8\), prior 1% and FPR \(10^{-2}\), the pair allows a precision of 0.5024, while the exact curve allows 0.1744: five flags out of six are false. So say who the attacker is. Against the \(\varepsilon = 2\) run, an insider who knows you are one of two candidates (prior 0.5) can reach 0.8808 on the worst output, while a stranger with prior 0.01 reaches at most 0.0695. The guarantee is the same; what it protects against depends on what the attacker knew before.

title: 44  Choosing ε
text:
44.5 Reconstruction
Many harms need more than membership: recovering a diagnosis or a face the attacker does not have (Reconstruction attacks). Give the attacker every other training record and a prior over the target, and let \(\kappa\) be its best success without the model, \(1/m\) for one of \(m\) equally likely candidates. Any reconstruction attack is also a membership test for its own guess, and averaged over the prior that test’s false positive rate is at most \(\kappa\), because a model trained without the target cannot help guess it. Because the curve is concave, averaging over the candidates cannot help, so reconstruction succeeds with probability at most the trade-off curve read at FPR \(\kappa\), or \(e^\varepsilon\kappa + \delta\) from the pair alone. Balle, Cherubin & Hayes (2022) introduced this informed adversary and its bounds from pure DP and RDP; Hayes, Mahloujifar & Balle (2023) gave the bound from DP-SGD’s whole curve.
A large prior uncertainty is a small FPR, exactly where DP-SGD’s curve lies far below the line. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) the pair gives no bound for any \(m\) up to 1,000, but the curve caps the success of choosing among 1,000 equally likely candidates at 0.0589, against 0.001 by guessing. Even \(\varepsilon = 16\) keeps it at most 0.2808. The catch is the prior. If the attacker can narrow the target to two values, as with one unknown binary field in an otherwise known record, \(\kappa = 0.5\) and reconstruction is as easy as membership at FPR 0.5. A defensible reconstruction claim names its prior: “an attacker who knows the target is one of \(m\) records”.

title: 44  Choosing ε
text:
44.6 How small δ must be
A deliberately bad mechanism shows what \(\delta\) permits: publish each record in full, independently with probability \(\delta\). It is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, yet it exposes at least one of \(n\) records with probability \(1 - (1 - \delta)^n\), which is 0.6321 at \(\delta = 1/n\) for \(n = 10{,}000\). So a meaningful guarantee needs \(n\delta \ll 1\), where \(n\) counts the privacy units, usually people (User-level differential privacy). NIST’s guidelines (SP 800-226) write that a common recommendation is \(\delta \le 1/n^2\), that \(1/(n\log n)\) is another sensible choice, and that values above \(10^{-5}\) are suspicious and should be justified. The running example’s \(10^{-5}\) with 10,000 records has \(n\delta = 0.1\).
DP-SGD spends its \(\delta\) very differently from that mechanism: on outputs whose loss is just above \(\varepsilon\), not on outputs that identify someone with certainty, because its loss has a light, nearly Gaussian tail. That is why shrinking \(\delta\) is cheap (Table 44.2). For the \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 4\) runs, every factor of 100 in \(\delta\) costs between about 0.2 and 0.9 in \(\varepsilon\). Meeting the \(1/n^2 = 10^{-8}\) rule makes the \(\varepsilon = 4\) run \((5.209, 10^{-8})\)-DP. When in doubt, use a smaller \(\delta\).

title: 44  Choosing ε
text:
44.7 Deployed values and their units
“Industry uses \(\varepsilon\) between 1 and 10” is a common justification. It hides two things every \(\varepsilon\) needs: the privacy unit, meaning what one neighbouring change is (one record, one user-day, one user forever), and the period over which the budget is spent. Table 44.3 lists documented deployments, and the units differ from row to row.
